compiled by the śramaṇa Jie Xian, a successor of the Fourth Patriarch at Mount Shuangfeng in Huangmei and a native of Eastern Wu.

to deviate from a single word of the scriptures is equivalent to the teaching of Māra. This is the unchanging Way. Yet those who merely eat with their ears remain stuck to stale explanations, claiming:

Since it is called "pointing upward," all streams are cut off; yet they rely on the words of others. Furthermore, it is said: "Since it is termed the 'Gate of the School' (Zongmen), whatever is brought forth is it;
how could there be any fixed rules? Thus, they cite the Sixth Patriarch’s illiteracy as a shortcut for evading the root of the matter.

Consequently, the heterodox and the orthodox are not distinguished, the crimson and the purple are mixed together, a multitude of voices create confusion, and common pots compete in their clamor, such that their speech does not touch upon the classics.
Chapter. Matters have fallen outside the bounds of propriety; street talk and vulgar colloquialisms have been accepted and adopted, thereby confusing the Way.

While the "Sun of Shu" and the "Snow of Yue" indulge in mutual derision and reproach, the affairs of the Zen school have undergone a profound transformation. Master Da’weng Yue and I were fellow countrymen and worked together for many years.
Subsequently, his Dharma heir Nanjian Xuancong succeeded him on the seat, where he served for four years. Alas, I deeply lament the state of the Dharma.

The gates of the great rivers are daily collapsing; there is no more Pillar of砥 (Dizhu) to stem them. The very life-force of the Buddhas and Patriarchs depends entirely upon the preaching of the Dharma.
Therefore, I have compiled the dharma-words of the successive patriarchs, categorizing and classifying them to form this collection.

From formal sermons, small-scale expositions, instructions to the assembly, and general discourses, down to spontaneous remarks given according to specific circumstances, each has its own formal structure. As for those instances appearing in their practical conduct, they number in the thousands.

I have brought together myriad strands and standardized them according to the *Baizhang Qinggui* of the Great Wisdom Patriarch. With the main framework raised and the details displayed, each section follows its own sequence.
This work is titled the *Liejuz Tigitang Lu* (Record of the Essential Rules of the Successive Patriarchs). When viewed by comparison, it is like the battle array of Xiaofu at Feiyu:

the discipline is precise and rigorous; or like Li Guangbi entering the army of Li Yili: the fortifications and formations are completely transformed. Thus, even those of later generations and junior standing may [attain clarity].

Furthermore, having seen this *Great Compendium of the Dharma* by the ancient masters, its merit is no small matter. Some may say: "Chan values what flows from the breast and what is uttered in accordance with one's nature.
Now, to compile and categorize meanings into fixed patterns is to provide a ladder for thieves to climb over;
it allows them to simply strike from the printing blocks and cast from the molds. Does this not further assist the bandits? I reply: Not so. This is the way of those who have mastered the school.

These are fabricated and incoherent ravings, arising solely from a failure to comprehend the essential principles. If one were willing to investigate this with diligence, one would naturally find that "those who know the Dharma are afraid.

It is like entering the Hall of Brightness or the Ancestral Temple, where one beholds the rites and music of the Three Dynasties; those who previously acted with negligence and contempt, treating the teachings as mere trifles, will feel ashamed of their childish play.

As for the superior practitioners, their golden chapters and jade-like phrases have stripped away the very marrow of their bones; even the secondary practitioners walk according to the compass and square, so that their speech does not [deviate].
Amidst the false proclamations and the clamor of foxes and wild dogs, this great salvation has been obtained.

To suspend it at the gates of the kingdom and to spread it across the assembly halls—will this not make it, together with the *Tongyao*, *Lianzhu*, and the various *Wudeng* collections, the very sun and moon of the Chan school?
Preface to the *Record of the Essential Teachings of the Successive Patriarchs*, compiled on the third day of the middle autumn month in the fifth year of the Kangxi era by the śramaṇa Dayi,
a successor of the ancestral lineage from ancient Min, residing at Qixia Monastery in Jinling.
From the Great Sage [the Buddha] down to Daizhi, the canonical models of our school were fully established; this is truly what is meant by the "rites and music of the Three Dynasties.

However, following the Southern Song, they gradually declined and grew feeble. During the more than two hundred years of the Ming dynasty, the lineage was in perilous straits, like the "Guangling San" melody, until the reign of Emperor Shizong.
Subsequently, several masters, one after another, raised high the banners and drums in Jiangdong, and their lineages were thus transmitted.
Members of the Imperial Secretariat: There is not one whose family has not produced a sword from Fengcheng, nor one who does not harbor the light that shoots toward the Dipper.

Yet, in the aftermath of decline, our institutions have been established in haste; the legal codes remain incomplete. Recently, a few mature elders who have taken an interest in the ancient statutes have already come to understand and clarify them through their own insight.

Nevertheless, the essential framework has not yet been raised up, and the underlying order remains as discordant as the stars Shen and Shang. I— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. This translation reflects the full extent of the available text.)

Twenty years ago, while I was studying under venerable masters of the Ji lineage together with the monk Daoweng, we would frequently debate this matter, each of us feeling such indignation that we could not contain our frustration.
Subsequently, the two of us became teachers in the north and south respectively;

the Master [Daoweng] settled in the distant regions of Wu and Chu, where he long presided over famous monasteries and became a refuge for the monastics of the southeast. One day, however, he suddenly shook out his robes and departed, maintaining his unique integrity.
Zhi traveled across the famous mountains and rivers of the world, searching extensively and gathering widely for twenty years, until the general outline of his ancestral teachings was completed.
Upon returning from Yue, he first arrived at Jinling and passed through my Sheshan, where we discussed the past while lighting lamps.

He then presented this book and requested me to write its preface. In the midst of this joyful occasion, I burned incense and read it once more; it was as if ascending the hall of Baizhang and hearing [the Dharma] in person.
The bells were struck and the drums beaten; fifteen hundred men, dignified and majestic, ran forward and prostrated themselves.
As for the transcendence of the Dharma words and the clarity of the spiritual eyes, more than four hundred people appeared as one, and the forty-odd fascicles [of the scripture] were [mastered].
Not a single word is superfluous; the compiler’s mental power truly forges both the ancient and the modern.
Some say: "Chan values sublime awakening; written words are but its fringe. What is the use of rules?

Suppose one were to command the World-Honored One to descend from heaven and sit or lie within the ashes of paper money, casting aside the offerings of flower rains and Brahma-music to instead enter the bamboo tubes of the kitchen.
If one seeks sustenance within [the palace], then for forty-nine years, what shall the hundreds of thousands of devas and humans look to for reliance? What shall they have for their awakening?

Furthermore, consider how the Duke of Pei’s [Li Bang’s] exploits on horseback ultimately led to the establishment of the system; or how Yue Fei’s wild battles were followed by the study of military formations.
How could there be such a thing as reaching Tongguan and claiming to see the Son of Heaven, while the outer palace walls alone could enrich the hundred officials? This is so.

These are the writings: over three hundred kinds and more than three thousand passages. Combining the people of past and present, ancient and modern, the exemplary models of the former are all present here.
The Way exists right before one's eyes. All of these are the very blood-heart of the Master; every fragment was held up by his own bare hands.

If you were to rely on words and get stuck on phrases, or manipulate these compositions, you would bring upon the dull-witted Master immeasurable transgressions, and the Ancestors as well would suffer.

The kōans and verses of the patriarchs of the Zen school are recorded in detail in various Zen lamp histories and records.

However, seeing that later students were rarely able to master them thoroughly, the venerable masters of the Song and Yuan dynasties further collected these kōans and appended their own verses and commentaries.

They compiled this distinct collection and circulated it within the monastic communities, so that students might examine and discern them with clarity as easily as looking at the palm of one's hand. This is truly...

It is the Great Dharma Banner of Radiant Light. His *Nianggu ji* (Anthology of Ancient Cases) is titled *Zongmen tongyao* (Essentials of the Chan School), and his *Songgu ji* (Anthology of Verses on Ancient Cases) is titled *Songgu lianzhu* (String of Pearls of Verses on Ancient Cases).
However, the *Tongyao* also appears in a *Xuji* (Continued Collection), and the *Lianzhu* likewise appears in a *Tongji* (Comprehensive Collection).

Yet, regarding the formal discourses and instructional outlines (*tengtang*) delivered by the successive patriarchs upon ascending the seat, those collected from past and present are lamentably lacking. Whenever I encountered senior masters of the monastic community, they all [lamented this].
I sighed with regret that people’s conduct is superficial and the Way has grown thin; that what they hear and see is meager and narrow.

Thus, I have endeavored to uphold the aspirations of my predecessors by borrowing from the *Baizhang Qinggui* and compiling the essential instructions of the various patriarchs regarding the daily affairs of a monastic abbot over the course of twenty years.

I have gathered various strategies through hunting for insights, collecting words according to their practical applications, and establishing matters based on those words. Whether referring to the present or the past, I have recorded them as they appeared;
thus, there is no distinction between high and low, nor chronological order, nor sectarian differences. It is much like the *Zhengfayan zang* (Treasury of the True Dharma Eye) of Miaoxi.

As for the arrangement and titles, I have generally followed established monastic regulations (*qinggui*). This collection from previous editions comprises four hundred masters who have provided expositions throughout the ages.

As for the other lineages: the Linji lineage ceased with the third generation after Patriarch Huanchu of Longchi; the Caodong lineage ceased with the third generation after Patriarch Jing of Shouchang;
and the Yunmen lineage ceased with the second generation after Patriarch Cheng. As for the Fayan and Yangshan lineages of Yunmen...
Furthermore, it includes the various patriarchs of the five schools and their collateral lineages from the early period, with each lineage’s records extending down to the *Lamp Records* (*Denglu*).
It compiles over three thousand instances of "extracting the essential points" (*chuti gangyu*) and more than three hundred essential matters appropriate for monastic communities.

This work is titled the *Record of the Essential Points Extracted by the Successive Patriarchs* (*Liezu Tiegang Lu*), consisting of forty-two fascicles. Although it sets forth the great principles and essential tenets of the Buddhadharma upheld by the successive patriarchs, it is indeed...
It is not present here; yet, regarding the principles of proclaiming the Way and establishing discourse, the general outlines are fully contained therein.

In the spring of the Gengzi year, upon resigning from my duties at the former Nanjian Monastery, I took this manuscript with me and traveled extensively through Guangdong. There, I met with the Regional Commander, Duke Xingran Li.
Furthermore, the two Dharma protectors, Mr. Liu Xin’an and Feng’an, rejoiced in the circulation of the Great Dharma and made the first offering of funds for its carving.
Also participating were the Governor of the great prefecture, Mr. Lu Xiaoshan; the Prefect of Jiayou, Mr. Min Jieyu;
the Magistrate of Baochang, Mr. Li Jiji; as well as Mr. Wang Manshou, Mr. Li Maoxian, and Mr. Zhang Bian’an.

Lord Xiao Gongsheng and others opened their purses and contributed their funds, joyfully providing assistance in great numbers. Once the woodblocks were completed, I have respectfully recorded this account of the origins on the right.
Written on the day of the Attainment of the Way, the twelfth month of the fifth year of the Kangxi era.

The *Tigang lu fanli* (General Rules for the *Tigang Lu*) is the essential outline of this work. It takes the various matters of the *qinggui* (rules of purity) as its main framework and the *tigang* (outlines) of the successive patriarchs as its headings.

However, since the successive patriarchs of antiquity upheld the essential principles of the Great Dharma, it would not have been appropriate to divide them into separate categories, as is done in worldly texts.
In works such as the *Shilü beiyào*, the subtle words and wondrous phrases bequeathed by our patriarchs since ancient times are scattered and inconsistent.
Although scholars may desire to read extensively, the texts of the Chan school are not necessarily complete; even if they were complete, [they would still be difficult to access].

It is not that I have fully mastered the vast teachings of the former masters; rather, I have borrowed from the *Qinggui* (Rules of Purity) to briefly detail the general outline of the daily affairs of an abbot.
This is like a single morsel from a full cauldron or a single drop from the great ocean, intended to serve those of beginner’s capacity while also providing a foundation for broad study.

The Imperial Birthday (Shengjie) is included within the *Chinggui* (Pure Rules) recompiled during the Zhizong era of the Zhiyuan period. However, it details only the ritual procedures for the formal lecture (*shangtang*) held upon the commencement of the festival;
regarding the concluding ceremony (*mansan*), apart from the wording of the memorial text (*shuyu*), everything else remains unclear.

Upon examining the various patriarchs such as Yuanwu, it appears that all possessed formal texts for the conclusion of the Imperial Birthday. I suspect that within the ancient *Chinggui* prior to the Zhiyuan era, such established precedents already existed.
I did not dare to omit this abruptly; therefore, I have established it as a single rite for the conclusion of the ceremony.
Furthermore, I observed that various masters of the lineage, such as Master Yan, did not distinguish between the opening and the conclusion, but simply titled it the "Sacred Festival" (Shengjie).

This particular form seems somewhat abrupt, so I have provisionally established it as the "Principal Festival. Instances such as these are frequent throughout this compilation. Generally speaking, regarding the extraction of the essential points—
As for their names, they were compiled and established only when they closely corresponded to the nine chapters of the *Chanyuan Qinggui*.

If they did not address urgent matters or respond to the needs of the occasion, or if they were too inconsistent with the nine chapters or merely redundant with the works of predecessors, they were all excluded from the record.

The opening of the *Tigang* (Outline) follows the single-item catalogs of former masters. When ascending the hall to instruct the assembly without establishing a separate title, these instances are all subsumed under the "Five Visits" (*wucan*).

Even if they appear repeatedly within the nine chapters, those that occur frequently are also largely included within the "Five Visits," the "Evening Visits," and the "Small Lectures" (*xiaocan*) of the four seasonal periods.
The "Universal Sermons" (pǔshuō) delivered prior to the summer retreat are rarely seen in the collected records of former masters.

Furthermore, those that conform to the formal protocols of the *Qinggui* are even more difficult to find. This compilation records only the words of the two venerable elders, Gulin and Yuejiang, in order to preserve their ancient spirit.
Moreover, the reason for specifically requesting that the Universal Sermons of Dahui be included as a standalone volume is to manifest his [spiritual] authority.
His eloquence was纵横 (unrestricted) and his discourse as vast as the great waves.

This compilation has no sectarian bias; it generally collects all the essential instructions of venerable masters that accord with the formal traditions of the past, provided their words and phrases are both concise and archaic, and capable of opening the eyes of practitioners.

Regarding the maintenance of the Buddha-Dharma through daily practices such as ascending the seat, formal sermons (*shàngtáng*), informal discourses (*xiǎocān*), and general expositions (*pǔshuō*), these have long been clearly detailed within the *Qīngguī* (Pure Rules) and ritual protocols.
Nowadays, however, various regions often transmit these erroneously and practice them in a confused manner;
some even go so far as to employ two titles concurrently. Although this does not significantly affect the gate of conversion, it is notably lacking in standard form. Therefore, the *Qīng*...
This single volume of regulations must always be kept at hand. Therefore, regarding the headings for the "Elevating to the Seat" (*shengzuō*) and "Ascending the Hall" (*shàngtáng*),
which are recorded at the beginning of this compilation, I have followed the original texts of the former masters exactly as they were and dare not alter them in the slightest.
The circumstantial details of these question-and-answer exchanges are not recorded at all, as the primary aim is to present the essential principles.
However, where they serve to illustrate the core teachings through the immediate dialogue, one or two instances are occasionally included.

When matters encounter their essential framework, those that are many are gathered in abundance, while those that are few do not hinder even a single rule; what is valued is simply the preservation of the matter itself.

As recorded in the *Ching-k’ui* (Pure Rules), regarding the request for the presiding mourner—such as a great master of the tradition—there is, within the Buddhist rites for the transition [of death], a ritual for chanting for the robes (*ti-i fo-shih fa-yü*). I have previously searched for this throughout ancient and modern sources.

It is missing. Nevertheless, the name of the "Robe-Exhortation" (Tiyi) remains recorded in various catalogs. First, this is so that later students may know that such a fundamental form exists within the Dharma-gate;
second, it awaits those of later generations who appreciate antiquity to supplement its practice. All other cases are similar to this.

Following the presentation of the essential themes (tígāng), there are generally two types of concluding sections: expressions of gratitude and the closing of the session; neither of these has been omitted.

Although I have compared various editions of the patriarchs’ essential themes found in the Great Canon or in various secular works, seeking out corresponding events and cross-referencing the commentaries, I am deeply aware that the vulgarities of errors, omissions, and redundancies cannot be entirely avoided. I truly regret that my mental and physical efforts have reached their limit.

My solitary wisdom is insufficient to encompass this; I humbly entreat the great masters of clear vision to graciously provide corrections and revisions for the General Table of Contents at the beginning of the *Lectures on the Essential Principles of the Ancestral Patriarchs*.

Chan Master Yuanwu Qin ascended the hall for the Imperial Birthday: "With heads reaching to heaven and feet treading the earth, we all share in the imperial grace. Possessing teeth..."

With our hair bound in caps, we all receive the Emperor’s grace; as the Divine Palace descends with blessings, the True Lord manifests his birth. With the sincere hearts of ten thousand nations, we pray for the Sage Sovereign’s longevity.
When the path to the throne is clear, the myriad streams flow toward their source; with this one word of impartiality, I offer my very liver and gall.
Do you understand this thoroughly? The imperial domain matches the North Pole; the Sage’s longevity equals the Southern Mountain.
On the occasion of the opening of the Dharma hall for the Tian-shen Festival: On the Tian-shen Festival of the fifth month, the True Man descended from the midst of heaven.

Zen Master Dahui Gaofeng ascends the hall for the Imperial Birthday. Having finished offering incense, a thunderclap suddenly strikes followed by torrential rain. He then says:

"I do not know. Beings who possess life receive the great creative force of existence yet offer no thanks. Furthermore, as for a man of the Way beneath the forest trees, how can he offer prayers of praise?

[He] strikes the whisk and says: "As soon as the Sleeping Dragon exerts himself, the Vermilion Phoenix soars aloft."

The Fifth Patriarch, Chan Master Yuan, provides the essential framework for the Correct Festival. On the occasion of the Imperial Birthday on the eighth day of the twelfth month, he ascends the hall and says:

Chan Master Zhenjing Wen ascended the hall for the Imperial Birthday: "All the soil under heaven belongs to the King's soil;

This is the day of the birth of His Majesty the Emperor. As it is said, "The former sages and the later sages share the same clarity of sacred virtue;

We humbly pray that Your Majesty, the Emperor, may live for ten thousand years, nay, ten million years. Again, he summoned the assembly, saying: "Recite the Buddha’s name in the Great Hall and offer prayers."
"May the Sage's life-span be extended. [The Master] descends from the seat.
Chan Master Foyuan of Yuan ascends the hall for the Imperial Birthday: "The Emperor takes the whole world as his home and the myriad people as his children."

Father and son are of one body; the world is a single family. When the ruler loves the people, the people revere the ruler. When love and reverence are thus shared, the Way of the King has no boundaries beyond it.

Therefore, the Buddha said: "It is as if the people have obtained their king," and also: "It is as if the people are the king. Furthermore, there are no people outside the king, and no king outside the people.
If the king were outside the people, the people would not receive his bounty; if the people were outside the king, the king [would not receive their reverence].
The Way is not broad. How can one be called a "min" (the people)? One who lacks knowledge is called a "min. How can one be called a "wang" (a king)?

One who is sagely and divine is called a "wang. His Majesty the Emperor is supremely divine and supremely sage. On the occasion of his birth as the parent of the people and the tranquility of Heaven, the sun, moon, and stars joined like pearls and merged like jade disks;

the Yangtze, Yellow, Huai, and Ji Rivers surged forth, clearing the turbid and exalting the pure; and the transformative power of Heaven and Earth brought forth all plants, trees, insects, and beasts.
"The fish present auspicious omens and manifest wonders; all these are brought about by the Emperor’s supreme virtue.

I humbly pray that his longevity may rival the Southern Mountains and his years match those of the Northern Peak—lasting ten thousand years forever, without end or limit. Thereupon, he descended from the meditation seat and performed a dance, saying, "Do you understand?

Ascending the hall for the Imperial Birthday: In the heavens there is no second sun; In Jambudvīpa, there is but one Supreme Honored One. The ten-thousand-year pine does not age; The Sage’s longevity equals Heaven and Earth.

Simply take this one flavor of the dharma of non-seeking and look up to pray for the Emperor’s longevity for ten million years.
Chan Master Miam Jie ascended the hall for the Imperial Birthday. "The Mahāyāna Dharma transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations;

Ascending the hall on the occasion of the Emperor’s Birthday: The Buddhas preach that which is not preached; the Patriarchs hear that which is not heard.

They have left behind a single turning word that shall forever stabilize heaven and earth for ten thousand ages. But tell me, what is that one turning word? Suddenly rising, straightening his body, and joining his palms, he said:
"Long live the Emperor! Ten thousand years, ten thousand ten thousand years!"

Ascending the hall on the anniversary of the Sage’s birthday: The numinous faculty is vast and penetrating; its wondrous resonance accords with the impartial. The mirror of wisdom is clear and bright; the universal path is free of tracks.
At every place, auspicious events manifest; seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are never obscured. Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the adamantine body emerges.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, throughout heaven and earth, all sing of the Way; across the five lakes and four seas, all rejoice in non-action.
"What means does a man of the Way beneath the forest have to repay his debt of gratitude? The message remains before the Many-Sons Stūpa; each time it is brought forth, it is ever new.
Ascending the hall on the occasion of the Emperor’s Birthday: "The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; he manifests dharmas equal to empty space; he realizes empty space."

At that time, there is neither "is" nor "non-dharma. Since there is neither right nor wrong, one takes empty space as the true essence (*dharmakāya*), the lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges as the wondrous function (*upāyakauśalya*), Mount Sumeru—the immovable mountain—as the mountain of longevity, and the ocean of profound merit as the sea of blessings.
Encompassing all existence and ferrying across the four modes of birth, this is truly the most sublime among heavens.
O Celestial One, the Sage among Sages, on this very month of your birth, we look up with the sincerity of sunflowers and heliotropes.
As you fully uphold a single phrase, a thousand auspicious signs converge. We pray for the longevity of Your Majesty, enduring as long as earth and heaven.
Ascending the hall on the occasion of the celebration of the Emperor’s Sacred Birthday: "The void can be measured and the wind can be bound, yet one cannot fully describe the Buddha’s merits.
Since the ocean of the Buddha’s merits is difficult to measure, so too is the sacred longevity of our Sovereign."
Ascending the Dharma Hall on the Emperor’s Birthday: Every day is a good day; every moment is a good moment.
Only on the twenty-second day of the tenth month, when auspicious stars shine their light down, is it most rare and precious.
Chan Master Xueyan Qin’s Outline for the Sacred Festival: The source of the myriad transformations, the mother of all things;

his virtue covers the sands of the Ganges, his capacity encompasses the universe. The sage among sages, the sovereign among sovereigns; a celebration of this rare occasion, a longevity that towers for a thousand ages.
Taking the Earth (Kun) as his own responsibility, the moon shines bright in the great void; taking the Heaven (Qian) as his son, the red sun stands at its zenith. It is exactly thus.

The Master composed a verse: "All dharmas are free from the marks of discrimination; relying on the former..."
The marks are themselves suchness. Within the shadows of the spring breeze, heaven and earth are vast; boundless rivers and mountains unfold like a painted scroll.
Regarding the "Qian" hexagram and the principle of "convergence": "Qian" refers to vigorous movement that never ceases; "convergence" refers to the myriad phenomena returning to the One.
Is it not only the Sage who can cause the myriad phenomena to converge within himself? Is it not only he who employs the virtue of Qian to occupy the position of Heaven?
Is this not the ultimate principle? It is the pinnacle of all principles. Its source lies in non-action; its manifestation is the sagehood of humanity. Its essence resides in non-being.
Thus, the wind of Yao blew vast and far-reaching, and the sun of Shun shone bright and serene.
Chan Master Zhongfeng Ben addressed the assembly on the occasion of the Imperial Birthday: "How great is the Primordial Source of Qian! How ultimate is the Primordial Source of Kun!
A single breath contains and encompasses all existence; the people have no name by which to designate it. Its merit transcends all previous sages; its virtue surpasses all former kings.
Vast indeed is its function; majestic indeed is its substance. The Dragon embraces the sun above the ninefold heavens; its true radiance..."
Its radiance shall shine for ten thousand years. Does the great assembly know this yet? On this very day, auspiciousness is distributed throughout the lands, and spring fills the entire realm.
From the crown of the Great Vairocana, his emanations appear; the Udumbara flower bursts forth in flames.

For this reason, the world calls it the "Excellent Festival of the Sage. Indeed, among all things that grow and flourish between heaven and earth, there are none that do not receive its grace. Only...

Among those of our Śākya clan, we are perhaps those who have received its benefits most profoundly. Why is this so? It is because we are solitary, humble, and weak, and thus unable to establish ourselves independently.
To speak of "solitude," it means we remain far removed from kinsmen and do not manage a family estate.

To speak of "humility," it means we rely on the generosity of donors for sustenance and dwell among the forested foothills. To speak of "weakness," it means we devote our minds to emptiness and stillness, maintaining our integrity and following the precepts.
I submit this proposal: if one’s strength is weak, one should protect the true nature and refrain from competing with worldly things.

Were it not for the Sages who, never forgetting the Buddha’s entrustment, graciously provide external protection, how would the monastic community dare to claim that its gardens and requisites are "permanently held" (zhǒngcháng), lest they be plundered by the hands of others?
It is because of this that our peaceful dwelling and leisurely meals—every moment, every instant—are all derived [from such protection].
Your Sacred Grace is such that even the heavens covering above and the earth supporting below are insufficient as metaphors for it.

To seek the Dharma for the remainder of one’s life and turn toward the Way until death, or even to forget one’s body and devote one’s life to it, would still not suffice to repay even a ten-thousandth part of it.

How could one permit oneself to be indolent or lax, to let the days pass in vain, and furthermore to direct one’s thoughts toward profit and desire? Now, encountering this auspicious occasion of the Imperial Birthday, [I]...

I cite this humble sincerity to encourage one another. It is recorded that Emperor Zhuangzong of the Later Tang asked Master Xinghua, "Since I reclaimed the Central Plains, I have obtained a treasure, yet no one dares to appraise its value. Xinghua said, "Please let Your Majesty show me this treasure.
The Emperor then reached out his hand and extended the ends of his *fuhou* (head-wrap). Xinghua said, "As for the treasure of a sovereign, who would dare to appraise its value?"
When the dragon roars, mist rises; when the tiger howls, wind is born. Thus, it is not that the Founding Emperor (Zhuangzong) failed to promote the Dharma.
Yet, as for the price of the treasure of the Central Plains, it has ultimately never been settled. I, a humble monk, facing the celestial court from afar, venture to compose this verse:

The treasure of the Central Plains covers heaven and earth; Without past and without present, it fills the great void. Its value exceeds that of heaven and earth, yet remains unredeemed— I wait in expectation.
Behold the Imperial Transformation surpassing that of Yao and Shun!
On the occasion of the Emperor’s Birthday, Chan Master Lirun of Tianmu ascended the hall and said: "What does Heaven say? The four seasons proceed.

Clear. At such a time as this, how is it? "The rustic elder knows nothing of the labors of Yao and Shun; once the sacrifice to Goumang is finished, he feeds the spring plowing.

On the occasion of the Imperial Birthday, he ascends the hall: sitting in the crystal palace, drawing the night-bright curtain, he is a unified whole that is difficult to encompass—obscure and profound.

Responding to all conditions without error, from the time of the ancient patriarchs down to the present, this station has been esteemed as supreme. For now, let us set aside the single phrase of total self-surrender and offer it with reverence:

how should one proclaim it? It wondrously accords with the myriad capacities, allowing all to enter the offering together; let the various paths be permitted to distinguish their own provisional functions.
Chan Master Chushi Qi ascended the hall on the occasion of the Imperial Birthday. He cited the dialogue between Wuzhuo and a non-Buddhist regarding the exposition of doctrine.
Wuzhuo said, "The world is at peace; may the King enjoy long life. The non-Buddhist was left speechless and unable to refute him. The Master offered this verse:
"The meanings are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, Yet they do not exceed this one sentence: A mosquito upon an iron ox— There is no place for you to bite."
Chan Master Wuyong Kuan ascended the hall on the auspicious occasion of the Emperor’s birthday: "The Buddha Vairocana of the Past (Wei-yin-wang) manifests his presence this very day;

his virtue covers all living beings, and his radiance shines across the seas and fields. Without the need for polishing or refinement, I, the subject-monk of Lake Tai, briefly open up a single thread:
May the Sage Emperor’s longevity equal that of heaven and earth; may his majestic divine light pervade everywhere. He then descended from the seat.
Chan Master Xiaoyin Yun ascends the hall for the Imperial Birthday: Descending from Tuṣita to Jambudvīpa, his fundamental essence and manifested traces are non-dual;

turning the golden wheel to proclaim the True Dharma, his provisional and ultimate teachings are fully revealed. Riding upon his vows to manifest birth, he expounds the transformation according to capacities;

the subtle pivot of spiritual power moves in secret, elevating our people to the midst of the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī), while the precious mirror is held high, placing the four seas within the crucible of the Great Potter.
Within [this state], beneath my groves and springs, the days of transformation stretch long; amidst the clarity of bells and drums, the profound wind spreads afar.
The three wheels do not abide, and both giver and receiver are relinquished. Ultimately, how can one offer praise? After a long silence, he said:
"The merit of non-action is inconceivable; the wondrously perfect body of pure wisdom is empty and still."
Ascending the hall on the Imperial Birthday: The transformative power of the Creator operates in secret, enshrining all living beings within the vast expanse of its protection;
with dignified non-action, he leads the four seas into a realm of benevolence and longevity. It is like the ocean of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, which integrates and encompasses the three thousand worlds;
it resembles the net of Indra, where the pearls interlace across ten billion mountains and rivers. At such a time as this, what is that which does not involve birth?
A single breath remains silent, yet it contains all forms; where could the myriad spirits fail to express their gratitude for this impartiality?
Chan Master Liaoyuan Yu ascends the hall on the auspicious occasion of the Emperor’s Birthday: "The true eye of Mahesvara penetrates the ten voids;
the celestial voice of the Kalavinka pervades the entire dharma-realm. It establishes the Three Powers and brings peace to the four seas. He continues his lineage...

The great design of the successive sages received the entrustment of Mount Ling; they crushed resentment and shattered the enemy by turning the Vajra-wheel, and they issued governance and bestowed benevolence by letting out the lion’s roar.

On this auspicious dawn of the rainbow-omen, we celebrate the flourishing era of ten thousand generations. Thus, with rattled drums of straw and earthen drums, all together rejoice in peace and prosperity;

even in the reigns of Kings Yao and Shun, there remained further transformation to be wrought—this is why it is said: [The text here concludes with a citation from the *Laozi*: “Even when the Way is lost, its traces remain.”
The upward path has not been transmitted by a thousand sages; atop a ten-thousand-fathom cliff, one attains mastery in all directions. Holding up his staff, he said:
"To offer this body and mind to every dust mote and land—this is what is called repaying the debt of national gratitude."
Ascending the hall on the Emperor’s Birthday: All phenomena are the radiance of the mind; all conditions are but the clarity of nature.
Fundamentally, there is no person who is deluded or awakened; it simply requires realization today. But tell me, what is it that is realized? After a long silence, he said:

"On the eleventh day of the first month of the Jiachen year, when the Son of Heaven of the Great Yuan was born, the oceans of lands and the hairs of dust all bowed their heads. May the ten-thousand-year pine grow ever taller."
On the anniversary of the Emperor’s birthday, he ascended the hall and said: "The adamantine true body penetrates the ten voids; the numinous light of prajñā encompasses all phenomena.
It is brilliantly manifest within the mind and eyes, yet its form cannot be seen; it shines radiantly amidst the sensory objects of form, yet..."

The Principle is indivisible. It shares with heaven and earth the same universal canopy; it shares with the sun and moon the same illuminating presence; it shares with the mountains and peaks the same lofty majesty;
it shares with the rivers and streams the same flowing current. This is what is meant by "Buddha to Buddha, hand to hand; Patriarch to Patriarch, transmission from one to another.

without establishing even a speck of dust, one may fully realize Vajra-wisdom. How much more so when the vegetables in the garden are green and the grain in the fields is ripe—is this not a time of abundant harvests and harmonious seasons?
When the mind is fused and the environment is tranquil, how can one possibly act apart from the single phrase "neither turning toward nor turning away"? How could one do so?
The Way arises. A single wild goose in the autumn Milky Way; a thousand households with their mortars and pestles at night.

Chan Master Mimang Jue ascended the hall on the fifteenth day of the month and said: "Before the fifteenth day, the pond is dug but does not wait for the moon;

Receiving the Imperial Decree and Fulfilling the Sacred Mandate:

and the Pratyekabuddhas and Solitary Realizers attain it here, appearing in worlds devoid of Buddhas to manifest supernatural powers.
Radiant light. Here, the assembly of śrāvakas and the five hundred arhats who came by night to offer their invitation attained it;
they attained the eight liberations and were endowed with the six supernormal powers. Here, devas and humans attained it; they increased in the ten wholesome deeds.
Here, asuras attained it; they eliminated their arrogance. Here, those in the hells attained it; they instantly transcended the ten stages. [The hungry ghosts...]
Animals, as well as those of the four modes of birth and the nine categories— all sentient beings— attain it here, each receiving its enjoyment according to their own faculties and natures.
After the World-Honored One of Immeasurable Life has finished performing all Buddha-works by emitting great rays of light,
he then pours the waters of the four great oceans upon the crown of the head of the World-Honored Maitreya, bestowing upon him the [prediction of] Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Prediction of Enlightenment: You shall perform great Buddha-work as a successor to the position.

World-Honored One Amitāyus possesses such supernormal powers, such mastery, and such majestic spiritual authority. Having arrived at this point, is there anyone here who knows how to acknowledge kindness and repay it?
If there is, come forth and meet with Jingshan; I shall bear witness for you. If not, listen to this one [verse]: [Verse omitted per instructions]
Verse: The Dharma-realm of the ten directions reaches the mouths of men; All that exists within the Dharma-realm is their very tongue.

Relying solely upon these mouths and tongues, May they pray for the longevity of our Sovereign without ceasing. For billions of years, may the source of blessings flow forth, Like the surging ocean, never to be exhausted.
Within the lion’s den, the *sūnī* is born; The *yuèzù* shall surely emerge from the caves of Mount Dan. As an auspicious omen...
Auspiciousness pervades the nine realms; plants, trees, and even insects all rejoice. I prostrate to this inconceivable matter, which is like the myriad stars bowing to the bright moon.
Therefore, I now proclaim these sublime gāthās, speaking of the truth within the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

On the nineteenth day of the twelfth month in the second year of the Huangyou era, Emperor Renzong summoned Chan Master Da Jue Lian to the Rear Garden to partake in a vegetarian feast at Huacheng Hall.
Upon the conclusion of the meal, an imperial edict was proclaimed, ordering him to follow the ritual protocols of the Southern Chan monasteries to open the hall and expound the Dharma.
Furthermore, the Master of Great Compassion (Ciyun Dashi), Qingman, Vice-Registrar of the Left Street, was commanded to perform the formal invocation (*kaibai*). Man offered his thanks.

The grace having been concluded, he then addressed the assembly, saying: "As spring returns to the imperial gardens and the royal assembly is convened, the Ten-Thousand Chariots have descended upon the Hall of Shun, and the two streets are honored by the presence of Yao’s brow.
This being a season of gentle warmth, it is truly the day for the proclamation and exaltation [of the Dharma]."
"It is fitting to discuss the Way of our Ancestors, so as to fully accord with the Imperial mind. Respectfully submitted. The Master then ascended the seat.
Having offered incense for the Emperor and finished the exchange of questions and answers, he said: "Within the hall of the Ancient Buddhas, there has never been any divergent teaching;

yet within the phrases that circulate, there are indeed many discourses. Those who attain them find their wondrous function unimpaired; those who lose them encounter obstructions at every turn. Thus, the streams, mountains, clouds, and moon..."
Abiding in the same wind, the water birds and forest trees manifest the Way at every turn.
If one enters the gate of Kāśyapa, one directly attains the vast sway of Yao’s wind and the brilliant clarity of Shun’s sun; the village elders sing their songs and the fishermen dance with joy.
At such a time, there is only the transformation of pure, non-action—how could one know of such a thing? Thereupon, he descended from his seat.

At the request of the Imperial Court, Chan Master Yuanwu Qin ascends the hall. At the request of Noble Consort Qiao, he ascends the hall: "A single phrase is fully raised; a thousand differences are simultaneously realized.
When a single flower blooms, ten thousand blessings arrive. Coming and going are uninterrupted yet have their source; movement and stillness do not shift, yet they are ever-present."
Quiescence! Everywhere is the Buddha; every head is the Way. If you can gain deep faith and reach this realization, you will no longer require the external assistance of others.

It is like a strong man extending or contracting his arm—in an instant, you fully manifest this dynamic power. Whether moving or still, whether emerging or dwelling, the most sublime appears within the sublime;
the most extraordinary appears within the extraordinary. This is not due to external conditions, but is entirely sustained by [one's own inherent capacity].
Such is his virtue. Thus it is said: "The multitudes of devas and human beings all receive this power of grace.

If one recognizes this grace, then every movement, pause, and action—manifesting in hundreds of thousands of transformations—will never fall into emptiness. At such a time as this, how do you speak a single phrase?
"In the presence of the sun, pervading the world without deviation; through a thousand layers and ten thousand turns, its radiance shines ever more brightly."
Lady Qiao Guifei: Please ascend the hall for the sake of Dharma Master Fazhen’s recovery from illness.

At Vulture Peak, the supreme teaching was held aloft; the myriad spirits met in harmony without consultation. At Shaoshi, the True Dharma Eye was secretly transmitted; the ten thousand phenomena are interfused in perfect penetration.

The seals of realization accord with one another, and causal conditions enter into one another. This divine efficacy is like the heavens and earth in their encompassing and supporting; it is wondrous—
Wisdom is like the illumination of the sun and moon; it is equal and level throughout the sands of the world-realms, without the slightest partiality or bias.
There is a Great Being of Liberation who has realized the Path of Great Liberation, opened the Gate of Great Liberation, and revealed the Matter of Great Liberation.

Now he manifests this ailment that cannot be fathomed even when all efforts are concentrated upon it, directly causing the thousand sages to seek its point of origin and yet find nothing. All Buddhas and sentient beings alike possess this ailment.
If the Buddhas were to fall ill, they would not be sentient beings; if sentient beings were to fall ill, they would not be Buddhas.
Therefore, because sentient beings are ill, he manifests this illness. Consequently, the people of Rājagṛha, each receiving light from the crown of his head, all came to inquire after his health.
Yet this Great Being, manifesting according to their needs, caused them to stand like a wall ten thousand fathoms high, until the multitude...
The illness has ended; the Great Liberated One is at peace.
Once he is at peace, there is a great donor who performs a great Dharma-giving, erects a great Dharma-banner, expounds the great meaning of the Dharma, and rains down the great rain of the Dharma.
Each element interlaces with the others, layer upon layer, inexhaustible. At such a time as this, how do you speak that single phrase which accords with the moment and the season? Do you understand?
The spiritual sprouts increase in refined vigor; the auspicious grasses emit a radiant light. Once more he composed a verse: "Vimalakīrti was fundamentally not ill when he manifested illness;
Mañjuśrī did not actually come when he inquired after his health. He erected the great banner of Dharma and opened the gate of great giving, Suddenly causing the thousand eyes to open all at once."

When Concubine Qiao established the Assembly of the Thousand Buddhas, he ascended the hall and said: "The thousand blossoms manifest auspicious responses; ten thousand virtues accumulate upon the spiritual terrace.
The gate of liberation is widely opened, and the priceless treasury is grandly revealed. He raises high the Eye of the True Dharma and manifests the causes of the thousand Buddhas.

Thus, the entire realm is severed from the net of entanglement; in the presence of reality, there is no grasping or rejecting. Penetrating sound and penetrating form, it spans from antiquity to the present."

Possessing the great faculty of faith, they cultivate the bodhisattva practices and give rise to inconceivable powers of aspiration. They open up pure adornments and establish the great site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Therein, they array all manner of rare delicacies; even a single incense stick, a single flower, a single cup of tea, or a single fruit is identical to the nature of dharmas, as vast as empty space.
In every atom and in every land, the thousand Buddhas radiate light; according to principle and according to phenomena, they universally respond throughout the ten directions.

Thus, the great artisan requires no marking line, and the fine timber has neither curvature nor straightness. As the crimson sun blazes through the vast void, the entire realm is brilliantly illuminated.

With the blooming of a single flower, a Buddha appears in the world; with the lifting of a single mote of dust, a Buddha attains enlightenment. Lords and attendants interpenetrate one another, and the myriad phenomena manifest in radiant clarity.
Accumulating boundless fortune and honor, may we pray for Your Majesty’s wisdom and longevity to be limitless. At such a time as this, how would you speak?
Within the chamber, a thousand lamps shine upon one another; beyond the heavens, the precious moon is even more clear and full.
At the request of Imperial Consort Da-nei, the Master ascended the hall and said: "A single phrase emerges from the crown of a thousand sages; a wondrous pivot issues from an inexhaustible treasury.
It is utterly without dependence and forever beyond all traces. It is neither form nor mind, neither suchness nor difference.
Throughout the entirety of empty space and the furthest reaches of the Dharma-realm, it is all, without exception, this one Great Gate of Liberation. You all are vast and expansive..."
As you enter and exit the earth, do you still feel your hair standing on end with cold?

If, beneath your heels, not a single thought arises and your whole being is fully revealed, then you will be pure and naked, alive and agile; when you wish to walk, you walk; when you wish to stay, you stay.
When you wish to act, act; when you wish to rest, rest. Do not point toward a secondary head; do not fall into a secondary view.

Upon reaching this state, from antiquity to the present, there is a profound, still, and luminous clarity. If you can step upon it, penetrating through and beyond birth and death—what a trivial matter that would be!
One can then, by means of the untainted faculties and powers, raise the banner of Dharma, establish the essential tenets, and clothe all sentient beings. To the end.
To the limits of the future, there is no end. At this very moment, tell me: by whose power of grace does one receive it? Do you understand thoroughly?
On the summit of the mountain of the five aggregates, the formless Buddha emits light that shakes the earth, pervading all lands. The verse says:

With a single mind free from dwelling or attachment, One is the sovereign of the Dharma-kingdom throughout the world. Having accomplished untainted merit, One sits upright upon the precious lotus flower.
Lady Da-in Kyōkoku requests the Master to ascend the hall. Everywhere there is truly no turning back or deviation; in every atom of dust there is discerning awareness.
The myriad phenomena are seen through non-seeing; the myriad dharmas are heard through non-hearing.
This seeing that is not seeing fills and pervades empty space; this hearing that is not hearing encompasses all existence. Depart from both seeing and non-seeing, hearing and non-hearing.
I have heard that there is another extraordinary matter. One must possess the mechanism of great liberation and the function of great liberation;
only then can one, wherever they arise, be entirely authentic. Have you not seen how a monk asked Yunmen, "What is the samādhi of every dust mote?
Yunmen replied, "Rice in the bowl, water in the bucket. Furthermore, a monk asked, "What are the Buddhas?"
Regarding his place of origin, the Master said: "The eastern mountain walks upon the water. At one and the same time, this is a moment of utter simplicity;
where it is plain and solid, it is truly plain and solid. Where it is solitary, perilous, and steep, it is truly solitary, perilous, and steep.
At such a time as this, with what do you uphold [the Dharma]? With what eyes do you discern? Do you understand? Try!
Jade must pass through fire; seeking pearls does not depart from the mud. Again, a verse says: This mind contains the Dharma-realm; its clarity accords with the person of original nature.
A thousand auspicious signs gather like mist; ten thousand virtues arrive like clouds.
The Feudal Lord requested Master Qín Yuánwù to provide the essential framework. At the request of the Great King of Yùn, he ascended the hall and said: "The ultimate principle is naturally so;

once, a thousand petals manifested as an auspicious omen. Neither existing nor non-existing, the ten directions are right before one's eyes. If you possess keen faculties and superior wisdom, with a single stroke—"
He immediately understood and took it upon himself. Being able to cut off the myriad streams, he could transcend the present and crown all antiquity.
With such wisdom, such power, such a mind, and such vows, his clarity was like the bright sun and his vastness was like the great void.
Therefore it is said: "It is like empty space; its essence is not comprised of manifold characteristics, yet it does not obstruct the manifestation of those various characteristics. It is also said:
"If a person wishes to thoroughly understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm as being entirely created by mind alone.
For this pure original source is free from going and coming, and free from sound and form. If one were to employ true and correct...

One perceives the quiescent suchness. Although throughout the twelve periods of the day and night one neither thinks nor deliberates, being without action or conditioning, from movement and stillness to speech and silence, and even amidst dreaming and waking, there is nothing that is not the radiant light of the original ground, the primordial face.

Various auspicious omens appear; various wonders appear. All of these arise from the cultivation of the Wisdom of All Modes throughout an ocean of immeasurable and boundless kalpas, manifesting through the wisdom of the pure and subtle faculties.

At such a time as this, how can it be that a thousand Buddhas appear within the light of formlessness? A single path of pure emptiness extends through past and present. Furthermore, he cites the Sage Śākyamuni. His spirit...
At the mountain assembly, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* was being expounded. Before the Buddha, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"If one speaks of the six *pāramitās* within a dream, is that the same as when awake, or is it different? Subhūti replied: "The meaning of this is profound and subtle; I am unable to explain it.
In this assembly there is the Great Being Maitreya, who shall succeed the Buddha; you should go and ask him. Maitreya—
Maitreya said, "Who is Maitreya? Who is the one called Maitreya? The Master picked it up and said, "Do you understand? A single phrase meets the mark;

ten thousand conditions are extinguished. Listen further to this verse: Preaching the Dharma within a dream is no different from awakening; The wondrous functioning of spiritual powers does not go beyond him.
Who is he? What is his name? All are Maitreya; Where auspicious light arises, the jewel of the mind appears."

King Xin requested [the Master] to ascend the seat. To the assembly: "To see the Buddha with the Buddha-eye is to have no differentiated seeing; to expound the Dharma with the Dharma is to have no distinct preaching.
The hearing and seeing of the Buddha-Dharma are entirely present and complete. Directly beneath the sun, one completely transcends.

This single stroke of the present moment is neither Buddha nor Dharma, neither seeing nor preaching, neither existent nor non-existent, neither different nor suchness. Vast as the great void, it is luminous."
It is like the bright sun. For this reason, the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time were born here, practiced here, awakened to the Way here, and attained Buddhahood here.
It was entirely not dependent on others; they alone relied upon its power. Even now, it has been extracted from the crown of the heads of the thousand sages.
It is not seen with the eyes, nor heard with the ears, nor proclaimed by words, nor grasped by the mind.
Understand. At this very moment, one must be such a person to succeed. Therefore it is said: "The great man possesses great vision; with great wisdom, he attains great function.
He raises one to clarify the three; he informs the past and knows the future.

At this very moment, how do you speak that single phrase which does not involve causal conditions? Do you understand? In the Chu marsh, the *míng* plant blooms once every five hundred years; the dragon coils...
The peach tree grows for a thousand years. Again, a verse says: "A single mote of dust is raised and a single land appears; when a single flower blooms, a single Buddha is born.
By attaining realization of the Vajra, one gains long life; the six sense faculties radiate light day and night."
At the request of Prince Ji, he ascended the seat. With his untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), he performed a wondrous feat; with the wisdom of liberation, he planted diamond-like conditions.
He did not manifest his body in another place, but remained forever revealed at the crown of the head. It is neither mind nor Buddha, neither different nor suchness.
In the midst of the ordinary, he took up a single blade of grass and made it a sixteen-foot golden body; in the midst of the ordinary, he spoke a single phrase that could serve as [the Dharma].
The Vajra-jewel sword: everyone receives this function, and each and every one receives this mind.
If you can reflect back and turn the light inward, it is the very essence of Vairocana. Have you not seen how King Prasenajit asked the Elder Śākyamuni:
"In the past, before I had attained Buddhahood, I consulted Kātyāyana, who told me that after the death of this body, there is annihilation. I...

Although he had met the Buddha, his mind remained full of doubt. "This body changes and transforms from moment to moment," he thought, "yet I do not know if there is anything within it that does not change.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni said to King Prasenajit, "Though you know that transformation never ceases, do you also know that there is something within the body that does not change?
The king joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying, "I truly do not know. The Buddha said:
"Great King, how old were you when you first saw the waters of the Ganges? The King replied, "I saw them when I was three years old. The Buddha asked, "How is it now?
The King replied, "Sixty-two years have passed since then; my vision is no different from what it was at age three.
The Buddha said, "Great King, although your face has wrinkled—wrinkling being a sign of change—the essence of this seeing-nature (*darśana-vidyā*) has never changed. Change..."
That which undergoes cessation is subject to change; that which is unchanging is fundamentally without birth or death.

Śākyamuni, atop the thousand-saints’ crown and the ten-thousand-fathom peak, pointed out the adamantine nature—unchanging and immutable, profoundly still and immovable, majestically and fully manifest.
Because of this, King Prasenajit recognized his original mind. He ventured to ask the great assembly: "Right now, all people see this mountain monk ascend the hall.
Tell me, from where does this seeing arise? Is it the same as, or different from, that which existed prior to the time of Vipaśyin, beyond the kalpa of emptiness?
If you can see that there is no difference and no distinction, then you see what is right before you. This is precisely the moment.
At such a time, how do you express it in a single phrase? "Face-to-face, he strikes open the inexhaustible treasury;
from every point, the night-jewel emerges. He further said: "The Great King Jiguo possesses great capacity and the lineage of the Supreme Vehicle.

Born as a prince, his status is most noble and glorious; yet he does not forget the entrustment of the Buddhas, knowing that there exists this great causal connection, and thus he has manifested his spiritual power."
The scriptural teachings provide profound insight into cause and effect; thus, in all that one undertakes, the source of the mind is clearly illuminated.

Therefore, by establishing these causes and conditions for performing good deeds and practicing virtuous protection, one’s wealth and status endure, and blessings and prosperity flourish ever more greatly.
Cultivating merit when one possesses it is like the great ocean receiving all streams. Only those of keen faculties and the seed of wisdom possess such capacity. This alone—
This is none other than the Hall of Universal Radiance; the formless body is Vairocana. The myriad practices are the flowers of the cause, and the perfect sea is the fruit;
the source of merit pours forth in a great torrent, overflowing the celestial river.
Chan Master Zhenjue Tian traveled to the capital at the beginning of the Yuanyou era. When Prince Xu Guo heard of the Master’s reputation for the Way, he dispatched an envoy one day to summon him.
Upon entering the palace and ascending the seat, the Master declared: "The true nature of Vairocana is no different from the fundamental nature of you all.
Since time immemorial, we have transmigrated through the Dharma-realm; amidst these births, there is neither beginning nor end."

There is no going and no coming; no nature and no characteristics; no past and no present. Not even a speck of dust can be established; not even a hair’s breadth can remain. There is no True Dharma to be divided;
how could there be any interval between the beginning and the end? Therefore, know that within the *dharmadhātu*, sentient beings neither arise nor perish;
the self-nature and original source are themselves the Buddha. Nevertheless, according to the gate of the patch-robed monks (*bhikṣu*), heaven and earth are as far apart as the poles.

It is extraordinary. Since there is arising and there is ceasing, and since there is departing and there is coming, the periods of the True Dharma, the Semblance Dharma, and the Final Dharma are without distinction;
their nature and characteristics are clearly manifest and can be seen. Within this interval, there is neither one who attains Buddhahood nor one who does not attain Buddhahood.
Within the treasury of Prajñā, there is nothing whatsoever that is obstructed. Even were it the Buddhas of the three periods, the six generations of patriarchs, or the old masters of the world—

"Upādhyāya, your spiritual power surpasses that of Śāriputra, and your discerning wisdom exceeds that of Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. Upon reaching this point, one must also bind the tongue and lose all sharpness of wit.
After a long silence, he said: "The imperial decree has already been proclaimed throughout the pure universe; every person celebrates the year of Great Peace."
The Imperial Edict for Master Daoti Wenshu Dao:
In the first year of the Xuanhua era, an edict was issued to change the title of "monk" (*bhikṣu*) to "Virtuous Man" (*deshi*). He ascended the hall and said:

"The matter of the Patriarch’s coming from the West is, this morning, exceptionally new. Formerly he had the appearance of a *bhikṣu*; now he has taken the form of the Lord Lao. [He wears] a crane-feather cloak..."
Clad in silver-brown robes and with a plantain-leaf turban wrapped around his head, this guest of the forest and springs has received the sovereign’s grace twice.
Thus it is said: "If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should contemplate the causes and conditions of time and season. But tell me, what is the current season?
Vairocana wears a jeweled crown to manifest the conventional within the ultimate; as for the elder Mañjuśrī, his body...
Donning the crane-feather cloak, one must likewise conform to the exigencies of the times. As it is for one person, so it is for many;
together we establish the monastic groves, rejoicing in this gathering of immortals. We shall jointly sip the *míxiān* libation and sing the *bùxū* hymns together.
At times we will read the *Língbǎo Dùrén Jīng*, or discuss the elixir of longevity and immortality. Under the moon, the zither is played, and the notes emerge from the fingertips.

The sounds of primordial antiquity are spread out like a chessboard before the hall; their subtlety manifests beyond the realm of divine mechanisms. Take one step forward and you arrive at the heavens of the Great Brahma;
take one step back and you enter the city of the Nine Shades of Darkness. As for that phrase of neither advancing nor retreating—how would you explain it?
Even if one were to transcend and transform upon the path of the Three Clarities, it remains ultimately but a delusory body within the cycle of rebirth.
Chan Master Fahai Li was ordered by the imperial court to convert his temple into the Shenxiao Palace. The Master ascended the seat;

after a long silence, he addressed the assembly, saying: "It is precisely because one has not yet attained thorough penetration that one speaks of right and wrong; it is because of a lack of true realization."
Thus, one proceeds to distinguish this from that. Since even my own body does not exist, what need is there to speak of anything outside the body?

Viewed with the True Eye, it is all a matter for laughter. Now, as the Sage Ruler has issued his decree to convert monasteries into shrines of Shenxiao, it is like adding a crown atop a Buddha’s head;
when calculated, what could be wrong with that? Today, this mountain monk cannot help but carry my staff across my shoulders.
Carrying my staff and hanging my alms-bag high, I shall settle my body and sustain my life within the seamless stupa.

Beneath the rootless tree, I shall whistle at the moon and chant with the wind, leaving it entirely to the cloud-riding immortals and the crane-mounted transcendents who may come here to recite incantations over water, write talismans, and perform rites by clapping their teeth.
In years to come, when I have attained the Way and ascended on a white cloud during the day, I shall be worthy to repay the unrepayable kindness and assist in [the Buddha's]... [unlimited merit].
He transformed for their sake, yet he feared it might not be jade; if it were jade, how truly marvelous! Nevertheless, tell me:
how would the mountain monk express his own turning-about? Do you understand? He cast down his whisk and immediately passed into stillness.

The Imperial Edict restored [Chen] to the tonsure and appointed him as the Abbot of Yuanwu Qin Chan Temple. After the monk had been restored to the tonsure and finished his expressions of gratitude, he ascended the seat. He is the God among gods, the Sage among sages;
he dwells within the great realm of the world yet transcends the venerable ones beyond the mundane. Holding the precious tally, he comes to face the people; with the golden canopy...

He ascended the throne and ruled the empire, sweeping clear the six realms and nourishing all quarters of the world. He then issued an imperial decree to once again revive the Buddha-dharma, whereby the śramaṇas throughout the heavens were restored to their monastic decorum.
They returned the ceremonial tablets to the late Minister Pei and resumed the crown and hairpins of the Great Being Fu.
Thus, the cranial protuberance of the Arhat was once more made whole, and the saffron robes of the Buddha were donned again in an instant.
The former splendor has been restored; Imperial grace is so profound and weighty that it exceeds mountains and hills ten thousand times over.
How could even the most minute things, such as grasses and trees, know how to repay it? I shall now pour forth my very heart and soul, offering but a tiny fraction of my being. O Great Assembly:

The First Buddha possessed the pivot of the *uṣṇīṣa*, like the spark struck from flint, like the flash of lightning. The Patriarch possessed the final phrase, which swallows the thorny *karkaṭaka* fruit and leaps through the diamond ring.
It can rival and surpass others, startling the multitudes; it can transform the mundane into the sacred. It soars through the present and manifests in antiquity, encompassing both form and sound.
Now, as I bring this forth before the assembly, I do not violate the proclamations of the past. Do you understand? The wondrous power of the Great Balance existed before heaven and earth;
the grace of its covering and supporting returns to the Great Sage.

The evening small discourse on the occasion of shaving the head and receiving the tonsure: To restore the monastic form once more and don the square robe is as rare an occurrence as the appearance of the *utpala* flower.
How can one repay such kindness, which is as vast as a mountain? I shall now briefly raise its essential principles:
throughout the entirety of the ten directions—whether long or short, vertical or horizontal, extending even to the seas of fragrant water—it is unspeakably, unspeakably infinite.
The ocean of lands is entirely contained within this single autumn hair. At times he manifests an infinite body; surging up in the east, it sinks in the west;

surging up in the south, it sinks in the north; surging up in the center, it sinks at the periphery. He performs immeasurable and boundless supernatural transformations, yet even these do not transcend this single autumn hair.
At other times, he is cold and silent, like withered wood, rotten stumps, cold ashes, or extinguished fire. In a single thought-moment—
Ten thousand years. Ten thousand years in a single thought-moment do not go beyond this single autumn hair.

Even performing immeasurable, boundless, extraordinary, and marvelous deeds, practicing difficult and painful austerities, transforming all beings, and attaining Buddhahood or becoming a Patriarch—none of these go beyond this single autumn hair.
Do you people still know this single autumn hair? If you know it, you have not yet opened your mouths.
Before this—before even the intention has been raised, before the Buddha has manifested even a sign, and before the empty kalpa itself—take it up well!
Once you have taken it up, then roll it inward and cherish it; let things proceed spontaneously, remaining as if a stump or as if dazed.
This is none other than a person of immeasurable capacity. If this is not yet the case, you must instead reflect back and turn the light within, whether in motion or stillness.
Whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, you must investigate the ultimate source before you can attain it.

Before your parents were born, and after they had given birth to you, your six sense organs and four great elements, along with your three hundred and sixty bones and joints, were fully formed. When cold, you knew cold;
when hot, you knew heat; when hungry, you knew hunger; when satiated, you knew satiety—extending from your head reaching toward heaven to your feet treading upon the earth.
All those who dwell upon this earth—those with teeth and those with hair—rely entirely upon this very power of grace. Now tell me, how does one turn toward this power of grace?
Do you know? A single breath speaks not, yet it contains all forms; where can the myriad spirits offer thanks for such impartiality?
Chan Master Wenshu Dao addressed the assembly upon his re-ordination as a monk: "I do not don the field-robes [of a layman], but wear the feathered garments [of an immortal].
My physical appearance is quite suited to that of the Old Lord (Laojun). For over a year and a half, I have reflected idly on this; in general, prosperity and decline each have their own time.

Our Buddha, the Tathāgata, foretold in advance that the Dharma would face difficulties; these are clearly recorded in the scriptures, so there is no one who does not know them. When calculating the years and eras, it is precisely..."
It is here that Māra finds his opportunity to confound the orthodox tradition. Monks alter their secular appearance; the Buddha’s name is changed;

false interpretations are fabricated; and the scriptural texts are edited and excised. Ritual bells are struck incessantly while the sound of the *ghaṇṭā* is silenced; begging bowls are made with extra bases. Through such manifold deceptions, they seek to mislead the Sagely Sovereign.
Fortunately, Your Majesty the Emperor, by virtue of your sagely merit and sagely wisdom, has not forgotten the sacred entrustment and has not permitted these practices to perish.

The Imperial Edict was specially bestowed, its divine calligraphy promulgated throughout the realm, and it was further permitted that monks and nuns might once again don their robes and shave their heads.

This is truly like cold ashes catching fire once more or withered wood flourishing anew. Without abandoning their secular forms, they have assumed the form of monastics; without departing from the realm of Māra, they have entered the realm of the Buddha.
The Dharma drum resounds once more, and the collapsing order is restored. Those who were lost in the wine of immortals now partake of the sweet dew and jade nectar.

The *Buxu Ci* (Verses on the Empty Walk) have been translated into the *Huanxiang Quzi* (Songs of Returning Home). Setting down the silver and wooden tablets, he picks up the *niśīdana* (sitting mat).
Yesterday morning there was bowing with hands clasped; today there is the greeting of *vaṃdanā* and the inquiry of well-being.
Only the old appearance has changed; the old person remains unchanged. I dare ask the assembly: Is this old person one, or is it two? After a long silence, he said: "The autumn wind."
The authorities, finding him difficult to manage, dispersed him; thus was the ash of the Way from those years blown away.

Later, during the reign of Emperor Gaozong, an imperial edict restored the status of monks and nuns throughout the empire, yet Master Daming Ying alone remained steadfast in his resolve not to change. This continued until the beginning of the Shaoxing era.
Rising at dawn, he donned a crown of birch bark and a crane-feather cloak; holding a ceremonial tablet of ivory and wearing vermilion shoes, he had the drum beaten to assemble the multitude.

Ascending the seat, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Orchids bloom in the spring valley, chrysanthemums flourish by the autumn fence; all things must surely experience their periods of flourishing and withering."

In the past, he disparaged the monks and nuns and devoted himself exclusively to the Way (Taoism). Later, upon the suppression of the Way and its sycophants, he restored the status of the monks and nuns.

He then asked, "As for the Way, how can one who has the form of a monk or nun [attain it]? He then took up a crown and showed it to the assembly, saying: "My head has always been as round as the full moon;
Though I wear this crown, my hair does not become immortal. Today I cast it down without obstruction; I release a divine light that pierces the azure sky. He then threw it away.

He stepped forward, exchanged his robes with the assembly, and then took up a crane-feather cloak (*he-chang*), saying: "In days of yore, the Tathāgata traded for a fur robe; for many years I have felt ashamed to wear this crane-feather cloak.
Return to me the garments of a manly tamer of men; you should know that this object is ill-suited. He cast it aside.

Then, raising a ceremonial tablet (*xiang-jian*), he said: "I was weary of the meditation board being so unreasonably stubborn; who would have thought it would be deceived by this ceremonial tablet? Today, because of..."
"Why do you suddenly let it go? You old retired immortal official of the whole world! He threw it down, picked up his vermilion shoes, and said: "Dharma carried one back with him;
from this day forth, sons and grandsons shall walk barefoot. Borrowing these vermilion shoes to substitute for hemp sandals—do not say that the times are difficult and hinder one's efforts.
To transform into a Peng bird before meeting its opportunity is no better than being a Kun; to paint a tiger and fail to complete it results in something resembling a dog. He threw them down.
He held his staff crosswise and said, "Today my staff has transformed into a dragon, splitting apart the tens of millions of peaks of Mount Hua.
He then leaned it against his shoulder and said, "Take care, O True Holy Sovereign with the Buddha-mind; may you well employ the virtue of Yao to revitalize our school.
He cast down the staff, closed his eyes, and passed away.

Chan Master Dahuì Gǎo was commanded by imperial decree to return to the monastic order. After offering his thanks for the grace and completing the incense offering to pray for the Emperor’s longevity, he took his seat and said:
“The blue felt mat is originally an object of our own house; today it is returned once more to the monk of old. How shall I repay this precious imperial grace?
A single branch of wisteria upon the ten-thousand-year-old pine. He then picked up his staff and said: “This single branch of wisteria is here.”
The inner meaning. Now, regarding the phrase "repaying kindness," how would you say it? If you can say it, then "Even grinding one's bones to powder would not suffice as recompense;
this single phrase, when clearly realized, transcends billions. If you have not yet reached this, I, this mountain monk, cannot help but reveal it for you all:
"I shall forever take the sun and moon as my celestial eyes, and point out Mount Sumeru as my mountain of longevity."
