Compiled by Xingyue of Loudong, Abbot of Lian’an Chan Monastery at Shiba Jian in Wulin.
The Outline for the National Memorial Service (Bao'en):
Chan Master Dahui Zonggao ascends the hall on the occasion of the Great Xiang (the anniversary of the Emperor Huizong’s passing). Having finished offering incense, he takes his seat and says:
The body arises from within the signless, just as various forms are produced by illusion. The mind-consciousness of the one who creates the illusion is fundamentally non-existent;
thus, both sin and merit are empty and have no place of abiding. Among the sages of antiquity, there were none who did not proceed from this state of non-abiding.
He brings sentient beings to maturity. In a state of non-abiding, he descends his spirit into the womb for ten months.
In a state of non-abiding, he manifests birth. In a state of non-abiding, he manifests walking seven steps.
In a state of non-abiding, he manifests dwelling in the royal palace. In a state of non-abiding, he manifests renouncing the world. In a state of non-abiding, he manifests...
He practices ascetic austerities. In a state of non-abiding, he manifests sitting beneath the Bodhi tree and attaining perfect enlightenment.

In a state of non-abiding, he manifests subduing the armies of Māra. In a state of non-abiding, he manifests sitting at the site of enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dharma, and delivering sentient beings.
In a state of non-abiding, he manifests bestowing the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon all bodhisattvas.

He received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Having performed the work of a Buddha while abiding nowhere, he manifested the entry into *parinirvāṇa* and addressed the great assembly, saying:
"Since the various sages of antiquity have all manifested in this manner, today I, the monk Zonggao, likewise preach the Dharma in this way;
I shall respectfully employ such a Dharma for the sake of Emperor Huizong, Sage of Virtuous Letters and Benevolent Deeds."

For Emperor Xianxiao and Empress Dowager Xiansu, to solemnize the celestial procession, we humbly pray that you do not abide in your own nature, but universally manifest the firm and dense body within the midst of the mundane world;
may you, like those noble beings, dwell in the ocean of inconceivable liberation. [Descend from the seat.]
Chan Master Tianmu ascended the hall after the Emperor Huizong had passed away and said: "The stars, the sun, and the moon assist the celestial vault;

Encompassing the earth’s boundaries, all is already in great harmony. The twelve jade towers have long since vanished of their own accord; Mountains and rivers remain forever within the bright moonlight."
Chan Master Xiaoyin Yun delivered a formal address upon the conclusion of the recitation of the Tripitaka for the anniversary of the late Emperor Wen’s passing.
"Venerable and unsurpassed, he transcends the primordial state beyond the Celestial Sovereign; noble and beyond naming, he sits at the summit of Vairocana.
In his essence, he encompasses the ten voids; in his function, he includes all myriad things—like the moon reflected in all waters."
There is no distinction between the pure and the defiled; spring resides within the hundred flowers. One does not perceive the marks of the orthodox or the biased;
wondrous existence is non-existence, and true emptiness is non-emptiness. Thus it is said: "The realms of infinite lands do not separate self and other by even a hair’s breadth;
ten ages of past and present, from beginning to end, do not depart from the present moment. One casts the great trichiliocosm beyond the four quarters and contains Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed.

Within this, one may perceive it. Thus, one sees Emperor Wenzong: formerly manifesting from the Buddha-ground in a royal palace, he governed the state and brought peace and stability to the imperial house.
Once his work of transformation and guidance was complete, he returned once more to the rank of Buddha.

Silent and unmoving, his wisdom universally responds throughout the ten directions; vast and impartial, his transformation has already encompassed the sands of all worlds. I, the monk, offer praise in this manner.
"Yang! Tell me, does this accord with the Sage’s intent or not? After a long silence, he said: "The celestial fragrance of the *utpala* flower blows on without ceasing;
again descending from Tuṣita to Jambudvīpa. He then spoke a verse: "The Buddha-mind awakens and illuminates, wondrously leaving nothing behind;

It encompasses heaven and earth, the pivot of transformation. Responding to myriad occasions, it is ever vivid and clear; In the Great Samādhi of the Nāga, it is as it is, just so. The three thousand [worlds]..."

Within the Vairocana-receptacle of the ocean of lands, there are ten billion mountains, rivers, and Indra’s net jewels; may you not forget the power of your compassionate wisdom, and once again open the sun of insight to illuminate the dark alleys of the world.

On the day of the memorial service for the Sage, concluding the offering of the Tripitaka, he ascended the hall and said: "Overturning the precious treasury, one does not involve oneself in verbal explanations; suddenly awakening to the King of Sutras, how could one be constrained by words?

Therefore it is said: 'In the state of a sage, one is the same as a sage; in the state of an ordinary person, one is the same as an ordinary person; in the state of a deva, one is the same as a deva; in the state of a human, one is the same as a human.
Dust mote by dust mote, world-system by world-system, thought-moment by thought-moment—it is thus. Without moving so much as a hair’s breadth of a mind of cultivation or realization."

One transcends directly and enters the stage of the Tathāgata. If all people can peruse this work in such a manner, they may then ascend to receive the divine presence of Emperor Wenzong, rein in their steeds at the wondrous field of Perfect Enlightenment (*Samantabhadra*), sport within the great ocean of the Flower Treasury (*Avataṃsaka*), and abide in the realm of the Buddha.

They share in the Buddha’s enjoyment. Or, manifesting a thousand, ten thousand, or a hundred million bodies, they cause the various capacities of the four classes of sages and the six realms of ordinary beings to converge together.

Or, appearing in the thirty-two transformations, their wondrous functions are fully revealed throughout lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Thus, they protect our nation and bring blessings to our people;
their merit is so great it cannot be repaid, and their kindness is so vast it is difficult to requite. At such a time as this, let us offer a single phrase in honor of the deceased.
"How would you say it? After a long silence, he said: "The void can be measured, the wind can be bound; none can fully describe the Buddha’s merit.
He then cited Emperor Wu of Liang, who invited the Great Master Fu to lecture on the sutras. The Master struck his ruler once and descended from the seat. The Teacher said:
"At this Dharma assembly, dragons and elephants listen as the teaching is fully upheld; why did the Great Master trouble himself to strike the ruler? Truth and convention are merged like..."

There is transformation; when ruler and minister are in accord through the Way, there is naturally non-action. Blown by the wind and scorched by the sun, the Vairocana-realm is revealed; the chirping of magpies and the cawing of crows are the mechanisms of all Buddhas.
At the Dragon Flower Assembly of the three gatherings, all gaze upward with longing; when will we return from the human and celestial realms?

On the day of the memorial service for the Sage’s passing, the Tripitaka was formally concluded. Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: “Śākyamuni Tathāgata appeared in the world for the sake of one great cause and condition.
For forty-nine years, he proclaimed the True Dharma to transform and guide all living beings.

Upon reaching the assembly at the Lotus Sūtra, he bestowed predictions of Buddhahood upon his disciples; only then did he fully realize his original intent. Thereafter, he entered parinirvāṇa to manifest the ritual of his transformation.”
That he has reached this consummation is like our Emperor Wenzong, who mounted the wheel of the Buddha’s vows to succeed to the imperial orthodox line.
With his spiritual pivot operating in secret, he cleared away the borders of demonic afflictions; with the precious seal fully raised, he inherited the divine regalia of his ancestors.

He repeatedly practiced righteousness and yielded his place to others, widely disseminating benevolence and compassion. His ministers served him with loyalty, establishing great achievements comparable to those of Yi Yin and Lü Shang;

he succeeded to the throne as a sage-king, attaining a state of perfect governance like that of Yao and Shun. The eight regions of the world submitted to his virtue, and the myriad states rejoiced in their occupations.

Yet, he has suddenly abandoned his ministers and subjects to return once more to the rank of a Buddha. Her Majesty the Empress Dowager has dispatched envoys to bestow gold and silk for the purpose of examining and reading the texts of the Great Tripitaka.

Above, they support the Imperial Chariot; the Buddha’s transformation and the King’s transformation both accord with a single principle. The Golden Wheel and the Dharma Wheel turn together at the pivot of the Way.
Within the tip of a single hair, the Jewel-King Realm is manifested; it is perfectly accomplished right where it is. By breaking open a single atom, a great scripture emerges.
Expounding in accordance with the nature of reality: in seeing form, every instance is Maitreya; in hearing sound, every place is Avalokiteśvara.
Mañjuśrī, through non-discriminative wisdom, manifests differentiated bodies; Samantabhadra, within differentiated objects, enters non-discriminative samādhi.
In every land there is spontaneous meditative absorption; in every particle of dust, there is the natural state of dhyāna. Where is there that is not thus?
“Where has the Perfectly Enlightened One not turned the Great Dharma Wheel? Where has he not transformed and guided sentient beings? Where has he not entered Parinirvāṇa?
And what merit has not been attained? What kindness has not been requited? Such proclamations are still but discourses on the unfolding of the vehicles of teaching.
As for that single phrase which does not fall into the mechanisms of the profound and mysterious—how shall it be revealed? Truly, it is excellent!

Jiuyun said: "The meritorious achievements of the late Emperor shall endure for eternity; may his holy descendants rule for ten million years. Furthermore, he recounted how the King of East India once invited Venerable Prajñātāra to a vegetarian feast.
During the meal, the King asked, "While the assembly of monks is reading the sutras, for what reason does the Venerable One not read?
The Venerable replied, "In my entrying breath, I do not dwell within the realms of the five aggregates; in my exiting breath, I do not involve myself with the myriad phenomena."

Conditioned phenomena. This sutra is constantly being turned in hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions, and billions of scrolls—not merely one or two scrolls. The Master’s verse says: "This sutra is constantly turned in hundreds of thousands of scrolls;
Transcending sages and surpassing ordinary folk, it spans from antiquity to the present.

The vermilion phoenix naturally dwells in the arched pavilion; How could the clear pool fear the coiled dragon’s roar? The Yangtze, Yellow, Huai, and Ji rivers all return to the sea; Hairpins, bracelets, vases, and basins are all one."
One Gold Coin. Even with a tongue as vast and long as space, one could never fully proclaim the profound depth of the Sage’s grace.
On the first anniversary of the passing of the late Emperor Yijong, Chan Master Hongjue Man ascended the seat and said: "The curtains hang at the yellow gate; the purple silk canopy is drawn shut.
His majesty is supreme and noble, yet he has not yet reached the present moment. You must know that there is another person above this, who wanders in leisure."
Traversing the path of birds, he waves his hand and departs from the profound way. Blending his traces among the common folk, let him leave behind his magnificent crown;

concealing himself within the charcoal, let the jewel palace be at the mercy of moss growth. Nevertheless, though he does not maintain a fixed position, the nine provinces and the four seas all receive his majestic spirit;
though he does not guard a great achievement, the entire earth and the heavens beneath all partake in the power of his grace. Thus it is said: "There is..."
The substance precedes heaven and earth; formless, it is fundamentally silent and vast. It can act as the sovereign of the myriad phenomena, yet it does not wither along with the four seasons.
Since it does not wither with the four seasons, tell me: how does this person now pay homage?
Following conditions, one observes with ease; where could one not be honored?

In the first year of the Jiàngzhōng Jìngguó era, when the Empress Dowager passed away, Chan Master Fórì Yuè was commanded by imperial decree to ascend the seat at Wéndé Hall together with the Elder of Liùchán Monastery.
He then said: "The one who preaches the Dharma at the beginning does not know the final phrase;
the one who preaches the Dharma at the end does not know the initial phrase. As for the initial phrase, it was just now [spoken] by Chan Master Huílín."
I have already spoken for all of you. Though I have spoken, how shall I speak of the final word?

If one relies upon the Three Vehicles, the twelve divisions of the teachings, the partial and the complete, the sudden and the gradual, or the half and the full within the single voice of the Buddha, one cannot avoid mistaking the pointing finger for the moon.
Entering the sea to count its sands is like the moon’s reflection in a clear pool or the sound of a bell at the dead of night:
it emits sound according to what strikes it and follows the waves without dispersing. Yet this remains a matter of the shore of birth and death.

Therefore, Bodhidharma observed the signs and saw that the land of China possessed the capacity for the Mahayana; thus he floated his cup across the thousand-fold surging waves and ascended ten thousand layers of mountains. At the outset—

He established the Liang dynasty. The Emperor of Liang posed inquiries concerning the conditioned phenomena of cause and effect; Bodhidharma responded by revealing the ultimate truth of the Noble Truths.
As the Emperor failed to grasp this, he departed for Mount Song and Mount Shao, where for nine years he sat facing a wall, eschewing written words.
Transcending the three vehicles, he pointed directly at the human mind, asserting that to see one's nature is to become a Buddha. At that time, the Second Patriarch, Shen Guang, stood...

Xuefeng severed his arm; he attained the marrow and clarified the mind. One flower and five petals; the fruit ripened of its own accord. The robe was transmitted through six generations, and later followers attained the Way.
From this point on, the people of Donghua finally believed that there exists the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the wondrous mind of Nirvana.

Among those of middling and inferior capacity, delusion and awakening were equally divided. It is known with certainty that this matter cannot be realized unless one possesses great roots and a great vessel. How so?
For this reason, when one perceives, hears, senses, or cognizes these dharmas, those dharmas are themselves apart from seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing.

Consequently, a mass of fire stands at the fork in the road and iron mountains block the path; naturally, before the peak of Shaoshi, there are cliffs standing ten thousand fathoms high, and along the road of Caoxi, not even a drop of water can pass through.
Amidst this, the ancestral wind has not failed to decline, and the collapsing framework is likewise about to lie prostrate upon the earth. Nevertheless...
Thus it is. The Dharma has no fixed characteristics; the Way relies upon temporal chapters to erect the great banner of the Dharma and expound the great meaning of the Dharma.

This great causal nexus for a single great event arises to benefit and bring joy to sentient beings—not at any other time, but only when one encounters the convergence of the thousand Buddhas before and after, knowing this today.
Fortunately, a Great Sage has now appeared in the world, widely disseminating [the teaching] so that it pervades the sands of the Ganges.

This realm is truly a rare encounter once in a thousand years. As for the likes of Yao, Shun, Yu, and Tang, they sat upright with robes trailing on the ground, and through their non-action, their transformative influence reached everywhere.
Yet, when it comes to opening the gate of skillful means and revealing the true aspect, this is a magnificent assembly from the ten directions.
The four assemblies gathered together to extend the ancestral style of the ancient Buddhas and to manifest the fundamental source of all living beings;

this cannot be discussed as being on the same level as what occurs today. Why is this so? When Śakra-devānām-indra and Subhūti elucidated the Prajñāpāramitā, they stopped at ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
When King Prasenajit spoke to Ānanda, he specifically pointed to the non-transiency [of phenomena], which still remained within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). It is only here...

The separate transmission outside the teachings, that ultimate point beyond the ordinary—its manifestation in the present day is surely a rare and auspicious occasion, one that ought to take place here in China.
Yet, while the streams and mountains differ, the clouds and moon are the same.

Like voices responding to one another and essences seeking their kin, we now know that this matter is neither ancient nor modern, neither there nor here. It is loftily unsurpassed and vast beyond limit—a profound abyss.
Yet it has no bottom; its depth is unfathomable. A single hair swallows the vast ocean; a mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru.
Among the heavens, it is identical with heaven; among humans, it is identical with humanity. In the heavens, it becomes the sun and the moon, providing illumination and clarity.

Among humans, it becomes the ruler and the minister, embodying loyalty and filial piety. By extending this principle, one understands the ten billion suns and moons, the ten billion Mount Sumerus, and the ten billion four...
The great ocean, the fundamental body, and the vessel-world—the sentient and the insentient—are of one and the same essence.
It is not that the benevolent who see it call it benevolence, nor that the wise who see it call it wisdom; rather, the common people use it daily without knowing it.
Is there anyone other than the Sage who can unify all phenomena within themselves? From this, lamp follows lamp in a continuous flame, and leaf follows leaf in mutual succession.

For a hundred thousand lifetimes, the moon-like lamp of wisdom has shone, its light harmonizing with the three realms; for a hundred thousand *li*, the stars are arrayed along the ancestral trunk, providing cool shade for the four modes of birth.
Thus we know that the Wheel of Dharma has turned again in China, and the Sun of the Emperor shines eternally upon Zhendan.

From this it is clear that the Dharma knows no distinction of great or small, and things have no preference of near or far; all are enveloped by its light, and all receive its bounty. To such an extent...

From grasses, trees, birds, and fish, there is none too distant that does not reach [this state]. It is just like the King of Śrāvastī, who, wishing to go to Vulture Peak to see the Buddha, commanded his ministers and officials:
"The mountains, rivers, the great earth, the grasses, trees, and forests must all go together to see him.
If even a single blade of grass or a single tree does not go, I shall not see the Buddha. O Great Assembly, within the present heavens and earth, throughout the universe—

In this very interval, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the grasses, trees, and forests—neither going nor coming, profoundly still and impartial, towering and unmoving—are both civil and martial, both Chan and Vinaya.
They all stand together before the Hall of Compassionate Virtue in the Ninefold Heavens, seeing the Buddha at one and the same time. Friends, it is not that you do not see; but how do you see? Truly.
Jiuyun said: "His double pupils shine with the inexhaustible light of the sun and moon; his prominent nose possesses the superlative beauty of the mountains and rivers.
Imperial Edict: At the request of the Empress Dowager, who has recently passed away, Chan Master Qingyin shall expound the Dharma in the Cide Hall on the fifth and seventh days of mourning."
After the exchange of questions and answers upon ascending the seat, he said: "Just now, Zen Master Jingyin said, 'The one who preaches the Dharma at the beginning does not know the final phrase;
the one who preaches the Dharma at the end does not know the initial phrase.

I, this humble monk, shall now preach the Dharma at the end, yet for the sake of the late Empress Dowager Daheng, I shall expound the initial phrase. Do you understand? The spiritual source is limpid and still."

All things and the self are identical in their suchness; the Buddha’s nature is true and authentic. Holy ones and ordinary beings share the same essence, pervading the ages and penetrating the vast void.
Fundamentally devoid of coming and going, how could there ever be arising or ceasing? Today, humans and devas meet; the realms of the hidden and the manifest are all present.
The imperial breeze blows gently in harmony with spring; the sun of the Emperor lingers long to nourish all creatures. The Ten-Thousand Chariots are now ascending the hall of Shun. Six...

The Zen school looks up to the sky of Yao; for the sake of the Empress Dowager, this Dharma assembly is established. Pointing to the heart of the ancient Buddhas and opening the eye of the True Dharma, if one can perceive it here:
within the vermilion towers and jade palaces, the pure Dharmakāya manifests in successive layers;

throughout the golden gates and jeweled ponds, the original face is revealed everywhere. Only Buddha and Buddha realize and know this together. I humbly pray that you will hold yourself in high esteem.
**The Outline for the Prayer for Fine Weather by Chan Master Tiantong Pu.** Praying for Fine Weather: Entering the Hall. Long rains have not ceased; one is half-asleep, half-awake.

This may be called heaven and earth harmonizing their virtue, the sun and moon harmonizing their brilliance, the four seasons harmonizing their order, and the ghosts and spirits harmonizing their auspiciousness and misfortune.

He then shouted, "Stop! Stop! The inner trigram is already formed; you seek yet another outer image. He planted his staff firmly and said, "Just now you cast *Leitian Dazhuang* (Thunder in Heaven, Great Strength);
now it has transformed into *Dihuo Mingyi* (Earth Fire, Obscuration)."
Chan Master Xueyan Qin ascended the hall to pray for clear weather. "It has not been sunny for a long time; it has soaked and rotted the nostrils of the patch-robed monks.
He asked, "What are the nostrils of a patch-robed monk? "The floating clouds have dispersed and the azure sky is vast; the brilliant golden basin surges from within the sea."
Chan Master Gaofeng Miao ascended the hall to pray for clear weather. "The celestial gate has been locked for long and will not open; day and night, torrential rain beats down with black winds.
Striking the meditation seat once with his whisk, he said: "With a single blow of the staff in a fit of indignation, it is all shattered to pieces;
from the crown of the head, a red orb bursts forth."
Chan Master Zhantang Zhun ascended the hall to pray for clear weather and issued this notice: "The long rain has not ceased;
it has reached the point where black clouds gather thickly atop Mount Wulao and white waves surge to the heavens within Lake Dongting. Great Master Yunmen could no longer restrain his impatience."
He burned incense inside the Buddha hall, joined his palms at the triple gate, and offered this prayer:
"May the Stone Woman of Huangmei give birth to a son; may mother and child be reunited. May the hornless iron ox of Shaoshi always find sweet water and grass.
With a shout, he said, "What connection is there? Looking at the assembly, he remarked, "Were it not for Yang Deyi, who would have seen Ma Xiangru?"
The Outline for the Prayer for Rain by Chan Master Yuanwu Qin. Entering the hall for the prayer for rain: On the path of Caoxi, heaven is high and earth is deep;
before the peak of Shaoshi, the land is vast and people are few. Sitting alone and upright, cold and desolate; stretching out across the great wilds, the wind whistles. [His] eyes—
To see it is to go blind; to hear it with the ears is to go deaf; to speak it with the mouth is to go mute. And yet, it does not emerge from the tip of a single hair.
It contains and exhales the ten directions of emptiness, without front or back. Since this is so, possessing such spiritual powers and such functional activity, why do you remain so dry and arid?
When a carp of the Eastern Sea is struck with a blow, it busily covers the earth and immediately becomes a rain-cloud.
Chan Master Yuan of Longmen ascended the hall when Governor Zeng Gongsheren entered the mountains to pray for rain.

He raised the case where Official Liu Yu asked Yunju, "From where does the rain come? Yunju replied, "It comes from where Official Liu asks. The Master said, "As for where the rain comes from, there is no need to seek it out;
it fills the void and rescues all that is withered and parched. It is surely a wondrous, responsive, and numinous manifestation."
[The Master] said, "Understood. You, Prefectural Secretary, have come here as one who truly brings rain and dews; there is none who does not rejoice and welcome this.

Now I ask you all: Is this the rain of certainty and clarity? Is it the rain of the Secretary? Or is it the rain of the common people? Can you determine which it is? After a long silence, [the Master continued]:
Zhuo struck his staff once and said, "Three. He then descended from the seat.
Chan Master Zhenjing Wen addressed the assembly regarding prayers for rain, saying: "A lion does not eat the remains left by a vulture;
a swift falcon does not strike a rabbit lying down. Let loose the great dragon of Linji; pull out Yunmen’s single glance. He then held up his staff and said, "The Dragon..."
When it rained, the three types of grass and two types of trees flourished.
Chan Master Daowei Tai of Dayu Monastery ascended the hall to pray for rain, saying: "The fire clouds scorch the field crops; the springs have ceased their flow.
The Great Dragon King Sāgara—where might he be? He struck the meditation seat with his staff and said: "He is right here! Look!"

"Look! Clouds rise from the Southern Mountain; rain falls upon the Northern Mountain. I, the old monk, shall further add the sound of a thunderclap to help spread this majestic brilliance far and wide.
Then, he cried out in a loud voice: "Chaos! Chaos!"
Chan Master Shiwu Hong ascended the hall to pray for rain, saying: "I recall last year in the fifth month, when fire-clouds scorched the fields and heaven sent no rain.

9. Chan Master Shuzhong Yun ascends the hall on the Buddha’s Birthday: "The bright pearl is in the palm; it divides its luster according to the various colors.

Spouting water to bathe his golden body; the earth surges forth golden lotuses to cradle his two feet. To those who say he has no pupils in his eyes, I say I am merely deceiving the common folk.
To those who say there is no blood beneath his skin, I say I am using shrimp to catch turtles. He plants his staff:

For three copper coins he married a dark old woman; she does not comb her hair nor wash her face—know you whether she is a commoner or a sage?

Examining this from the perspective of the future, what a fine man indeed! Is there anyone present now who can surpass Śākyamuni and leap over Maitreya?

If there were, they too would deserve thirty blows. Having completed the dedication of merit, he spoke again: "The Tuṣita Heaven palace is not a place of leisurely joy; I have instead come to be born here."
This is the suffering of Sahā. Pointing to heaven, pointing to earth—what business is that? It only adds to the turmoil and commotion of the monastic groves.
Stolid and blunt; simple and harmonious. A tree without shadow for a thousand years; a shoe without a bottom in these times.
Chan Master Nan Shiyou’s Hall Discourse on the Buddha’s Birthday: Chan Master Dongshan Wuzu Yan was once asked by a monk, "What is the place where all Buddhas emerge?

"He too deserves thirty blows. Where the Old Śākyamuni passed, Original Awakening surely knows it of itself;

Pure as empty space—where would you all go to apply even one or two ladles?

To act as a substitute for one’s descendants by taking the first bite while they peck at the shell—those who are not true men are all drenched with foul water.

who is the one who repays kindness when one gives up their own body only to receive another? [He strikes the whisk and descends from his seat.]
On the eighth day of the fourth month, Chan Master Miyun Wu ascended the hall and said: "A single cry at birth alone makes one supreme;

When he declared, "In the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am honored"—was this not Śākyamuni?
Since he is indeed Śākyamuni, where is Śākyamuni right now? If you say he is not Śākyamuni, then where is Śākyamuni?
[He] strikes the meditation staff and says: "The wind carries wild clouds back to the azure cavern;

Why, then, did Yunmen insist on beating him to death with a staff and feeding him to a dog? Householder!
Fatty soil produces filial sons; a state achieves hegemony through strategic ministers.

This is that which distinguishes dragons from snakes throughout antiquity and the present, forging the ordinary from the sage, discerning the heterodox from the orthodox, and analyzing the black from the white.
This is a fundamental and great pivot. Those who have penetrated it may act in this way, they may act otherwise, or they may act both ways—everything is permissible.
Those who have not yet penetrated it cannot act in this way, they cannot act otherwise, and they cannot act both ways—nothing is permissible.
Therefore, one who studies the Way must be an iron man; as soon as it touches his heart-mind, he makes the judgment.

Directly advance toward unsurpassed Bodhi. Do not concern yourself with any right or wrong. Since you do not concern yourself with any right or wrong, you do not concern yourself with whether one is ordinary or holy;
you do not concern yourself with whether it be Buddha or Māra; you do not concern yourself with whether it be ancient or modern; you do not concern yourself with whether it be that or this.
Charge straight ahead and enter directly, disregarding danger or ruin. Exerting valor and striving for precedence, seize whatever opportunity presents itself and employ it immediately.
It is not an obstacle that at times he manifests as ordinary beings or sages; at times he appears as Buddhas or demons; at times he cites the ancients or the present;
and at times he distinguishes between "that" and "this. Yet, for the time being, neither sages nor ordinary beings can confine him;
neither Buddhas nor demons can bind him; neither the past nor the present can measure him; and neither "this" nor "that" can accommodate him. Only then, at every turn...
In its application, one encounters the source from both left and right. One may freely call it ordinary, or call it sage; call it Buddha, or call it Mara;
call it ancient, or call it present; call it that, or call it this.
Pervading every atom and every land, it attains the wondrous as it flows with the current. This matter is a matter beyond measure; the person must be a person beyond measure.
If one is an overqualified person, they know their own overqualification.
Today, on the anniversary of the birth of Old Śākyamuni, although this mountain monk stands head and shoulders above him, I dare not bury even a single bit of that old fellow.

If you could truly see the face of this Old Man, then Linji’s Three Mysteries and Three Essentials, as well as Dongshan’s Five Ranks, would all be contained therein.
The sovereign and his ministers are also within this. Yunmen’s "one arrow through three barriers" is also within this.
Baizhang Huaiyang’s ninety-six circular diagrams are also within this. Fayan’s "there is no dharma outside the mind" is also within this.
Since all of these are entirely within this, why did that lame monk want to strike them dead with a single blow and feed them to a dog? [He] suddenly picked up [his staff].
Holding his staff, he does not avoid the sparks flying from the furnace; when speaking, he does not fear having his tongue cut out.

This staff—today it has fallen into the hands of this mountain monk. For now, I shall carry it on my shoulder. (He strikes the ground with his staff.
Iron oxen, pair by pair, with golden horns; wooden horses, twin by twin, with white jade hooves.

From antiquity to the present, how many great spiritual friends have sat upon the curved wooden bed? On the eighth day of the fourth month, they all play with the little old man Gautama."
As for the foul stench of the arrows, there is indeed a distinction. Have you ever dreamed of Gautama’s teacher?
If you can distinguish the black from the white here, it matters not whether you have shaved your head or not; you will not have come in vain to Baolin.

"Thus it is. One person is not thus. We have arrived together at Baoen; tell me, which one would you keep?
There are some fellows who say that a wise host accepts neither the Goddess of Fortune nor the Woman of Darkness.
Such a person as this is exactly the kind who should be seized and beaten three thousand times in the morning and eight hundred times in the evening. Why? Because the great ocean..."
[The Master] did not accept it. [If he had,] the hundred rivers would have flowed backward.
At the end of Master Ziji Chan’s discourse on the Buddha’s birth, having finished citing the story of the World-Honored One’s first appearance in the world, the Master said:
"All the venerable masters of past and present have said that Yunmen’s words are extraordinary, claiming they mean: 'To offer this body and mind to every dust mote and land.'"
This is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness. If we examine it according to Dongming today, both the great and small Yunmen possess only a single eye.
Why? Because they merely look ahead and fail to reflect upon what lies behind.
Today at dawn, Dongming rose at the fifth watch, burned a stick of incense, offered a cup of water, and recited the name of Śākyamuni Tathāgata three times.
Again, I spread out my sitting mat and performed nine prostrations. This was neither for a specific occasion or festival, nor was it to repay virtue or requite kindness.
Let those who possess the eye that discerns the Dharma try to examine this for me, both monastics and laypeople alike.
On the morning of the Buddha-Bathing Festival, Chan Master Chaosong ascended the hall. Within Amitābha Temple, Śākyamuni was born;

at the firm request of both monastics and laypeople, he ascended the high Dharma seat. All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas bowed their heads in unison; the defiled lands and pure lands were equalized as one path.
Thus, he took seven steps and looked around, pointing to heaven and pointing to earth to proclaim his supremacy. The Tathāgata appeared.

World, do not engage in other matters. Within the vast emptiness and the great earth, there is no other person. Great assembly, recognize the meaning at the tip of the hook; do not mistake it for the fixed weight on a scale.

Siding with Yunmen, [Tiantong] would strike him dead with a single blow of the staff. To covet another’s fragrant bait and fall for another’s hook—such is Tiantong’s judgment.

Although he is indeed beating the drum to match the tune of his guest, it is still like feasting heartily while facing a butcher’s door. Yet, since this is a celebration and praise offered on account of the meal, [I shall speak thus].

as for Yunmen’s single blow—tell me, did it kill him or not? If it killed him,"

On the Buddha’s Day of Enlightenment, Chan Master Xueyan Qin gave a formal discourse on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month. "The Yellow-Faced Old Man labored for six years until he found his own nostrils, yet he lost his eyesight.
Tell me, where did it end up? In the midnight snow mountains, a single star in the sky."
The Buddha ascends the hall after attaining the Way. The Way is fundamentally formless and fundamentally nameless. Since its destruction has never been heard of, how could there be its attainment?
You "Yellow-Faced Barbarian," you ought not to fabricate such demonic and grotesque things.

Pointing out a single star at midnight, you have brought misfortune upon your descendants of later generations, all of whom are merely feeding on dregs and drinking diluted wine. Vague and indistinct, they remain in a drunken dream to this day. As for me, the mountain monk...
This staff—let me not fail to open another eye for you all. It makes one cry of a golden cock announcing dawn.
(He strikes the ground with the staff. "The red sun rises in the heavens, and the ten thousand lands are bright."

at that time, how could his eyes have ever opened? Only when he truly saw the morning star appear did he realize that before reaching this gate, the courtyard was as cold as ash."
Chan Master Yancui Wen ascended the hall at Focheng Monastery and said: "Mistake! Mistake! Six years of binding oneself with straw ropes were all in vain;

when the eyes are opened, the heavens are wide awake. The heavens and earth of past, present, and future; the sun and moon of past, present, and future; the stars and constellations of past, present, and future."
He patted his knee and said: "The sword has long since gone; one must strictly avoid marking the boat.

Because rewards go to those who have merit."

The pearl remains even unto this day, yet it has turned into mere idle talk. Before Vulture Peak, the morning star shines brilliantly;

With his single sandal returning to the West, he lost his own wretched life. "I originally came to this land"—he lost that too. No? No! He has not lost it. Why? Because he was already here before he came. If you can see it thus, you will know that the Patriarch’s coming and going were both like a dream. Having attained great liberation and exercised great supernormal powers, he held a golden staff in his hand and supported a dragon bowl in his palm; he went to the gates of hell and stood there in solemn contemplation, whereupon he beheld—
The compassionate mother wept immeasurably; this was the filial piety of Maudgalyāyana.
But what is the filial piety of Xinghua? After a long silence, he said: "Today Xinghua does not ascend to heaven, nor does he enter hell.
In the Hall of Good Dharma, upon the Lion Throne of King Lamp, I shall preach the Dharma for my mother to repay her labors. Now tell me, where is my mother right now?
[The Master] said, "Where? My mother had sufficient roots of goodness during her life; there is no need to trouble the Buddha, for she has certainly been reborn in heaven.
Among humans, a long life is rare in all ages; ninety years is already one year short. [Having finished speaking, he] descended from his seat.

I venture to trouble the assembly to burn a single stick of incense to assist this mountain monk in repaying my filial debt. Since she was the mother of this mountain monk, why then do you trouble yourselves?"

A person burns incense, yet does not see the Way. When a member of the eastern household dies, the members of the western household join in their mourning, beating their breasts with their hands and crying out, "Heaven! Heaven!"

The Outline for the Five Visits (Zhuchi ○ The outline for the five visits consists only of a collection from various records of the *Chandeng*; the rest are so vast that they cannot be fully recorded here).
The Great Master Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch, ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying: "All you good friends, each of you should purify your mind."
Listen to my teaching of the Dharma. You all, people of this world, your own minds are the Buddha; do not harbor further doubt. There is not a single thing externally that can be established;
all are the myriad phenomena produced by the fundamental mind. Therefore, a sutra says: "When the mind arises, the myriad phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, the myriad phenomena cease.
If you wish to achieve the wisdom of all modes (sarvajñā), you must attain the samādhi of the single characteristic. One...
Practicing samādhi: if, in all places, one does not dwell upon signs, and within those signs neither gives rise to aversion nor attachment, and is without grasping or rejecting;
if one does not contemplate matters such as benefit or ruin, success or failure, but remains at ease, tranquil, empty, harmonious, and serene—this is called the Samādhi of One Mark.
If, in all places—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—one maintains a purely straightforward mind without wavering.
The site of enlightenment is truly the Pure Land; it is called the Samādhi of Single Practice. If a person possesses these two samādhis, it is like the earth having seeds:
it can contain and nurture them until their fruit is brought to fruition. A single mark and a single practice are also like this.
My preaching of the Dharma now is like a timely rain, universally moistening the great earth; your Buddha-nature is like various seeds, which, upon encountering this—
When moistened and saturated, all things are able to sprout and grow. Those who receive my intent will certainly attain *bodhi*; those who follow my practice will surely realize the wondrous fruit.
National Teacher Zhong of Nanyang ascended the hall and said: "Students of the Chan school should follow the Buddha’s words; the definitive meaning of the One Vehicle accords with [reality]."
Those who do not understand the source of their own minds will not grant each other’s validity, like parasites within a lion’s body.

Now, if one who serves as a teacher for others pursues fame and profit or opens up heterodox paths, what benefit is there for oneself or others? It is like a master craftsman whose axe and adze do not injure his hands;
or like the load carried by a fragrant elephant, which a donkey cannot endure.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The green vines wind their way straight up to the crest of the cold pine; the white clouds drift lazily, appearing and disappearing within the vast void.
All phenomena are fundamentally at rest, yet it is people themselves who create the clamor."
The Master was engaged in debate with the Imperial Attendant Zilin. As the Master ascended the seat, the Attendant said, "I request that you establish a thesis;
I shall refute it. The Master replied, "The thesis has already been established. The Attendant asked, "What is this thesis? The Master said, "Indeed, you do not see it.
It is not within your realm. Thereupon, he descended from the seat.
Chan Master Si of Nanyue addressed the assembly, saying: "The source of the Way is not far; the ocean of nature is not remote. Simply seek it within yourself; do not look for it elsewhere.
If you seek it, you will not find it; even if you were to find it, it would not be real."
The Ancient Buddha Koubing ascended the hall. As the fourfold assembly gathered like clouds, he asked, "What shall this old monk say? and immediately descended from the seat.
Master Mazu Daoyi ascended the hall and said, "All of you, believe that your own mind is the Buddha; this very mind is the Buddha-mind.
The Great Master Bodhidharma came from Southern India to China to transmit the One Vehicle of the Supreme Teaching."
The Dharma of the mind is intended to bring you all to awakening. Furthermore, I cite the text of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to seal the ground of the minds of sentient beings.
Fearing that you might be deluded and lack self-confidence regarding this Dharma of the One Mind—which each and every one of you possesses—the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* [states]:

Taking the Heart of the Buddha’s Words as the fundamental principle, and having no gate as the Dharma-gate: those who seek the Dharma should have nothing to seek. Outside the mind there is no separate Buddha;
outside the Buddha there is no separate mind. Do not grasp at good, do not abandon evil. Do not rely upon either of the two extremes of purity or defilement.
Realize that the nature of sin is empty and cannot be apprehended in every thought-moment, because it lacks intrinsic nature. Therefore, the triple world is only...
The mind encompasses the myriad phenomena; it is the seal of the single Dharma. Whatever forms you perceive are all perceptions of the mind.

The mind does not exist as a mind in itself; it exists because of form. You need only speak in accordance with the occasion, whether dealing with phenomena or principles, and there will be no obstruction whatsoever.
The path and fruit of Bodhi are likewise thus. That which arises within the mind is immediately termed "form" (*rūpa*); because one knows form to be empty, arising is itself non-arising.
If one realizes this meaning, then one may, according to the occasion, put on robes and eat food, thereby nourishing the holy embryo.
Time passed naturally; what further matters were there?

Chan Master Baizhang Hai ascended the hall and said: "The numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects. Its essence reveals the true and eternal, unconstrained by words and letters.
The nature of mind is undefiled, fundamentally perfected from the beginning. Simply by detaching from delusive conditions, one is the Buddha of Suchness."

Chan Master Banshan Ji addressed the assembly from the high seat: "If the mind is free from affairs, the myriad dharmas do not arise. If the intellect is cut off from subtle mechanisms, even a speck of dust has no place to stand.
The Way is fundamentally without substance; it is because of substance that a name is established. The Way is fundamentally without name; it is because of the name that a designation is obtained.
If one says 'this very mind is Buddha,' one has not yet entered the profound mystery of the present age. If one says 'neither mind nor Buddha,' it is still..."
This refers to the ultimate trace and the path beyond, which not even a thousand sages have transmitted. Students exhaust themselves, like a monkey grasping at a reflection in the water.

[He ascended the hall: "Now, the moon of the mind is solitary and perfect; its light swallows the ten thousand phenomena. The light does not illuminate objects, nor do objects exist as such. The light...
When both object and subject have vanished, what further thing could there be? Zen Master, it is like throwing a sword into the air; one need not discuss whether it reaches its mark or not.

This is the traceless whirling of the void, where the edge of the blade remains unimpaired. If you can thus maintain a mind-moment after mind-moment free from cognition, then the total mind is the Buddha, and the total Buddha is the person.
When person and Buddha are without distinction, only then does one truly enter the Way.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The virtue of Chan can be cultivated within this very practice. It is like the earth supporting a mountain, unaware of the mountain’s towering loftiness;
or like a stone containing jade, unaware of the jade’s flawlessness. If one is thus, this is called 'leaving home. Therefore, the Guide said:"
Phenomena are fundamentally non-obstructive, and the three periods of time are likewise so. Even for one who is unconditioned and free from affairs, it remains as difficult as a golden chain.
Thus, the numinous source shines alone; the Way is severed and birthless. Great wisdom is not "bright," and true emptiness leaves no trace.
True Suchness, ordinary beings, and sages are all but dream-like words; Buddhas and *nirvāṇa* are both merely figurative designations. Zen practitioners, you must simply look within yourselves.
There is no one to replace me. Entering the hall:
In the Three Realms there is no dharma; where can one seek the mind? The four great elements are originally empty; upon what does the Buddha rely to dwell?
The celestial sphere is unmoving; it is still and silent, beyond words. Face-to-face presentation—there is nothing more. Take care.

Chan Master Yangqi Shou addressed the assembly from the high seat: "The single source of all sentient beings is provisionally named 'Buddha. Though its substance is exhausted and its form dissolves, it does not perish;
though gold flows and the ingot disperses, it remains ever-present. When the ocean of nature is windless, the golden waves surge spontaneously;

when the spiritual mind is free of duality, the myriad phenomena are simultaneously illumined. One who realizes this principle traverses the sands of the world-realms without speaking, and accomplishes their work without effort."

This further deepens the mysterious transformation. How can one turn one's back on awakening and instead conform to worldly toil? Within the aggregates and realms, one falsely imprisons oneself through attachment.
Chan Master Maitou Zang ascended the hall and said: "To know while being without knowing is not a case of being without knowing; it is to speak of being without knowing."
Chan Master Nanquan Yuan was ascending the hall when he said: "Dīpaṃkara Buddha’s Way is finished.
If one gives rise to all phenomena through the conceptualization of mental states, they are false and unreal. Why is this? Since the mind itself does not exist, how can it give rise to all phenomena?
It is like distinguishing forms and shadows within empty space, or like a person trying to catch sound and place it inside a casket, or like blowing on a net [to make it move]."
This causes the vital energy to become full. Thus, the veteran elders said: "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing.

For now, let me speak to you brothers regarding the practice of conduct: according to the teachings, Bodhisattvas of the Tenth Ground dwell in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, attain the secret Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas, and naturally acquire all dhyānas, liberations, and the wondrous functions of supernormal powers, reaching all worlds.
The Universal Manifestation Body (sambhoga-kāya) may manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment, the turning of the Great Wheel of Dharma, and entry into nirvāṇa.

It causes immeasurable beings to enter into a single pore, where a single phrase of scripture is expounded for immeasurable eons without its meaning being exhausted, thereby teaching and transforming immeasurable billions of sentient beings so that they attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Yet, this is still termed "ignorance regarding the knowable" (jñeya-āvaraṇa), specifically the most subtle ignorance regarding the knowable.
This is utterly contrary to the Way. A great difficulty, a great difficulty!

Take care. He ascended the hall and said: "Master Wang has raised a water buffalo since childhood. If I intend to graze it on the east bank of the stream, I cannot avoid consuming the king’s water and grass;
if I intend to graze it on the west bank of the stream, I likewise cannot avoid consuming the king’s water and grass."
"Grass! It is better to accept a little according to one's lot; otherwise, nothing at all will be seen. Entering the hall, he said:
"To speak of 'suchness' (tathatā) is already to have changed it. The teachers and monks of these times must walk among the heterodox classes.
Guizong said, "Though one performs the actions of an animal, one does not receive the retribution of an animal. The Master said, "Alas, you fellow Meng!"
"Furthermore, going thus.
He ascended the hall and said: "Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra fought each other last night at the third watch; I gave each of them twenty blows and drove them out of the monastery.
Zhaozhou asked, "Whom does the Master’s staff intend for to eat? The Master said, "Now tell me, where was Old Wang’s fault?"
At Shenchu, he ascended the hall for formal instruction.
"Master Wang is selling himself; is there anyone who will buy him? A monk stepped forward and said, "I will buy him.
The Master asked, "Neither as something precious nor as something cheap—how will you buy him? The monk was speechless.
National Teacher Anguo of Yanguan ascended the hall and said to the assembly, "Taking empty space as the drum and Mount Sumeru as the mallet—what person can strike it?
The assembly was silent; no one responded.
Chan Master Guizong Chang ascended the hall and said: "The ancient worthies of old were not without understanding;
they were men of lofty character who did not conform to the common run. People of today cannot achieve self-reliance and instead waste their time in vain.
My sons, do not apply your minds in error. No one can take your place, nor is there any place for you to apply your mind. Do not seek it from others. From the very beginning..."
This is reliance on others for understanding; when speaking, words are all obstructed, and light does not penetrate through, simply because there is something before one’s eyes.
Entering the hall, he said: "I now wish to speak of Chan; all you sons, come forward together. The assembly came forward, and the Master said:

"Listen to the practice of Avalokiteśvara, which skillfully responds to questions from all quarters. "What is the practice of Avalokiteśvara? The Master then snapped his fingers and said: [Avalokiteśvara].
"Did you all hear that? they asked. "We heard it," they replied. The Master said, "You lot! What are you looking for here?
He drove them out with his staff, laughed loudly, and returned to the abbot's quarters.
Master Zhuyou ascended the hall. Holding up a piece of bamboo, he said, "Is there anyone who can drive a stake into empty space?
At that time, the senior monk Lingxu stepped forward from the assembly and said, "Empty space itself is the stake. The Master threw down the bamboo and immediately descended from his seat.
Chan Master Damei Chang addressed the assembly, saying: "All of you, each must turn your minds back to realize the fundamental source; do not pursue its branches.

If you attain the root, the branches will follow of their own accord. If you wish to recognize the root, simply understand your own mind, for this mind is fundamentally the root of all mundane and supramundane dharmas.
When the mind arises, all manner of dharmas arise; when the mind ceases..."
The various dharmas cease; furthermore, they do not arise in dependence upon any good or evil. The myriad dharmas are fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*).
Master Huangbo Xiyun ascended the hall. As the assembly gathered like clouds, he said, "All of you here, what is it that you seek?
He then drove them away with his staff, yet the assembly did not disperse. The Master sat back down and said, "All of you..."
"You are a fellow who eats dregs of wine! To travel on pilgrimage in such a manner is to become a laughingstock to others.
You simply go wherever you see eight hundred or a thousand people; you cannot help but seek out their clamor.

When I was traveling on pilgrimage, if I encountered a man even beneath a patch of grass, I would strike him with a single blow from the crown of his head to see if he knew pain or itch. If he had known it, I could have spread the teaching."
"Carrying a bag of rice to offer to others—this is entirely like you. How easy it is! Where else could there be such a thing as this today?
Since you all claim to be wandering monks (*caryā-yātrika*), you ought to apply some spirit to your practice.
Do you even know that within the Great Tang there is no Zen master? At that time, a monk asked, "The venerable elders of all quarters gather assemblies everywhere to teach and transform."
"Why do you say there is no Chan master? The Master said, "I do not say there is no Chan; it is simply that there are no masters.

You, O Kalyāṇamitra, have not seen that under the Great Master Mazu, there were eighty-four people who sat at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), yet those who attained Mazu’s True Dharma Eye numbered only two or three.
The Venerable Guizong of Mount Lu was one of them. Indeed, those who have left the household life must know this."
There are matters that can only be understood from the perspective of the "transcending" (shangxiang) stage.

For instance, those under the Fourth Patriarch, such as Niutou, spoke both horizontally and vertically, yet they still did not know the pivotal mechanism of the "transcending" stage. Only with this kind of insight can one distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.

As for the various schools, they merely attend to worldly affairs and are unable to realize the essence; they only know how to study words and phrases, which they then carry around in their leather bags.
"You go everywhere claiming you practice Chan. But can you truly take charge of your own birth and death? To treat an old master with such contempt—you will enter hell as fast as an arrow.
As soon as I saw you step through the gate, I recognized you for who you were. Do you understand? You must exert yourself urgently; do not treat this as a trivial matter.
If you spend a lifetime in vain, wearing but a single robe and subsisting on mere mouthfuls of food, those with clear eyes will laugh at you. Long.
Afterwards, you will all be calculated away by worldly people. You should look for yourselves at what is near and what is far; whose business is this?
If you understand, then understand; if you do not understand, then disperse. Take care.
Chan Master Xiangyan Deng was ascending the hall when a monk asked, "What is the direct source?
The Master then cast down his staff and immediately returned to his quarters.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Speech is slander; silence is deception. Beyond speech and silence, there is a path. This old monk’s mouth is too narrow;
I cannot explain it to you. He then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "For what reason is there nothing? The Master said, "I have never paused.
He then continued, "Even if one were to peel away layer after layer until everything is exhausted and nothing remains, such a provisional arrangement is merely a skillful means for guiding people."
"If it were a matter of 'that side,' such a thing would be impossible.
Master Tianlong of Hangzhou ascended the hall and addressed the assembly: "Everyone, do not wait for this old monk; when he comes up, come up; when he goes down, go down.
Each of you possesses the ocean of the nature of the Flower Treasury (Huazang), complete with all merits and unimpeded radiance. Each and every one...
Take this up. Cherish it. Chan Master Jiushan Gu said in a formal lecture:
"A movement of expression or a blink of an eye—nothing emerges outside of the person themselves. A single thought of pure mind is, from the very beginning, the Buddha.
He then spoke a verse: "The mind is fundamentally free from dust; what need is there to wash it? The body contains no illness; why seek a cure?"
Physician: If one wishes to know whether this Buddha is a physical body or not, it is like a bright mirror hanging high that has not yet reflected anything.

Zen Master An of Huangzhou ascended the hall and said: "When words do not fall into fixed phrases, Buddhas and patriarchs have nothing to offer; when the profound resonance does not decline, who can truly know it?"
Chan Master Daci Zhong addressed the assembly from the high seat, saying: "I, this mountain monk, am unable to answer questions; I can only recognize the illness.
At that time, a monk came forward, and the Master immediately returned to his quarters.
Chan Master Zhaozhou Shen spoke from the hall: "It is like a bright pearl held in the palm; when a barbarian comes, it appears as a barbarian; when a Han person comes, it appears as a Han person.
This old monk takes a blade of grass and uses it as the sixteen-foot golden body of the Buddha; he takes the sixteen-foot golden body of the Buddha and uses it as a blade of grass.
The Buddha is affliction; affliction is the Buddha. A monk asked, "I do not understand: of whom is this the affliction?"
The Master said, "It causes affliction for all people. [The monk] asked, "How can one avoid it? The Master said, "What need is there to avoid it? He ascended the hall and said:
"The golden Buddha does not pass through the furnace; the wooden Buddha does not pass through fire; the clay Buddha does not pass through water. The true Buddha sits within.
Bodhi, nirvana, suchness, and buddha-nature—all these are but garments upon the body, and they are also called afflictions."
In the ground of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), where can anything be placed? When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault.
You need only investigate this principle and sit and watch for twenty or thirty years. If you do not understand, cut off the old monk’s head and take it with you!

Dream-visions, illusions, and empty flowers—vain is the effort to grasp them. If the mind is not different from the myriad dharmas, they are all as one; since this is not obtained from without, why further cling to them and create [distinctions]?
It is like a sheep that indiscriminately picks up things and puts them into its mouth.
When I saw Master Yaoshan say, "If someone asks you something, simply tell them to shut their dog's mouth," I also told them to shut their dog's mouth. To grasp at me is defilement;
not grasping at me is purity. It is just like a hunting dog whose sole desire is to obtain something—where is there any Buddha-dharma in such a thing?

In this place, among thousands and tens of thousands of people, all are men seeking the Buddha; yet among them, if one seeks a true man of the Way, there is none like me who has become a disciple of the Empty King.
Do not let the sickness of the mind be the most difficult to cure. Before the world existed, this nature already existed;
when the world perishes, this nature does not perish. From the moment you first saw this old monk, it has been nothing other than this.
People are simply this very host. Why seek it further outward? At this very moment, do not turn your head or change your mind;
if you turn your head or change your mind, you will lose it. A monk asked, "I have heard your teacher say that when the world is destroyed, this nature is not destroyed.
What is this nature? The Master said, "The four elements and the five aggregates. The monk said, "This..."

The monk asked, "How is it when one does not come from the West? The Master said, "The cypress tree in the courtyard. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "The cypress tree in the courtyard. The monk asked, "How is it when one does not come from the West? The Master said, "The cypress tree in the courtyard. The monk asked, "If someone comes from the West, what do you say to them? The Master said, "The cypress tree in the courtyard. The monk asked, "How is it when one does not come from the West? The Master said, "The cypress tree in the courtyard. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "
[The monk] said, "In the south, there are many who lose their bodies and forfeit their lives. [The Master] said, "I ask the Master to cite an example.
As soon as the Master had uttered the previous words, the monk pointed to a monk nearby and said, "This monk, having finished his meal, speaks such talk. The Master then desisted.

Ascending the hall, he said: "When a person of integrity speaks of deviant teachings, those deviant teachings are entirely correct. When a deviant person speaks of orthodox teachings, those orthodox teachings are entirely deviant.
Elsewhere, they are difficult to see but easy to recognize; here, they are easy to see but difficult to recognize."
Ascending the hall, he addressed the assembly, saying: "When I was traveling southward on pilgrimage, there was a 'guestless host' koan at the head of my fire-hearth.
To this very day, no one has brought it forth."
Ascending the hall, the Master said: "The Ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes picking and choosing. As soon as there are words, that is picking and choosing;
that is making things clear. This old monk does not abide within clarity. Do you still cherish and protect anything?
At that time, a monk asked, "If you do not abide within clarity, what is it that you cherish and protect? The Master said, "I do not know either. The monk said, "Since the Master..."
"I do not know," he replied. "How can it be said that the Way does not reside within clarity? The Master said, "If you wish to inquire about the matter, you may;
however, after you have prostrated, withdraw. Another monk asked, "The Supreme Way is not difficult; it only dislikes picking and choosing. Is this the conceptual nest of people of this age?
The Master said, "Someone once asked me this, and for five years I was unable to explain it away. He asked again, "The Supreme Way is not difficult..."
"I only dislike making discriminations. What is non-discrimination? The Master said, "Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored.
The monk said, "This is still discrimination. The Master said, "You slave, where is the discrimination here? The monk was speechless.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Brothers, if you come from the south, I shall unload for you; if you come from the north, I shall load for you.
Therefore it is said: 'If one approaches a superior person and asks about the Way, one loses the Way; if one approaches an inferior person and asks about the Way, one attains the Way.'"

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Brothers, do not stand for long. If you have matters to discuss, deliberate; if you have no matters, sit beneath the robes and bowls and investigate the principle thoroughly.
When I was traveling on pilgrimage, apart from the two times of rice gruel and meals, these were the only occasions where my mind was occupied with various concerns.
Aside from these, there was no other place where my mind was occupied. If it is not like this, you will be far astray."
Ascending the hall, he said to the assembly: "If you were to spend your entire life never leaving the monastic groves and not speaking for five or ten years, no one would call you a mute.
Later on, even the Buddha would be powerless against you. If you do not believe me, cut off the old monk's head and take it with you!"
Master Dameo ascended the hall and said: "If you wish to recognize the Teacher of all Buddhas, recognize him within the mind of ignorance.
If you wish to recognize the eternally abiding, non-decaying nature, recognize it in the midst of the shifting and changing of all things."
Chan Master Cunen ascended the hall and said: "I saw Baizhang not knowing good from bad. As soon as the assembly had gathered, he struck them all down at once with his staff.
He then called out to the assembly; when they turned their heads, he said, 'What is this? There was no way for them to engage him in conversation.
Huangbo the Master did the same: he called out to the assembly; when they turned their heads, he said, 'The moon is like a bow...'"
A bow. Little rain, much wind; it is still somewhat better than this.
Ascending the hall, he said: "To split it open is up to me; to fold it back together is up to me. At that time, a monk asked:
"What is 'splitting it open'? The Master said: "Three times nine is twenty-seven. Bodhi and Nirvana. Suchness and Liberation. This very mind is Buddha."
"I shall speak thus for now; how would you speak? He replied, "I do not speak thus.
The Master said, "The cup falls to the ground, and the plate shatters into seven pieces. He asked, "What is 'gathering together'? The Master then sat with his hands folded.
Chan Master Daisuizhen ascended the hall and said: "This nature is fundamentally pure and replete with myriad virtues.

It is only due to the two conditions of defilement and purity that distinctions arise. Therefore, the sages, having awakened to it, employ it exclusively in its pure aspect to realize the Way of Enlightenment."
Ordinary beings are deluded by this; they engage exclusively in defiled activity and sink into the cycle of saṃsāra. Since its essence is non-dual, the Prajñāpāramitā states:
"There is no duality, nor two parts; there is no distinction, nor any interruption."
Chan Master Danxia Yan addressed the assembly: "All of you, you must carefully protect that single spiritual essence.
It is not something created by you or something to be described in words; how much more so can one speak of 'realizing' it or 'not realizing' it? In my past days, when I saw Shitou..."
Furthermore, you must simply protect yourself; this matter is not something you can discuss.
Each of you has your own patch of ground; what more is there to doubt regarding Zen? Is it something you can intellectually grasp? How could there be a Buddha to be realized?
The very word "Buddha" is never pleasing to hear. Look for yourselves! Skillful means and compassion—[this is the way].
Joyful relinquishment is not obtained from without; it does not abide within the mind. Skillful means is Mañjuśrī; expedient means is Samantabhadra.
What more do you intend to pursue? There is no need for seeking through scriptures, lest you fall into emptiness.

Scholars nowadays are in a state of constant turmoil, all of them engaged in "investigating Zen" and "inquiring about the Way. In my place here, there is no Way to be cultivated and no Dharma to be realized.
Every sip of drink and every morsel of food has its own allotted portion; there is no need for doubt. In every place and at every time, there are those who are like this.
If you can recognize Śākyamuni, he is but an old ordinary person. You must examine this for yourself;
do not let one blind man lead a crowd of blind men, leading them all together into a pit of fire. Playing double-six in the dark of night—how could you ever win? Take care.
Zen Master Sanpei Gicho ascended the hall and said: "The people of these times all come forth to study running after things and creating fabrications, taking them to be their own eyes and ears.
What adequacy is there in this? Do you wish to learn? It requires nothing else.
Each of you has your own fundamental matter; why do you not realize it? Why are you so frustrated in mind and so stammering in speech? What is there [to gain]?"

What benefit is there? I shall explain it clearly to you. If you seek the path of cultivation, as well as the various gates of transformation established by the sages, there are already the texts of the Great Canon (Tripitaka) available for that.
However, if this concerns the matter of the School of the Patriarchs (Zongmen), you must not, under any circumstances, apply your mind incorrectly.
A monk asked, "In the School of the Patriarchs, is there still a path of study? The Master said, "There is one path as slippery as moss."
[The monk] asked, "Can a student still grasp it? The Master said, "If you do not direct your mind toward it, look for yourself.
Chan Master Benkong of Majia Mountain ascended the hall and said: "As for these very activities and movements, do they accord with one's original ancestral nature?
If they do accord, there is no principle of wasting any of the twelve periods of the day. If they do not accord—"
Regarding the expression "drinking tea and conversing," it is often referred to as "tea-talk. A monk then asked, "How can one avoid it being considered mere tea-talk?
The Master said, "Do you even know what a mouth is? The monk asked, "What is the mouth? The Master said, "You do not even recognize two pieces of skin.
The monk asked, "What is the original patriarch? The Master said, "Do not drag this up before the assembly."
The Master, relying on his mother, said: "The assembly has departed with joy. The Master said: "Try to point out the nature of the assembly for me.
The monk bowed. The Master said: "He often says that 'one nature is all natures. The monk was about to offer a word when the Master said: [Stop].
"You have betrayed the eye of your lifelong pilgrimage.
Master Bensheng held up his staff and showed it to the assembly, saying: "If I hold it up, you immediately begin to apply intellectual reasoning to the time before it was held up.
If I do not hold it up, you immediately attempt to exercise mastery over the time when it is held up. Now tell me—"
"Wherein does this old monk serve others? At that time, a monk stepped forward and said, "I dare not arbitrarily create complications.

The Master said, "I know you, Dharma brother, do not go beyond the bounds. The monk said, "In low places there is more than enough to level them; in high places one observes that they are insufficient.
The Master said, "To add complications upon complications. The monk was speechless. The Master said, "Covering one's nose while stealing the fragrance."
Vainly inviting blame.

Chan Master Heshan Hui said in a formal address: "Since the time of the Patriarchs, people have misunderstood; this has been handed down to the present day, using the words and phrases of Buddhas and patriarchs as models for teachers.
If one proceeds in this manner, it instead makes one a madman or an ignorant person."
He merely points this out to you: that the essence of all dharmas is the Way. In the Way, there is not a single dharma;

there is no Buddha to be realized, no Way to be attained, no dharma to be grasped, and no dharma to be abandoned. Therefore, the old monk says: "Before one's eyes there is no dharma, yet the meaning lies before one's eyes.
This is not a dharma of the present moment. If you seek to learn from the Buddhas and patriarchs, such a person has not yet possessed the eye.

Wherein? For what reason? Because all are subject to their basis and lack autonomy; fundamentally, they are merely lost in the vast expanse of birth and death, and the nature of consciousness has no portion of freedom.
Traveling thousands of miles to seek a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), one must possess the correct eye to seek liberation from erroneous views.
One must definitively examine the birth and death before one’s eyes: do they truly exist, or do they truly not exist? If there is anyone who...
I grant you permission to emerge from [this state]. Those of superior capacity realize the Way upon hearing a single word; those of middling or inferior capacity wander like waves upon waves.
Why not settle decisively within birth and death? Where else could you seek, doubting the Buddhas and the Patriarchs?

A person of wisdom would laugh at you for trying to substitute someone else for your own birth and death. If you do not understand, listen to another verse: "Toiling to uphold the dharmas of birth and death... Only...
He seeks it from the Buddha’s side, yet is currently deluded regarding the correct principle; he strikes out at fire seeking a bubble.
Entering the hall: Not knowing when dawn breaks, awakening does not depend on a teacher. Leaping with its scales at the Dragon Gate, it does not fall into the hands of the fisherman.

It is simply that the mind does not lodge in private attachments and the tongue does not cling to the profound essence. This is precisely when one is fit to know the sound; this is called the "congenital dialogue.
If you harbor doubt regarding the profound essence, you will only bring ruin upon yourself, O Kalyāṇamitra. A weary fish stays in the pond; a dull bird perches on the reeds.
You, Kalyāṇamitra, are not the clouds and waters; the clouds and waters are not you, Kalyāṇamitra. As for me, an old monk, I have attained mastery over the clouds and waters. And you, Kalyāṇamitra...

"How is it? [The Master] ascended the hall and said: "To form an understanding from what one hears is to paint with brush and ink upon the surface of the mind. While it may seem beautiful at first glance, harboring it for long becomes a sickness.
The green mountains and white clouds have never met; the shuttle-head is unattached to the warp-thread—this is the meaning of the free and unrestrained display of literary brilliance."
This is distinct. Jiaxiang’s single path was understood by Zhiyi in his commentaries; yet, like a miraculous herb without roots, it is not esteemed by the wise.
Entering the hall: The golden crow and jade hare vie with one another for brilliance; when the sun is sat upon, the world falls into darkness.
Upper lip and lower lip have never known each other. I tell you clearly: do not let your eyes look back. Why is this?
The sun and moon are not sufficient to be called luminous; heaven and earth are not sufficient to be called great. The axe does not move through the air; the skillful craftsman leaves no trace.
Seeing one's nature, one does not retain the Buddha; awakening to the Way, one does not preserve the teacher. An ordinary old monk says:
"To see Gautama with one's own eyes is like [viewing] yellow leaves. The entire Tripitaka is this old monk’s sitting mat; the profound intent of the Patriarchs is for breaking [delusions]."
Straw sandals: it is better to go barefoot than to wear these; this is best.

Entering the hall for discourse, [the Master said]: "I have lived on this mountain for twenty years, yet I have never once raised a matter concerning the School of the Patriarchs. A monk asked: [Why not?]
The monk said, "I have heard it said that you, Master, have lived on this mountain for twenty years without ever having raised a single matter concerning the School of the Ancestors.

Is this true? The Master replied, "It is. The monk then overturned the meditation seat, whereupon the Master ceased speaking. On the following day, the Master went out for communal labor and had a pit dug;
he then sent his attendant to invite the monk from the previous day, saying to him, "For twenty years, this old monk has spoken nothing but meaningless words. Now—"
"Please, Venerable Elder, strike and kill this old monk and bury me in a pit.

If you do not strike and kill this old monk, it will only be right for you, Venerable Elder, to strike and kill yourself and bury yourself in the pit. The monk returned to the hall, packed his belongings, and departed in secret.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Apprehend the old monk at the tips of the hundred grasses; recognize the Son of Heaven in the midst of the bustling marketplace.

Ascending the hall again, he said: "The eye does not hang upon the door; the mind does not dwell in the profound mystery. Even when the numinous grasses do not grow, this is still but the rank of the Five Heavens.
The radiance of the pearl and the essence of the moon are not the time for them to emerge. Here there is no old monk; at the crossroads of the five paths there is none."
Ācārya, Chan Master Jiufeng Qian ascended the hall and said: "Brothers, do you yet recognize life? If you wish to know life, flowing springs are life;
