profound stillness is the body. The surging of a thousand waves is the realm of Mañjuśrī; the single expanse of the clear sky is..."
The Universal Worthy’s (Samantabhadra) couch and bed. Next, borrowing a single phrase refers to the finger pointing at the moon;
herein, the matter is the discourse on the moon from within the ancestral school of the Gate of the Patriarchs. It is like the signal banner of a military commander.

For instance, when the former worthies of various quarters had not yet established so many designations, what standard or framework did they rely upon to deliberate with their fellow practitioners prior to that? Upon reaching [this point]—
In this matter, try to speak and understand without relying on the "three inches. Try to listen and discern without relying on the ears. Try to distinguish and clarify without relying on the eyes.
Therefore it is said: "Before the sound, nothing can be cast out; after the phrase, no form is hidden.
Throughout the entire universe and great earth, it is all the very essence of you, the person here and now. Where, then, would you place your eyes, ears, nose, and tongue? Do not—
If you merely attempt to fathom and construct an understanding through the faculty of the mind, you will never find rest, even until the end of the future.
Therefore, Dongshan said: "To seek to study the profound mystery with the mind and intellect is much like heading west while facing east. Take heed.
Chan Master Yongquan Xin ascended the hall and said: "I have been here for forty-nine years, yet I still occasionally stumble.
You people must not open your mouths too wide; those with intellectual understanding are many, but those who possess both realization and practice are not one in ten thousand."
This insight and these words must all be thoroughly understood and penetrated. If your realization is not complete, I dare say you will remain in the cycle of rebirth.

Why is this so? It is because the outflows of your consciousness have not been exhausted. You need only exhaust them; only then will you be established in the present moment. This is also called "achieving merit within establishment.
To turn that merit over toward him is also called "achieving merit within conformity. To personally abandon oneself and go toward him is what is meant.
Therefore it is said: "A relative cannot be saved; he himself does not save his relatives. If you are like this, even a parable will not be understood. Realize the whole lump.
Just manage to keep your nature from being disturbed and moving about. You do not even see the tip of the tongue [of the teaching].
Dongshan said: "Continuity is also very difficult. You must know that there is this matter. If you do not know it exists, there will be days of weeping.
Chan Master Lupu An ascended the hall and said: "The final phrase reaches the ultimate barrier; it locks off the vital passageway, allowing neither ordinary people nor sages to pass through.
I have always told everyone: 'Let the world rejoice as it pleases, yet I alone do not consent.'"

If you wish to know those who are superior practitioners, they do not take the words and teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and paste them upon their foreheads, like a tortoise carrying a map—this is nothing but a sign of its own impending death.
Or like a phoenix entangled in a golden net, though it soars toward the heavens, what expectation of directness can there be?

You must clarify the essence beyond the words; do not seek it within the words themselves. In this way, the mechanism of the stone man will resemble yours. Only then can you sing the *bā* [of the partridge].
Song: "If you were like a stone man, you would sing the snow song; you should harmonize with the single path of the Guide. The wise know the commentary.
Chan Master Weizheng of Niutou entered the hall and said: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time could not manage it with even a single bit of artifice;

they could not reach the mouths of the teachers of the world. As for you all, who are like those carrying a flat pole—how will you do? It is not at all easy. Unless one knows 'that which is,' there is nothing else."
No one could understand this.
Chan Master Molamou ascended the hall. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of Baizhang rolling up his mat?
The Master said, "Take care," and then descended from the hall.
Chan Master Deshan Jian addressed the assembly from the high seat: "If you have no affairs within yourself, do not seek them falsely.

Even if you were to obtain something through false seeking, it would still not be attainment. You need only be without affairs in your mind and without mind in your affairs; then you will be spirit-like in your emptiness and wondrous in your voidness.
To speak of beginning and end regarding even a hair’s breadth of this is to deceive oneself. Why? Because a single hair’s tip binds [one]."

Reflect: the karmic causes of the three miserable realms arise from a mere flicker of emotion, yet they bind one in shackles for ten thousand kalpas. Holy names and mundane titles are all but empty sounds;
extraordinary features and inferior forms are all but illusory colors. If you seek them, will you not be burdened?
And when you grow weary of them, they become a great affliction. In the end, they are of no benefit.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The realization of my ancestors was not like this. Here, there is neither ancestor nor Buddha.
Bodhidharma is an old bald-headed barbarian; Śākyamuni is a dried-up dung-club. Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are dung-carriers;
Equal Enlightenment and Wondrous Enlightenment are deluded ordinary people; Bodhi and Nirvāṇa are hitching posts for donkeys. The twelve divisions of the teachings are..."

The "Register of Ghosts and Spirits" uses paper to wipe away sores and warts. Those at the stages of the four fruits and three worthies, as well as those at the initial mind of the ten bhūmis, are ghosts guarding ancient tombs;
they cannot even save themselves.
Chan Master Yantou Huo ascended the hall and said: "I have studied the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for seven or eight years and have seen only two or three passages."
[The Master] said, "This meaning is like the talk of a monk. He added, "When it is time to rest, rest. At that time, a monk came forward, bowed, and requested the Master to provide an illustration.
The Master said, "The intent of my teaching is like the three dots of the character for 'profound' (∴). The first dot is placed toward the east; it opens the eyes of all Bodhisattvas.
The second dot is placed toward the west; it strikes the life-root of all Bodhisattvas. The third..."
Pointing slightly downward from above, he touches the crowns of the various Bodhisattvas’ heads; this is the meaning of the first section. Furthermore, it is said:
"The intent of my teaching is like Maheśvara, who splits open his face and raises one eye; this is the meaning of the second section. Again, it is said:
"The intent of my teaching is like a drum smeared with lethal poison; when struck once, all who hear it, whether far or near, [perish]."
"Farewell. This is the meaning of the third section. At that time, the Elder Xiaoyan asked, "What is the 'poison-coated drum'?
The Master pressed his two hands against his knees, leaned forward his body, and said, "This is the one who faced the court when Han Xin was about to ascend. Xiaoyan was speechless.
Chan Master Xuefeng Cun ascended the hall and said, "On South Mountain there is a turtle-nosed snake;
you all must look at it very carefully. Changqing stepped forward and said, "Today, many in this hall will lose their lives.
Yunmen brandished his staff, thrust it toward the Master, and made a gesture of fear. A monk reported this to Xuansha, who said, "One must indeed..."
"Brother Ling has only now attained it. "Even so, I am not like that. [The student] asked, "How about you, Master?
The Master said, "What use is Nanshan?"
Ascending the hall, the Master said: "This matter is like a single field of land. It is left entirely to you all to plow and sow;
there is no one who does not receive the power of this grace. Xuansha asked, "And what, pray tell, is this field? The Master said, "Look!
Xuansha said, "It is indeed so, yet I do not see it that way. The Master asked, "How do you see it? Xuansha replied, "It is simply 'man'."
[The Master] ascended the hall for the assembly. "The entire earth is this gate of liberation. I hold out my hand and pull you toward it, yet you refuse to enter.
At that time, a monk stepped forward and said, "Master, you cannot blame me. Another monk said, "What is the use of entering? The Master then—
[The Master] struck [the gavel]. He ascended the seat. Once the assembly had settled, the Master rolled out a wooden ball. Xuansha then seized it and placed it back in its original position.
Chan Master Xuansha Bei addressed the assembly: "The Way of the Buddha is vast and open; there are no set paths. It is the liberation through the gateless."
This gate is not the intention of the man who speaks of intentions; it does not abide within the three periods of time, and thus it cannot be subject to rising or sinking.

To establish a system is to deviate from the truth; it does not belong to the realm of conditioned creation. To move is to give rise to the root of birth and death; to be still is to be intoxicated in the land of dullness and stupor.

If both movement and stillness are extinguished, one falls into a void of non-existence. If both movement and stillness are grasped together, one remains muddled regarding Buddha-nature. One must necessarily face the dust of the world and confront all sensory objects.
Like withered wood or cold ashes, they are applied as the occasion demands, never failing to be appropriate. A mirror reflects all images without its radiance becoming confused;

a bird flies through space without mixing its form with the color of the void. Thus, throughout the ten directions there are no reflected images, and within the three realms there are no traces of movement.

One does not fall into the mechanism of coming and going, nor does one dwell in the mind of the intermediate state. Within a bell there is no sound of a drum; within a drum there is no sound of a bell.
Sound: the bell and drum do not intersect; in every phrase there is no before or after. It is like a strong man extending his arm, requiring no external force;
it is like a lion roaming, seeking no companion. When the nine heavens are free of obscuration, where is there any need for piercing through? This is a single segment of radiant light.

It has never been obscured or darkened. If one reaches this state, the essence is profoundly still and eternally lucid. The sun’s blazing radiance is boundless, its perfect enlightenment manifesting beyond all limits;

unmoving within the void, it devours and illuminates heaven and earth with a transcendent clarity. Now, as for the Buddha appearing in the world: fundamentally, there is no coming or going. Names and forms have no substance;
the Way is originally suchness (*tathatā*). The Dharma is naturally so, the true nature of Heaven; it is not something attained through cultivation or realization. It is simply...

One must be empty and at ease; yet one’s function must not be obscured, nor should one be entangled in the mud of worldly dust. Within this state, even a hair’s breadth left unspoken constitutes being a member of the Māra king’s retinue.
The space before a phrase and the space after a phrase are the difficult points for the student.

Therefore, when a single phrase accords with the Way, the eighty thousand gates forever cut off birth and death. Even if you attain a state like the moon’s reflection in an autumn pond or the sound of a bell in a still night—responding to every strike—[you have not yet reached it].
Striking it without flaw, touching the waves without scattering—this is still merely a matter of the shore of birth and death.
Where the Path-walker dwells, it is like fire melting ice; the ice will never turn back into ice again. Once an arrow has left the bowstring, it has no power to return.
Therefore, he will not stay when caged and does not turn his head when called. The ancient sages made no arrangements, and thus to this day there is no fixed location.

If one arrives here, at every step one ascends the profound mystery. It does not belong to the categories of the heterodox or the orthodox; consciousness cannot perceive it, and wisdom cannot know it. To stir is to lose the source;

to awaken is to become deluded regarding the ultimate intent. The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas tremble with fear, and those of the ten stages are struck with terror; the pathways of speech are utterly cut off.

Where the movements of the mind cease, one directly attains that Śākyamuni closed his room in Magadha, Vimalakīrti silenced his mouth in Vaiśālī, Subhūti proclaimed "no teaching" to manifest the Way, and Śakra and Brahmā ceased their listening as flowers rained down.

If you see it in this way before you, what else could you doubt? With no place to settle and free from coming and going, now there is no limit or restriction; the paths of thought and reason are cut off.
It is absolute. It does not depend on adornment; it is fundamentally true and pure. Whether in movement, speech, or laughter, it is clearly manifest everywhere, lacking nothing at all.
People of the present day do not awaken to this underlying principle; they recklessly involve themselves in worldly affairs and sensory dust, becoming stained and attached everywhere.
Every aspect is bound by fetters. Even if you achieve some degree of awakening, the sensory realms will remain in chaotic turmoil and names and forms will prove to be unreal.

Consequently, you may attempt to settle the mind and withdraw thoughts, seeking to subsume all phenomena into emptiness; you may close your eyes and hide your gaze, intending to suppress every arising thought as soon as it occurs and to stifle every subtle conception the moment it emerges.
Such a view is precisely that of an externalist who has fallen into nihilism—a state where the soul has not yet dispersed.

Those who are dead at the very root exist in a state of profound darkness and vast obscurity; they are without awareness or cognition, like someone who plugs their ears and steals a bell—merely deceiving themselves.
To engage in conceptual discrimination here is not the way. This is not a matter of hiding behind doors or lurking by windows; every word is manifest before one.

It cannot be deliberated upon, nor does it involve written characters. By nature it is utterly free from the realm of dust, and by nature it has no stages or ranks. For the sake of expediency, we provisionally call such a person "one who has left the home-life. Thus it is concluded.
In the end, there is no trace to be found. True Suchness, ordinary beings and sages, hell-beings and devas—these are merely expedient means for healing the madness of a wayward son.
Even empty space undergoes no change; how could the Great Way have any rising or sinking? To realize this is to move with total freedom, never departing from the fundamental limit.
If you reach this point, there is no place for ordinary beings or sages to stand. If you attempt to apply intentional thought to these words, you will be drowned and destroyed.

If you run outward in pursuit, you will again fall into the realm of Māra. As for that which is above, there is nothing to be arranged; it is like a glowing furnace that harbors no mosquitoes or gnats.
This principle is fundamentally level—what need is there for excavation or removal? Whether in motion or stillness, the raising of an eyebrow is the true path of liberation.
Do not forcibly apply mental calculations; to establish such constructs deviates from the truth. If you reach this point, there is not even a hair’s breadth of [duality].
"Receiving [the teaching]—if one points to the mind, it is already off the mark. Even if a thousand sages were to appear, they could not place a single word upon it. Do not stand for long;
take care.
Chan Master Ling of Changqing ascended the hall. After a long silence, he said, "Do not say that tonight’s [teaching] is only slightly different," and then he descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall: "If you encounter a fellow traveler on the Way, you may pass your entire life with shoulders touching;
your studies will then be complete. Ascending the hall: "When everything has been swept clean and put away, you step forward and question me.
I shall strike you across the spine. If there were a blow that reached you, you would surely feel shame and remorse; if no blow reached you, then where would you turn?"
"Where do you understand this?
Guishan Yan, the National Teacher, ascended the hall and after a long silence said: "In the days when Nanquan was alive, there were also those who raised this essential point.
Yet they did not recognize Nanquan even then; is there anyone here now who recognizes Nanquan? Come forth and let us test you before the assembly."

At that time, a monk came forth. As he was just rising from his prostrations, the Master said, "What is it? The monk stepped forward and said, "I ask the Master. The Master said, "Incompetent! Please withdraw.
Then he said, "The Sūtras have masters of the Sūtras; the Treatises have masters of the Treatises; the Vinaya has masters of the Vinaya."
There are cases where there are caskets and titles, and cases where there are sections and volumes, each transmitted and upheld by individuals.

Furthermore, the Buddha-dharma is established as both teaching (śāsana) and the path of meditation (dhyāna-mārga), yet it is a discourse intended to stop the crying [of the ignorant]. When other sages appeared in the world, they did so because the dispositions of people’s minds were not uniform;

thus, they skillfully opened up various expedient means (upāya), resulting in many different gateways. Just as those who suffer from different ailments receive different prescriptions, so too do those dwelling in existence (bhava) refute existence, while those dwelling in emptiness (śūnyatā) refute emptiness.
"Chiding the void. Once these two afflictions are removed, the middle way must also be discarded. This is why Gushan said: "Phrases do not meet the occasion;
words do not unfold the reality. Those who rely on words perish; those who linger in phrases are deluded. If one does not sing before the word, how can one speak after the phrase?
This leads directly to Śākyamuni closing his room and Vimalakīrti sealing his mouth, to the Great Being of the Liang dynasty and the Boy of that very day—one question and two [answers].
The question was asked three times; everyone has reached the end of it. How should you all proceed?

Chan Master Mingzhao Qian ascended the hall and said: "When the golden blade meets its superior match, those who can recognize it are rare. To die together and live together—there is not one in ten thousand.
Those who seek words and pursue phrases are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. To cite the ancients and cite the present is to destroy the lineage of the Buddha. Toward...
Up until now, the "beak and eggshell" [metaphor] has remained discordant. When Confucian scholars meet, they grasp their whips and look back;
what the śramaṇas perceive is truly a bitter affair—casting away true gold to follow the crowd in gathering mere soil. I tell you, young ones: do not waste your efforts in vain waves of striving!
Even if you could unravel his mysteries, it would still be nothing more than tiles and rubble. It is better to cast it all aside and leap straight across the great void. This very sharp blade—A!
"Who dares to approach? Let the master come with his arrows; only then will he be called a man of honor. If you intend to swallow your words in silence, a single blow of the mattock will suffice.
Chan Master Luohan Chen ascended the hall and said: "The profound mysteries of our school—do they consist merely of this, or is there something else extraordinary?
If there is something else extraordinary, bring it forth for me to see. If not, then do not attempt to carry two [loads] at once."

The single word "this" (ge) suffices to encompass the entire vehicle of the school (zongcheng). Why? Because there are two words: namely, the vehicle of the school and the vehicle of the teachings (jiaocheng).
As soon as you speak of the vehicle of the school, it is the vehicle of the school; as soon as you speak of the vehicle of the teachings, it is the vehicle of the teachings.
O Chan masters, the vehicle of the school of the Buddha-dharma has, from the beginning, been established by names within your own mouths; it is simply a matter of taking up and speaking of them.
Just a moment ago, we spoke of the level and the real; we spoke of the perfect and the eternal. Zen masters, what do you call "the level and the real"?
What do you take to be "the perfect and the eternal"? Having traveled as pilgrims to other houses, you must distinguish these principles; do not allow yourselves to be obscured by them.
You have obtained a mere fragment of sound, form, name, and designation, and stored it in your heart, saying, "I understand; I am well able to discern. But what is it that you understand?
What is it that you discern? That which you can memorize and retain is merely names;
that which you can distinguish and select is merely sound and form. If it were not for sound, form, name, and designation, how would you go about memorizing or discerning? It is like the wind.
The blowing of the pine trees. This sound is the croaking of frogs and the cawing of old crows. Why do you not listen there and discern it?
If you have some mental calculation or conceptual model there, then consider the mouth of this old teacher as well:
how much mental calculation is there? Do not mistake it, Upādhyāya. Right now, sounds and forms are resounding clearly; are they actually reaching you?
They do not reach one another. If they did reach one another, then your numinous spirit—the adamantine secret—would surely undergo destruction and departure. Why is it so?

Because the cause and condition of sound piercing through your ears and form boring through your eyes immediately blocks your illusory delusions and runs away, killing the very substance of sound and form;
you must not allow this. If they do not reach one another, then how much more so!
"Where do you find sound and form to understand them? Whether they meet or do not meet—try to discern this for a moment.
Later, he also said, "It is perfectly constant and level and real. Who is it that speaks thus? Such a person is not yet a man from a village of commoners who understands how to speak in this way.
It was those ancient sages who bestowed a little bit [of teaching] to assist and manifest [the truth]. People of today do not recognize good from evil.

He then settled into a state of complacency, saying, "I have a distinct school tradition that is profound and subtle; Śākyamuni Buddha has no tongue, for he is not even equal to a mere fraction of you.

He then patted his chest in such a manner. If one were to discuss the offenses of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, though they are grave, they are still relatively light and there is still a time when they may cease.
But this slander of Prajñāpāramitā blinds the eyes of sentient beings, leading them into the Avīci Hell to swallow iron pellets.

"Do not treat this as something trivial. Thus the ancients said: "The fault lies with the master of the transformation; it is not your business. Be careful! Chan Master An-guo Qiu ascended the hall and said:
"The circumstances of the rice and gruel here are for the sake of you, my brothers, whom I bring forth and proclaim. In the end, these are not permanent.
If you wish to attain the essential, it is rather the mountains, rivers, and the great earth that reveal it to you. Since that Way..."

It is eternal and can also bring one to ultimate fulfillment. If you enter through the gate of Mañjuśrī, all inanimate things—earth, wood, tiles, and pebbles—will assist you in triggering your awakening.
If you enter through the gate of Avalokiteśvara, all sounds and voices—even those of frogs and earthworms—will assist you in triggering your awakening.
If you enter through the gate of Samantabhadra, you arrive without moving a step. It is by means of these three gates that [one enters].
I shall show it to you. It is like taking a single broken chopstick and stirring the waters of the great ocean, so that the fish and dragons therein know water as their very life.

Do you understand? If one lacks the eye of wisdom to examine this with discernment, then no matter how many hundreds of clever and ingenious methods you employ, they will not lead to the ultimate realization.

Chan Master Shuilü Yan ascended the hall. Once the assembly had gathered in stillness, the Master descended from his seat, took up the incense burner, and walked before the assembly, saying, "I offer this to the Buddhas of the ten directions," and then returned to his quarters.
Chan Master Longji Xiu ascended the hall and said: "The ordinary person possesses the dharma of an ordinary person, yet the ordinary person does not know it;
the sage possesses the dharma of a sage, yet the sage does not realize it. If the sage were to realize it, he would be an ordinary person;

if the ordinary person were to know it, he would be a sage. These two phrases share one principle but have two meanings. If anyone can discern this, they will undoubtedly find something within the Buddha-dharma."
Regarding the sense bases (*āyatana*): if you cannot discern them, do not say that you have no doubts.

Be careful. Entering the Hall: Opening the curtain removes obstructions; closing the door creates hindrances. As for these very obstructions and hindrances, from ancient times until now, no one has understood them.
To understand them is to be obstructed; not to understand them is to lack freedom.
Chan Master Guishan Lingyou ascended the hall and said: "The mind of a man of the Way is straightforward and without artifice; it has no back and no front, and no heart of deceit or falsehood.
At all times, seeing and hearing are ordinary, with no further contrivance. Nor does one close the eyes or block the ears;

it is simply that the emotions do not cling to objects, and thus one attains [the state of the sages]. All the saints of the past have only spoken of the faults and afflictions on the side of turbidity."
There is none. All such matters as evil thoughts, emotional views, perceptions, and habitual tendencies are like the autumn waters—tranquil and still, pure and unconditioned, limpid and unobstructed.
To call such a person a "Way-man" (Dao-ren) is also to call him a "man of nothingness" (wu-shi-ren). At that time, there was a monk who asked:
"Does one who has attained sudden enlightenment still have further cultivation to perform? The Master said, "If one has truly awakened to the source, they know it for themselves;

then 'cultivation' and 'non-cultivation' are dualistic terms. Although those with the initial resolve may, through conditions, attain sudden enlightenment in a single thought-moment, their own nature is not yet free from the habitual tendencies accumulated over beginningless kalpas, which cannot be instantly purified.
One must therefore teach them to cleanse and eliminate these manifest karmic activities."

The flowing of consciousness is itself cultivation. There is no separate dharma or teaching that can lead one toward practice; rather, one enters the principle through hearing. When the principle heard is profound and subtle, the mind becomes spontaneously perfect and luminous, no longer dwelling in the realm of delusion.

Even if there are hundreds or thousands of wondrous meanings, they may be emphasized or suppressed as the occasion demands; this is like finding one’s own clothes and putting them on by oneself—only when one has established one’s own livelihood does it truly work. To speak of the essentials: [The flowing of consciousness is itself cultivation. There is no separate dharma or teaching that can lead one toward practice; rather, one enters the principle through hearing.

When the principle heard is profound and subtle, the mind becomes spontaneously perfect and luminous, no longer dwelling in the realm of delusion. Even if there are hundreds or thousands of wondrous meanings, they may be emphasized or suppressed as the occasion demands; this is like finding one’s own clothes and putting them on by oneself—only when one has established one’s own livelihood does it truly work. To speak of the essentials:
Thus, on the ground of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not a single speck of dust is accepted; within the gateway of the myriad practices, not a single dharma is abandoned.

If one enters directly with a single blade, then the sentiments of ordinary and sage are exhausted, the essence reveals true permanence, principle and phenomena are non-dual, and this is precisely the Tathāgata.
Ascending the hall, a monk stepped forward and said, "I request the Master to preach the Dharma for the assembly.
The Master replied, "I have already exhausted you thoroughly. The monk bowed.
Ascending the hall, the Master said: "The mid-winter is bitterly cold; year after year, the movement of the sun’s course shifts. As for this matter, how do you understand it?
Yangshan stepped forward, stood with his hands clasped, and remained there. The Master said, "I knew well that you would not be able to answer this question.

Xiangyan said, "I am uniquely able to answer this question. The Master repeated the previous question. Xiangyan also stepped forward, stood with his hands clasped, and remained there. The Master said, "Fortunately..."
When Yunju met Jizang, he did not understand him.
He ascended the hall and said: "People of the present day simply take that which is 'not understanding' directly as their realization; this is precisely your mind, and this is precisely your Buddha.
If you seek outwardly for a single bit of knowledge or understanding and take it to be the Way of Chan, you are utterly out of touch—this is called 'carrying manure.'"
[He] entered. It is not called "carrying out excrement"; it defiles your mind-field. Therefore it is said: "It is not the Way.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "After this old monk has passed away, I shall become a water buffalo on the mountain below. On its left flank, I shall write five characters:
'A certain monk of Mt. Gui. At such a time, if you call me a monk of Mt. Gui, I am also a water buffalo."
An ox. To call it a "water-ox" is yet another monk from Mount Gui. Ultimately, what should it be called?
Yangshan came forward, bowed, and withdrew. Yunju Ying spoke on his behalf, saying: "The Master has no other title. Zifubao said: [The Master has no other title.]
At that time, [Baizhang] simply made this [circle] seal and presented it. The Silla Master made this [circle with a "cow" inside] seal and presented it.
He further said: "Only those on the same path will understand. Baizhang Chao made this [circle with a "clothing" and "Buddha" inside] seal and presented it.
He further said: "The explanation has been given; the commentary has been provided. You must realize it for yourself! Thereupon he composed a verse, saying: "This is not [the teaching of] Guishan."
It is not a cow. To have two names for one body is truly difficult to account for. Setting aside these two extremes, you must speak:
how can you express that which flows eternally?
When Chan Master Jì of Yǎngshān was residing at Dōngpíng, Wéishān sent a monk with a letter and a mirror to the Master. The Master—
Ascending the hall, he held up an object and showed it to the assembly, saying: "Tell me, is this the mirror of Mount Huai or the mirror of Dongping?
If you say it is the mirror of Dongping, yet it was sent by Mount Huai. If you say it is the mirror of Mount Huai, yet it is currently in the hands of Dongping."
"If you can speak it, keep it; if you cannot speak it, smash it to pieces. The assembly remained silent. The Master then smashed [the bowl] and descended from his seat.
He then ascended the hall and said: "All of you, each turn the light inward and reflect back upon yourselves. Do not merely memorize my words. You have been thus since beginningless kalpas..."
Come! You have turned your back on the light and cast yourself into darkness; your deluded thoughts are so deeply rooted that they cannot be uprooted all at once.
Therefore, we provisionally establish skillful means to seize your coarse consciousness, much like using yellow leaves to stop a child’s crying—what validity is there in such a thing?

It is also like a person who sets up a single shop with a hundred kinds of goods alongside gold and jewels for sale, intending only to gauge the capacity and weight of those who come. Thus it is said: "The Stone..."
"The head is a shop of pure gold; here, I am a general store. If someone comes seeking mouse droppings, I likewise pick them up and give them to him.
If he comes seeking pure gold, I likewise pick it up and give it to him. At another time, a monk asked, "I do not want the mouse droppings; please give me the Master’s pure gold.
The Master said, "To bite the bullet and intend to open one's mouth—even in a donkey-year, one will still not understand. The monk was speechless.
[The monk] replied, “Yes. The Master said: “If you call out for something, there is a transaction; if you do not call out, there is no self.
If one speaks of the vicinity of the Chan school, even a single person to accompany you cannot be found, let alone a multitude of five hundred or seven hundred.
If I were to speak of this or that, people would scramble forward to seize it, like using an empty fist to deceive a small child—it is entirely without substance.”
"Regarding this matter, I shall now clearly explain to you the affairs pertaining to the limit of the holy. For now, do not allow your mind to settle upon external objects;

simply practice according to reality within the ocean of your own nature. You need not seek the three insights or the six supernatural powers. Why? Because these are merely secondary matters of the holy.
At present, you must first recognize the mind and penetrate the source. Once you have attained the source, you need not worry about the branches. In time..."
On a later day, I shall explain this in detail myself. If you have not yet attained the fundamental source, then even if you apply your emotions and imitate others, you will still not achieve it.

Have you not seen what the Venerable Master of Mt. Gui said: "When the sentiments of both ordinary beings and sages are exhausted, the true permanence is revealed; when phenomena and principle are non-dual..."
This is precisely the Buddha of Suchness.

Chan Master Xiangyan Xian ascended the hall and said: "If one discusses this matter, it is like a person climbing a tree, with a branch held in his mouth, his feet not treading on branches, and his hands not grasping branches.
Suddenly, someone from beneath the tree asks: 'What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?'"
[The Master said: "If you do not answer him, you contradict his question; if you do answer him, you will lose your body and forfeit your life.
At such a time, what can be done? At that moment, the Venerable Houtou Zhao stepped forward from the assembly and said, "I do not ask about [the tiger] on the tree;
please, Master, speak of it before it has climbed the tree. The Master then let out a great laugh.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Way is attained through awakening; it does not reside in words and phrases. Moreover, this is profound and majestic, never subject to interruption.
There is no need for mental effort; simply borrow the returning light for a moment. This is the full efficacy of daily life, yet those on the path of delusion turn their backs upon it."
Chan Master Bazhao Qing addressed the assembly from the high seat. Holding up his staff, he said to the congregation:
"If you have a staff, I will give you a staff; if you have no staff, I will take yours away. He leaned on the staff and descended from the seat.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "Suppose a person is walking along when suddenly they encounter a ten-thousand-fathom deep pit ahead, while a wild fire presses from behind, and on both sides are thickets of thorns.
If they move forward, they will fall into the pit; if they retreat..."
Then a wild fire will burn your body. If you try to turn over, you will be obstructed by the thorny brambles. At such a time, how can you avoid it?
If you can avoid it, you must possess a way to emerge from this state. If you cannot avoid it, you are a man who has fallen and died.
Ascending the hall, he said: "I was twenty-eight years old when I went to Yangshan to visit Nanta.
He ascended the hall and said, 'If you people here are true men, as soon as you emerge from your mother's womb, you should let out a lion’s roar—how about that?
At these words, my body and mind came to rest, and I stayed there for five years."
Master Lüyuan ascended the hall and, spreading his hands, said: "The life-roots of all the old monks and venerable seniors under heaven are all here.
A monk stepped forward and asked, "Have you gathered them in yet? The Master said, "Beside the Stone Bridge at Tiantai.
[The monk] said, "I do not think so. The Master said, "I humbly pray that you will continue to enjoy [this teaching]."
Chan Master Bājiāyuán addressed the assembly from the high seat: "The great trichiliocosm was rolled up by this old monk last night into a single lump and hurled toward the summit of Mount Sumeru.
Śakra, Lord of Devas, grew greatly incensed, seized it, and smashed it into dust and fragments.
Do you all feel a headache yet? After a long silence, he said: 'Do not fail to recognize pain and itchiness. Take care."
Chan Master Chengtian Que addressed the assembly: "To uphold the true command and grasp the guiding principle is still to manipulate a mold and fabricate a pseudo-Buddhism.
To respond with such extraordinary artifice merely deceives those of the highest caliber. If questioned, they falter; if answered, they become entangled.
Where, O Virtuous Ones, do you intend to set your teeth? Yet, in such matters, there is no fixed authority held in hand; one must employ both concession and seizure."

On one occasion, when there was doubt regarding how to act in the moment, Zen Master Zifu Su ascended the hall. Seeing the monastery bannerpole of Zifu from across the river, a monk immediately turned back;

he would have deserved thirty blows to his heels for that. How much more so when he had actually come across the river! As soon as another monk stepped forward, the Master said, "He is not fit to converse with."

Chan Master Bājīchè addressed the assembly from the high seat: "When there is no film in the eye, there are no flowers in the sky. When the water rises, the boat floats higher; when the mud is deep, the Buddha is larger.
Do not bring questions, for I have no answers. Do you understand? The question is in the place of the answer;
the answer is in the place of the question. He then descended from the seat.
Chan Master Linji Xuan ascended the hall. A monk asked, "What is the true Buddha, the true Dharma, and the true Way?
We beg the Master for instruction. The Master said, "The Buddha is the purity of the mind; the Dharma is the radiance of the mind; the Way is the pure light that is unimpeded everywhere.
These three are one; they are all empty names without substantial reality. It is like acting with true integrity."

The practitioner’s mindfulness continues from moment to moment without interruption. Since Master Bodhidharma came from the Western Land, he sought nothing other than a person who would not be deluded by others.
Later, upon meeting the Second Patriarch, he attained realization in a single word; only then did he realize that all his previous efforts had been in vain.
My present understanding is no different from that of the Patriarchs and Buddhas: if you can attain realization within the first phrase, [you have found it].
"One who realizes it in the first phrase is fit to be a teacher of the patriarchs and Buddhas. One who realizes it in the second phrase is fit to be a teacher of devas and humans.
One who realizes it in the third phrase cannot even save themselves. A monk then asked, "What is the first phrase? The Master said, "The seal of the three essentials opens;
the vermilion dot is narrow. There is no room for hesitation; host and guest are distinguished. [The monk asked,] "What is the second phrase?"

[The Master] spoke two phrases. The Master said: "How could a wondrous understanding fail to admit the question of Wuzhuo? How could the *upāya* (skillful means) fail to match the mechanism that cuts through the stream?
[A monk] asked: "What is the third phrase? The Master said: "Just look at the puppets performing on the stage; their every movement depends entirely upon the person inside. He then said:
"In general, when expounding the Dharma of the *zongmen* (the school of the essence), one must possess the three mysteries within a single phrase. This is the first mystery."
One must possess three essentials: there must be the provisional and the real; there must be illumination and function. How do you all understand this?
To those who study under me, I say: you must be extremely careful. It is like the meeting of host and guest, where there is an exchange of words;
or it may be manifesting form in response to things, or functioning with one's entire being, or employing skillful means through expressions of joy or anger, or appearing in partial form.
[The Master] manifested his body, sometimes riding a lion and sometimes riding an elephant king. When a true student of the Way let out a shout, [the Master] first produced a lacquer basin.
The spiritual friend (the Master), failing to discern it as an objective environment, stepped onto that environment and began to affect various poses.
Thereupon, the student shouted again. The former person refused to relinquish [the posture]. This is a terminal illness; it cannot be cured.

This is capable of being treated. To call this "the guest looking at the host" means that perhaps a good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) does not bring forth an object, but simply seizes [the student] right where the student asks.
The student, having been seized, resists to the death and refuses to let go; this is "the host looking at the guest.
Or, there may be a student who encounters a single pure object before a spiritual friend, and the spiritual friend is able to discern that it is such an object.
He seized it and threw it into a pit. The student said, "Excellent, O Good Knowledge-Keeper (Kalyāṇamitra)! The Master immediately said, "Shame!
You do not distinguish between good and evil. The student then prostrated. This is called "the host looking at the host.

Or, there may be a student who comes before the Good Knowledge-Keeper while wearing a cangue and shackles; the Knowledge-Keeper then places another layer of cangue and shackles upon him, and the student rejoices.

"Joy! When this and that cannot be distinguished, it is called 'viewing the guest'—O Great Virtue! All that I, this mountain monk, have raised is for the purpose of discerning demons, selecting the extraordinary, and knowing what is heterodox and what is orthodox."
Ascending the hall, he said: "There is one person who, for kalpas, remains on the road yet never leaves home; there is another person who leaves home yet is not on the road.
Which of these two deserves to receive the offerings of devas and humans?"
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "One person stands atop a solitary peak with no way out; another person stands at the crossroads with neither front nor back.
Now tell me, which one is in front and which one is behind? Do not act as Vimalakīrti;
do not act as Fu Dashi. Take care."
Addressing the assembly: At times I first manifest illumination and subsequently employ function; at times I first employ function and subsequently manifest illumination;

at times illumination and function occur simultaneously; and at times illumination and function do not occur simultaneously. When I first manifest illumination and subsequently employ function, there is a person present. When I first employ function and subsequently manifest illumination, there is a Dharma present.
When illumination and function occur simultaneously, I drive the ox of the plowman and snatch the food from the hungry man; I strike the bone to extract the marrow.

They strike with the needle and the chisel with great force. Illumination and function do not occur simultaneously; there is questioning and answering, the establishing of guest and host, and the blending of water and mud to form a paste.
To respond to capacities and engage with beings—if one is a person of transcendent capacity—one should seize the moment before the question is even raised and depart immediately;
this would still be a slight advantage.
Ascending the hall, he said: "O Great Assembly! Those who act for the sake of the Dharma do not shrink from losing body or life.
At the place of my late teacher Huangbo, I asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma three times, and each time I was struck with a staff as if by a bundle of mugwort."
"Now I am thinking of one more meal; who will take the first stroke? At that time, a monk came forward and said, "I will take the first stroke.
The Master handed him his staff. As the monk reached out to receive it, the Master struck him immediately.
Chan Master Xinghua Jiang addressed the assembly: "I hear that they shout in the front corridor and they shout in the back quarters.

My sons, do not shout blindly or shout recklessly. Even if you were to shout Xinghua into the void so that he fell down with not a breath of life left, and waited for me to recover and rise up, I would still say to you: 'Not yet. Why is this? Because I—"
"I have never scattered pearls inside a purple silk curtain. "I am going with you all," he said. "Why do you shout so wildly and recklessly?
Chan Master Sansheng Ran ascended the hall and said: "Whenever I meet someone, I come forth; yet when I come forth, I do not act for the sake of others. He then descended from his seat.
Chan Master Guankui Xian addressed the assembly, saying: "I received half a ladle from my grandfather Linji and half a ladle from my grandmother Moshan;
together they made one full ladle which I have consumed. To this very day, I remain satiated and never hungry."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The ten directions have no walls; the four sides have no gates. Bare and naked, clear and open—there is nothing to grasp.
He then descended from his seat.
Master Kung of Youzhou ascended the hall. When the assembly had gathered, a monk came forward and said, "What is it like when one intends to ask but does not ask?
The Master said, "Aha! The monk then gave a shout. The Master said, "Hmph! The monk shouted again. The Master picked up his staff. The monk said, "Blind!
The Master threw down the staff and said, "Today I have lost. The monk said, "The grass-robber has been utterly defeated," and returned to the assembly. The Master—
He pointed his hand toward the sky, made a single dot, and said, "Does anyone in the assembly discern this? If there is one who can discern it, come forth and speak before the assembly.
After a long silence, the Master said, "The eye upon the crown of the head cannot even perceive it," and then he descended from his seat.
Chan Master Yong of Nanyuan ascended the hall and said: "Upon the bare flesh-ball, it stands like a thousand-fathom cliff.
A monk asked, "Is it not you, Master, who said that upon the bare flesh-ball, it stands like a thousand-fathom cliff? The Master replied, "Yes. The monk then overturned the meditation seat.
The Master said, "This blind donkey is causing a disturbance. As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him.

Ascending the hall, he said, "People everywhere possess only the eye for the simultaneous act of pecking and hatching, but they do not possess the function of the simultaneous act of pecking and hatching.
A monk then asked, "What is the function of the simultaneous act of pecking and hatching? The Master said, "A master does not peck or hatch; it is the simultaneous act of pecking and hatching."
[The monk] said, "I lost it. [The Master] said, "This is still not where you asked me. How was it at the place where you asked?
The monk said, "I lost it. The Master then struck him. That monk did not accept this; later, while under Yunmen’s assembly, he heard two monks cite this story.
One monk asked, "At that time, why did Nan-yuan break his staff? Suddenly, the monk attained enlightenment.
Chan Master Fengxue Zhao ascended the hall and said: "As for the eye of study, when facing a critical moment, you must have the great function manifest before you."
Do not confine yourself to minor details. Even if you were to attain realization before a word is spoken, you would still be stuck in the shell, lost in its seal.

Though you might be thoroughly proficient in the meaning of a phrase, you could not avoid encountering wild views wherever you go. It must have been that until now you have relied on others for your understanding, like a bright pearl split in two.
I shall sweep all this away from you at once, so that each and every one of you becomes like a lion cub, letting out a roar of "Tsa-ha! with a gaping mouth.
He let out a roar. Standing like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high, who would dare look him straight in the eye? To look is to blind one's own eyes.
At that time, a monk asked, "What is the True Dharma Eye? The Master said, "I am already blind. The monk asked, "After you are blind, what then?
The Master said, "Reaching for the sky and groping on the ground."
Ascending the hall, he cited a poem by Hanshan: "The Brahmin has passed away, His soul and consciousness meet the Old Man Yan.
Though he has read all the books of a hundred kings, He cannot yet escape the beatings and interrogations. But with one invocation of 'Namo Buddha,' All shall attain the Way of Buddhahood.
A monk asked, "What is this one invocation of 'Namo Buddha'? The Master said, "The lamp connects to the phoenix wings, illuminating the hall; the moon reflects the lady's蛾眉 (yumei) brows."
Looking with a stern face, he ascended the hall and said:
"If even a single speck of dust is established, the state and its family will flourish, yet the village elders will frown.

If not even a single speck of dust is established, the state and its family will perish, yet the village elders will be at ease. If you can understand this clearly, you have no share in it; it is entirely the old monk’s. At this—

[The Master] said, "I do not understand. Yet, you, the Venerable One, are indeed the *ācārya*. You, the *ācārya*, and I can both enlighten the people of the world, and we can both blind the people of the world.
Do you wish to recognize the *ācārya*? [He] clapped once to the right—this is he.
Do you wish to recognize me, the old monk? [He] clapped once to the left—this is I."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "If you belong to the highest class of practitioners, each possesses personal verification; you need only briefly reach the required standard.

As for those of middling and lower capacities, each must be exceptionally talented. Birth occurs right where it is; extinction follows wherever one goes. It is like cracking a tortoise shell: if it cracks, a pattern is formed;
if it does not crack, it remains dull. If you wish to crack it, do not hesitate—crack it directly right here."
Ascending the hall: The three thousand swordsmen were ashamed to appear before Zhuang Zhou. With a vermilion eyebrow across his shoulder, could there be any error?
When he transforms into a leopard at a later time, look in five days. Take care!
Chan Master Shoushan Nian addressed the assembly from the high seat: "If you can realize the first phrase, you are fit to be a teacher to Buddhas and patriarchs.
If you can realize the second phrase, you are fit to be a teacher to devas and humans. If you can realize the third phrase, you will not even be able to save yourself.
At that time, a monk asked, "What is the first phrase? The Master said, "The great function does not raise an eyebrow; under the staff, blood must flow."
[The monk] asked, "Wherein lies compassion? The Master said, "I have sent you out through the three gates.

[The monk] asked, "What is the second phrase? The Master said, "I would not strike such a donkey-like fellow. [The monk] asked, "Whom do you intend to receive? The Master said, "If it is someone like this, what can be done? [The monk] asked, "What is the third phrase?
The Master said, "You understand how to ask, but no one can answer. [The monk] said, "The one responding right now is [the answer]."
"Who? The Master said, "Do not let outsiders know. [The monk] asked, "Of which phrase does the Master recommend one gain realization?
The Master said, "The moon sets at the third watch as he passes through the marketplace. [The monk] asked, "Vimalakīrti remained silent, and Mañjuśrī praised it as excellent.

What was the meaning of this? The Master said, "At that time, the audience surely did not think so. [The monk] asked, "If they did not think so, why did Vimalakīrti remain silent? The Master said, "Because he was not like them."
Furthermore, how is it so? The Master said, "Those who recognize kindness are few; those who betray kindness are many.
He then added, "If one were to discuss this matter, it is truly not even the footstep of a single original son. Thereupon, he descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, the Master said: "The three essentials must be attained with intimacy. First, do not bring questions to ask.
Do you understand? The question lies within the answer; the answer lies within the question. If you bring a question to ask, I, the old monk, am already beneath your feet.
If you hesitate or deliberate, there is no connection. At that time, a monk came forward and bowed. The Master struck him. The monk then asked: "Hanging up the staff in seclusion..."
"What about at the moment of the rock? The Master said, "Wrong. The monk said, "Wrong. The Master struck him again.
Chan Master Fenyang Shanzhao ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying: "In the gate of Fenyang there is a lion of the West River, crouching right at the entrance.
Whenever anyone comes, it bites them to death immediately. What skillful means is there to enter the gate of Fenyang?"
If you can see the man of Fenyang, you are fit to serve as a teacher to the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
If you do not see the man of Fenyang, you are all but standing dead on the spot. Is there anyone who can enter right now? You must enter quickly!
"Lest you fail your lifelong endeavor. You are not a guest of Longmen; take care not to suffer the 'dotting of the forehead.
Who, then, is a guest of Longmen? He pointed his staff at them all at once and said, "Withdraw quickly! Withdraw quickly! Be careful!"
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The ancient sages said: 'A single phrase must possess the three mysteries; each mystery must possess the three essentials.
Which phrase possesses these three mysteries and three essentials? Understand it quickly! Each of you should reflect: have you attained a sense of stability yet?
When the ancients of old went on pilgrimage, if they heard a single causal condition that was not yet clear within their minds, they would go directly [to seek its resolution].
Below, food and drink lack flavor, and sleep is restless. You must resolve this with urgency; do not treat it as a minor matter.
This is why the Great Awakened Elder appeared in the world for the sake of the one great cause.

Consider that when those of former times traveled on foot, it was not to roam mountains or play by the water, nor to view the splendors of prefectures and capitals. Their single garment and meager sustenance were all for the sake of the sacred mind.

Not yet having attained penetration, I have traveled far and wide on foot to resolve the profound mysteries, to transmit and propagate the teachings, to consult extensively with those of prior realization, and to draw near to those of high virtue.
This was solely for the purpose of continuing the lamp of the Buddha’s mind, to perpetuate the legacy of the patriarchs, to exalt the sacred lineage, and to guide future practitioners.
To benefit oneself and others, I have not forgotten the traces of my predecessors. Is there anyone present now who would engage in such deliberation? If there is—then [speak].
Come forth! Let us all deliberate. A monk asked, "What is the phrase for receiving a beginner?
The Master said, "You are a wandering monk. The monk asked, "What is the phrase for discerning a patch-robed monk? The Master said, "The sun rises in the west at dawn.

The monk asked, "What is the phrase for the true command being exercised? The Master said, "Having come from a thousand miles away, I look longingly upon your familiar face. The monk asked, "What is..."
"This is the sentence that establishes Heaven and Earth. The Master said, "In the continent of Uttarakuru, there grows long-grained rice; those who eat it have neither greed nor anger.
He then said, "Use these four turning phrases to test the monks of the world. As soon as you step forward, they are already tested. A monk asked, "What is the place where a student exerts effort?
The Master said, "At Jia Prefecture, they beat the great elephant. He then said: [The four turning phrases follow].
"What is the place where the student turns their body? The Master said, "In Shanfu, they water the iron ox. [The student] asked, "What is the place where the student attains intimacy?
The Master said, "In Xihe, they play with lions. He then said, "If a person understands these three phrases, they have already discerned the Three Mysteries.
There are further words of the Three Essentials remaining; you must certainly realize them. This is no trivial matter; I speak this for the sake of the great assembly."
The Verse says: The Three Mysteries and Three Essentials are difficult to distinguish; When the meaning is grasped, the Way is easy to approach.
A single phrase clearly encompasses all phenomena; On the Double Ninth, the chrysanthemums are fresh.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "Every single phrase must possess the three gates of mystery (*san-hsüan*). Each gate of mystery must possess the three essentials (*san-yao*). There is illumination and there is function;
sometimes illumination precedes function, sometimes function precedes illumination, sometimes illumination and function are simultaneous, and sometimes illumination and function are not simultaneous.
When illumination precedes function, I shall first consult with you; when function precedes illumination, you too..."
One must be such a person to achieve this. If illumination and function are simultaneous, how do you respond?
If illumination and function are not simultaneous, how do you then find your place?
Ascending the hall, the Master said: "Fenyang has three secrets; it is difficult for monks to discern them. If you intend to ask how they are, I shall drive my staff right through your head.
At that time, a monk asked, "What are the three secrets? The Master struck him. The monk bowed, and the Master said, "I shall provide a verse for all of them at once.
The First Secret: Guiding others is without fixed timing; clever words cannot fully express it. The clouds part..."

The moon in the blue sky. This is the second secret instruction. Radiating light to distinguish the worthy and the wise, through questions and answers, one nurtures the mind that benefits living beings and extracts the wedge from the eye.
This is the third secret instruction, spoken by a man from the Western Regions. The water of the Ji River flows past Silla; in the northern lands, they use tempered steel.
He asked again: "Is there anyone who understands? Let those who understand come forth and convey a message. If you wish to know the distance, do not merely—"
"Such as this! To merely record words and phrases and take them as the entirety of one's life—what benefit is there in that? Do not stand here for long; take care.
He ascended the hall and said to the assembly: "Now, one who expounds the Dharma must possess the Ten Wisdoms of Identical Reality. If one does not possess these Ten Wisdoms..."

The same in truth, yet unable to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, or to differentiate between the monastic and the lay; they cannot serve as eyes for gods and humans to discern right from wrong.
They are like a bird flying through the sky with broken wings, or like an arrow shot at a target with a severed string. Because the string is severed, the arrow does not hit the mark;
because the wings are broken, the bird cannot fly through the sky. If the string is strong and the wings firm, then both the arrow and the bird will pierce the target and the void. How so?
Birth is the ten wisdoms sharing the same reality. Together with the various elders, they are pointed out as follows: first, sharing the same substance; second, sharing the same great task;

third, sharing the same companionship in practice; fourth, sharing the same true aspiration; fifth, sharing the same universal pervasiveness; sixth, sharing the same fullness; seventh, sharing the same gains and losses.
Eighth, the same birth and killing; ninth, the same sound of roaring; tenth, the same entry. It is further asked: "With what kind of person does one enter together?
With whom does one roar with the same voice? What is this 'same birth and killing'? What thing is it that shares in gain and loss?"
Who is it that is equally endowed? What is it that is equally pervasive and universal? Who possesses an equally true resolve? Who is able to participate as an equal colleague?
Who is it that shares the same great matter? What object is of the same substance? Is there anyone who can point this out?
To those who can point it out, I shall not withhold my compassion; yet for those who cannot point it out, they have not yet attained the eye of study. You must discern this with utmost care.
You must recognize right from wrong; the true face is present right before you—it cannot be maintained for long. Be careful!

Master Xiangshan Xue of Ye County ascended the hall and said: "The lifeblood of the ancestral teachers—whether ordinary or holy, Nāgārjuna and Aśvaghoṣa, heaven and hell, the boiling cauldrons and burning furnaces, the ox-headed jailers, the myriad phenomena of the universe, the sun and moon and the stars—all these are [the Buddha-nature]."
Within this land, both sentient and insentient beings—pointing with his hand and drawing a single line—he said:
"All enter this school. Within this school, one can kill people, and one can also bring people to life. To kill people, one must possess the sword that kills;
to bring people to life, one must possess the phrase that brings them to life. What is the sword that kills? What is the phrase that brings to life? Come forth and speak it before the assembly!
"Look at the Way! If you cannot speak of it, you will have brought your entire life to naught.
Take care. He ascended the hall and, after a long silence, said: "Now, those who travel as Zen practitioners must truly reflect upon themselves. To study, one must possess the eye of a student;
to perceive the ground, one must attain the phrase of the ground. Only then is there a possibility of mutual intimacy, such that one is not deluded by various external conditions."
Nor does one fall into the evil realms. How can this be fully understood? At times, the words reach [the mind] but the meaning does not;
one falsely conditions upon external objects and discriminates among reflected phenomena. At times, the meaning reaches [the mind] but the words do not;

it is like the blind men feeling an elephant, each asserting a different conclusion. At times, both meaning and words reach [the mind]; the realm of empty space is shattered, and radiance illuminates the ten directions. At times...
Neither thought nor words can reach it; a blind man runs hither and thither. Suddenly, without realizing it, he falls into a deep pit.
Chan Master Shending Yin ascended the hall. Jue said of Dongshan: "Greed, anger, and ignorance are utterly ignorant; fortunately, today I have come to recognize them.
When they walk, I strike; when they sit, I beat them. Entrust this to the Mind-Prince to investigate minutely. For immeasurable kalpas.
"Coming, they are not liberated. He asked, "Do you three know this or not? The Master said, "The ancients spoke thus; at Shending, it is not so.

Greed, anger, and ignorance truly have no knowing. Throughout the twelve hours of the day, let them be as they are: when walking, they go; when sitting, they follow. Entrusted to the mind-king, what could one possibly do?
Since immeasurable kalpas past, there has been primordial liberation; why need one ask further?"
"Knowing and not knowing.
Chan Master Cong of Guyin addressed the assembly: "If you can speak the first phrase, you have burst forth from within the stone.
If you can speak the second phrase, you have been brought forward by the inquiry. If you can speak the third phrase, you will not even be able to save yourself."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "A white cat with five claws, fierce and predatory; raised in the hall, it leaves no trace of insects.

This is clearly the method for securing one's position atop a tree; take care not to grant outsiders the right to claim it. "What is the phrase that grants outsiders the right to claim it? Do not misrepresent it."
Chan Master Guanghui Lian ascended the hall and said: "When the two head seats of Linji saw each other, they both let out a shout at the same time.
Everyone, tell me: was there a guest and a host, or not? If you say there was, you are nothing but a blind fellow; if you say there was not..."
This too is a blind fellow. Neither existent nor non-existent. Ten thousand *li* to Yaizhou.
If you can speak here, I will give you thirty blows; if you cannot speak, I will also give you thirty blows. When a monk reaches this point—
"How can one emerge from this mountain monk's circle? After a long silence, he said: "Alas!
The frogs and earthworms leap up to the Thirty-three Heavens and crash into Mount Sumeru, shattering it into a hundred pieces. Taking up his staff, he said:
"A troop of unperforated iron hammers! Retreat quickly, retreat quickly!"
Chan Master Sanjiao Song ascended the hall and said: "Mañjuśrī wields his sword and traverses Mount Wutai; Tang Ming blocks the path at once, cutting off all delusions.
The Buddhas of the three periods have not yet emerged from the vehicle of the teachings; like fish swimming beneath a net, it is difficult to pass through the Dragon Gate.

He casts his hook across the four seas, seeking only the fierce dragon. To discourse on the profound beyond the categories is to seek out those with true knowledge. If one were to proclaim the essence of the School..."
The essential point is this: Sumeru must be ground to dust; if one speaks of Buddhas or Patriarchs, the waters of the sea must dry up.

When the precious sword is brandished, its radiance extends ten thousand miles. I grant you a single path for speaking in accordance with the universal principle, yet when the throat is seized, where can all of you draw breath?
Chan Master Shishuang Yuan addressed the assembly from the high seat: "All Buddhas, as well as the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* dharma of all Buddhas, all emerge from this sutra.
He then held up his staff and said, "This is Nan-yuan’s staff; which one is the sutra?
After a long silence, he said, "The subsequent text is lengthy; it shall be entrusted to a future day. He then gave a shout.
One shout. Descending from the seat.
Ascending the hall, Baoying of old said: "If you can realize it through the first phrase, you are fit to be a teacher to the Buddhas and patriarchs.

If you can realize it through the second phrase, you are fit to be a teacher to gods and humans. If you can realize it through the third phrase, you will not even be able to save yourself. Daowu, however—
Not so. In the first phrase, you grasp it and it is like mixing mud with water. In the second phrase, you grasp it and you bind yourself with no rope.
In the third phrase, you grasp it and all four corners touch the ground. Therefore it is said: "When he arises, the seas are calm and the rivers clear, and travelers clear the way;
when he stays, heaven and earth lose their color, and the sun and moon have no light. Where, then, do you people find a place to vent your breath?
"Is there anyone here who still has breath to vent? If there is, come forth and vent it before the assembly.
If there is none, I, Daowu, shall go out and vent it for you. He then let out a single sigh, set down his staff, and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Daowu beats the drum; those from the four great continents are fellow practitioners. When the staff is held horizontally, it encompasses the heavens and the earth;
when the alms bowl is turned upside down, it covers the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Now I ask you all: where do you establish yourselves and find your livelihood? If you know, then go to the northern continent of Kuru and eat your porridge and rice. If you do not..."
"Understood. [The Master] ascended the long couch, partook of gruel and rice, and entered the hall.

With a single shout he distinguished guest from host; illumination and function were exercised simultaneously. "If you wish to understand the meaning within this, it is like striking the third watch at noon.
He then let out a shout and said: "Tell me, is this the guest or the host? Is there anyone here who can distinguish them? If...

It is also divided thus: "Three thousand blows in the morning, eight hundred blows in the evening. If you have not yet attained this, the old monk has lost his advantage. [He] ascended the hall and said:
"Now, as for a patriarchal teacher, they snatch away the jewel from the poor man’s garment and investigate the point of realization of those who have reached the Way.
If it were not so, they would all be nothing but fellows who merely mix mud and water. After a long silence, he said: "When meeting a swordsman on the road, one must present one's sword. Not...
"Is this a poem? Do not offer poems. He gave a shout. Entering the hall, he said:
"I have a word that cuts off deliberation and forgets conditions; it cannot be skillfully explained, it requires only mind-to-mind transmission.
Furthermore, there is one more phrase: nothing surpasses a direct presentation. But what is this one phrase of direct presentation? After a long silence, he struck with his staff.
He drew a line and gave a shout.
Entering the hall, he faced west while walking toward the east. "The Big Dipper is precisely in the Palace of Separation. Where has the Way ever gone?
A cowherd boy lies asleep astride his ox. "Take care!"
Ascending the hall, he said: "I do not ask you about spring’s growth and summer’s increase; tell me, what is the single phrase beneath the feet of all of you?
After a long pause, he said, "The Abbot of Huaguang Temple," and then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The medicine is abundant, yet the illness is grave; the net is fine, yet the fish are dense.
He then descended from his seat and addressed the assembly, striking the meditation seat once with his staff and saying: "Does the assembly understand? It is not said:
'With one strike, all that is known is forgotten; there is no longer any need for cultivation. Those who have realized the Way in all quarters declare this to be the highest capacity. Incense.
Yan has awakened in this way; he has clearly realized the Tathāgata-dhyāna, yet he has not even dreamed of the Patriarchal-dhyāna.
Tell me, what excellence does the Patriarchal-dhyāna possess? If you seek its principles within words, you will mislead future generations.

Even if one were to accept it under the staff, one would still betray the former sages. All phenomena are fundamentally tranquil; it is only people who create their own clamor. Therefore, I, this mountain monk—
He resided at Fuyan. There he beheld only the realm of Fuyan: rising late and sleeping early, sometimes clouds would arise over the azure cliffs and the moon would set into the cold pond.
The kalavinka birds flew and sang before the Prajna Terrace; the fragrance of the śāla flowers wafted from the slopes of Mount Zhurong.
Grasping a slender staff, he sat upon a flat rock and occasionally discussed the profound and subtle with the monks of the Five Lakes. His head was ashen and his face was covered in dust.
Dwelling in Xinghua, one sees only the house style of Xinghua: welcoming guests and seeing them off; the gates connect with the city, where carriages and horses throng.
One hears the songs of fishermen on the Xiao and Xiang rivers, the cries of monkeys at Mount Lu, and the melodies of stringed and bamboo instruments entering the ears from time to time.

Furthermore, one daily discusses the Way of Chan with eminent figures from all quarters, forgetting the passage of years and months. Now tell me: is this dwelling in deep mountains or residing in the city? Is it still...?
"Is there superiority and inferiority, or not? Try to say something. After a long silence, he said: "In every place is Maitreya; there is no gate and no Sudhana.
He ascended the hall and said: "The Heart-Seal of the Patriarchs: one seal seals the sky, one seal seals the water, and one seal seals the mud. Now..."
"Is there anyone who cannot be sealed? Try and bring forth a single phrase from beneath your heels.
Even if you could speak it—boldly and clearly—you must not, above all, pass through the gate of a patch-robed monk. Now tell me, what excellence does this patch-robed monk possess?
After a long silence, he said: "The three-inch blade of the king of men; everywhere are swords and spears. He gave a shout.
[The Master] leaned on his staff and descended from the seat. He ascended the hall and said:
"The sky has already brightened; the drum has already sounded. The assembly of noble ones has gathered in full, with palms joined. Is there anyone here now who does not join their palms?
If there is, the Nirgrantha will rejoice; if there is none, Gautama will be provoked to anger. I have stood for a long time; take care."
Ascending the hall: North of the mountain, south of the mountain; north of the mountain, south of the mountain. Sun and moon shine together, yet heaven and earth are dark.
The great oceans and rivers all emit light; meeting Avalokiteśvara, one asks about Maitreya. Take care!
Chan Master Jue of Langya ascended the hall and said: "How marvelous! The Buddhas of the ten directions are originally but flowers in the eye.

If you wish to recognize the flowers in the eye, they are originally the Buddhas of the ten directions. If you wish to recognize the Buddhas of the ten directions, they are not the flowers in the eye.

If you wish to recognize the flowers in the eye, they are not the Buddhas of the ten directions. If you understand this clearly, the fault lies with the Buddhas of the ten directions; if you have not yet understood this..."
The śrāvakas break into dance; the pratyekabuddhas prepare their makeup. Take care! Entering the hall:
If you wish to know the eternally abiding body, you should contemplate this decaying physical form. If you wish to know the eternally abiding nature, you should contemplate this staff.
This staff swallows up Mount Sumeru; Mount Sumeru swallows up the staff. When a monk reaches this point—
If you hesitate or deliberate, the sword will fall from the shoulder and the wheel descend; with an iron heart, one reaches the furthest corner of the sea.
[He] struck the meditation seat and descended from it.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are all causes of birth and death; yet seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are precisely the very foundation of liberation.
It is like a lion’s backward leap: north, south, east, and west, it knows no fixed stopping place. You people of this assembly—"
If you still do not understand, do not fail the Elder Śākyamuni. Hūṃ!
Entering the hall, the mountain monk has today explained it through for all of you. O clear-eyed monks, do not sit in meditation in the mud. Take care.

Ascending the hall, he said: "The heavens are so high they cannot be measured; the earth is so vast it can never be known. Flakes of white clouds fly over the mountain peaks; the green waters murmur swiftly down the mountain ravines.
I shall not ask you about the phrase 'rising in the east and sinking in the west. But as for the phrase 'before birth and after death,' how do you speak of it?
After a long silence, he said: "The weather is cold; go drink some tea."
Ascending the hall, he said: "A-he-he! What is this? When the mouth opens, it is already a transgression to close it. A light boat with a short oar floats upon the heart of the waves;
let the raincoat and bamboo hat wear out as they may. Heh!"
Ascending the hall, he said: "To eliminate wild bandits and sweep away the portents of chaos—this is still a matter of military merit.

For ruler and minister to be in accord, for the seas to be calm and the rivers clear—this is still a matter of the realm of Dharma. What, then, is the fundamental business of a monk? After a long silence, he said:
'The golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net still lingers in the water; the stone horse on its return path emerges from the silken cage.'"
Ascending the hall, he said: "When receiving words, you must understand the fundamental source; do not establish your own rules and regulations.
If anyone can deliver a phrase that penetrates all directions, I shall cut my own throat to apologize to them."
Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said: "Sometimes this mountain monk’s single blow acts as a net that covers the heavens, striking down the handsome hawks and swift falcons.
Sometimes this single blow acts as a fine-meshed net, scooping up clams and catching shrimp. And sometimes this single blow—"
Sometimes he manifests as a golden-haired lion; at other times, with a single blow of his staff, he becomes a frog or an earthworm.

When I, this mountain monk, strike you once, how will you deliberate upon it? If you can distinguish the black from the white, then the eye upon the tip of my staff will open and illuminate the four quarters of the world.
If you have not yet attained this, let him remain standing by the ancient screen, waiting for the brushstrokes of the artist to enter.
A painted image. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The fish in the water suffer pain; the birds nesting in the forest are startled. At twilight, no drum is struck; at midday, the third watch is beaten.
"O Zen practitioners, since it is already midday, why is the third watch being struck? After a long silence, he said: "Yesterday I saw..."
The willows hang green; now we encounter the falling leaves turning yellow.
Entering the hall, he said: "To advance is death; to retreat is extinction. To neither advance nor retreat is again to fall into the realm of 'nothingness.
Why? Though Chang’an is pleasant, it is not a place for long-term residence."
