"This single point has already washed away the waters of the four seas, yet it cannot be cast off."

Ascending the hall, he said: "To exhaust the subtle is to lose the root; to embody the wondrous is to forfeit the source. A single phrase cuts off the current, reaching the ultimate depth of the profound and mysterious.
Thus, where the golden needle is held in secret, its brilliance is not revealed; when the jade thread passes through, it silently unfolds extraordinary colors. Even so."
This is still a case of mutual illumination through both [aspects]. But tell me, when skill and clumsiness reach their limit, how can they be entrusted? After a long silence, he said:
"Where the cloud-vines are exquisite, the green shadows close together; on the high and low crag-trees, the emerald locks are deep."

Ascending the hall, he said: "To turn one's function to accord with the station is for those who are heading forward; it is like 'Jade hidden in the Jingshan Mountains'—precious. To turn one's station to accord with the function is for those who are returning;
it is like 'a flake of snow on a red furnace'—springtime. When both function and station are turned, the whole body is unimpeded; letting go of the hand, one departs from dependence.
The stone woman ascends the loom at night; the secret chamber has no one to sweep it. At this very moment, breath is utterly stilled."
"How do you entrust this phrase? After a long silence, he said: "Returning to the root, the wind drops the leaves; the moon shines everywhere, the pond is empty.
Chan Master Tiantong Jue ascended the hall and said: "The yellow gate curtains hang down—who transmits the family message?

The purple silk curtain is closed—secretly scattering precious pearls. At such a time, there is nothing that sight or hearing can reach, and nothing that words or explanations can attain. It is like..."
How can one attain the news? Returning from a dream, the night colors dawn with indistinct clarity; smiling, he points to the family tradition—a spring in full and profuse bloom.
Entering the hall, he said: "The mind cannot conceive it; the mouth cannot discuss it. Even if you step back and take up the burden, you must strictly avoid facing it head-on."
Avoiding the taboo: Wind and moon, cold and clear, at the ancient ferryhead; the night boat turns upon the crystal ground.
Entering the Hall: The True School exists from the empty kalpa; before sound, one asks of one’s own person. A destitute new livelihood, a pure and white ancestral style.
Truly beyond the Three Vehicles, it is within the single seal of vast silence. Yet coming back to act as a different species, the ten thousand streams flow forth of their own accord.
Facing east, Master Chan Daohong Yu ascended the hall and said: "I cite the story of Shipin instructing Jiashan: 'You must ensure there are no traces where you hide your body;
do not hide your body where there are no traces. For thirty years at Yaoshan, I have clarified nothing other than this matter."
Why do people nowadays act so hastily? The Cinnabar Mountain has no variegated phoenixes; the precious palace does not retain its crowns.
At times he is doltish, at times he is deluded; who among those on their own paths could know this?

Chan Master Zhifeng of Taimu ascended the hall and said: "Leisurely strolling within the wondrously luminous home of ultimate reality, A step taken and the body shifts, pointing toward the setting clouds.
Though boundless white clouds remain unseen, One rides the bright moon at night out among the reeds."
Chan Master Zhēnrú ascended the hall and said: "If you personally accept and take responsibility for the affairs of the void kalpa, then in daily life everything is fully manifest;
what leakage could there be? It is precisely right to return home and sit in peace, letting the snow cover the green mountains, without leaving behind a single character to hang upon your breast.

Who cares about the waves tossing upon the surface of the water? But tell me: how is it when the orthodox does not establish the mysterious and the partial does not attach itself to things? (He paused) "A single phrase like this—"
How can one bring this up for comparison? When the shuttle-head is not caught by the warp-threads, the patterns unfold freely and the meaning is naturally distinct.
Master Zhintong Shen addressed the assembly from the high seat: "Coming, he does not enter the gate; going, he does not leave the house. With no trace of coming or going, how can one proclaim this?
It reaches the point where the ancient path is sealed with moss and the rhesus monkey leaves no tracks; the moon of Cangwu locks the vermilion phoenix away."
"Resting. This is why it is said: "Where the body is hidden, there are no traces; where there are no traces, do not hide the body.
If you can act thus, going and staying will be without dependence, and there will be no facing or turning away. Do you understand this thoroughly? Now they disperse like clouds and cranes.
When you and I forget one another, the profound mystery is present in every encounter.
Master Chan Zong of Xuedou ascended the hall and said: "Every person has a nostril; only Shanquan has none."
Why does he have none? Twenty years ago, they were snatched away by someone. Everyone has two eyes, yet only Shanquan has no eyes.
Why does he have none? They were exchanged for *muhangzi* (wooden prayer beads) by someone.
Every person has a skull; only Shanquan has no skull. Why does he have none? Because he has borrowed someone else’s to serve as a dung-scoop.
He then called to the assembly, saying: "There are no nostrils, there are no eyes, and there is no skull.
Do you all recognize Shanquan? If you do not recognize him, it is you who are burying Shanquan."
Perhaps not yet so. Listen further to this verse: A mud ox at the bottom of the ravine has its face gilded with gold; A stone woman on the mountain peak wears true crimson.
Mushrooms grow upon the hitching stake for donkeys; It is not merely the misty clouds at Mount Xianglu.
Chan Master Huí of Jingci ascended the hall and said: "Nests know the wind; burrows know the rain. What is sweet is sweet; what is bitter is bitter.
There is no need for calculation or deliberation. Five times five has always been twenty-five. All manner of arrangements ultimately arrive at the ordinary.
These are the words of those who have thoroughly studied in the monastic groves. Do you all understand? The rustic elder knows nothing of Yao or Shun."
Power! Drumming the drums with a deep *dong-dong* sound, they sacrifice to the River God.
Ascending the hall: "The spirit of the valley; the pivot of the essential. Within this, one may investigate from the side and find the marvel by returning to the path.

Though the clouds move, they are ever at rest; though the moon is obscured, it shines all the more clearly. Guest and host intersect; the orthodox and the deviant are both reached. When spring ends in the Ten Islands...
The flowers wither and fall. The coral groves are bathed in the brilliant radiance of the sun. Entering the hall:
When skin and flesh have fallen away, all boundaries are severed; clearly understanding body and mind, not a single thing exists.

Wondrously entering the profound and tranquil realm of the Way, the jade-like person uprightly drives the white ox-cart. In this field of wondrous clarity, those who reach it are rare; ordinary consciousness and emotion—

It cannot be reached by the intellect; only through direct realization can it be known. The child of white clouds shines with self-illumination; the father of green mountains stands tall and ever-present.
The pivot of the mechanism is the light behind the crown; the wisdom accords with the eye before the kalpas. Thus it is said: "The road of Xinfeng is steep and rugged."
The caves of Xinfeng are profound and lush; those who ascend do so without wavering, and those who roam do so without haste.
Though there are pavilions and halls, visitors are rare; though groves and springs abound, they do not grow with ordinary trees.

O virtuous practitioners of Zen: the supreme point beyond is noble and difficult to clarify. Upon the crystal palace, one does not claim supremacy; before the emerald curtain, one must still keep company.
At such a time, when the needle and thread have pierced through and the True School remains undiminished, how should one act?
With a head full of white hair, he leaves the mountain valleys; at midnight, he pierces the clouds to enter the marketplace.
Ascending the hall, he cited the Dharma-body verse of Master Fu: "Empty-handed, one grasps a hoe; Walking, one rides a water buffalo.
A person passes over the bridge; The bridge flows, but the water does not flow. Master Yunmen said:
"Whether you come from the east, west, south, or north, each of you comes riding a water buffalo. Although this is so, even if there were a thousand heads..."
"Of ten thousand heads, one only needs to recognize this single head. The Master said, "Yunmen is usually dry and parched, so that a probe cannot penetrate him;
yet here, he is able to drag through mud and water. Do you all wish to see this single head right now?
The weather is somewhat cold; each of you return to the hall."

Ascending the hall, the Master raised the dialogue concerning the wind and the banner. He said: "If you can place an eye upon the very place where the wind and banner move, then you are indeed the patriarch (the monk).
If you lose that eye at the place where the wind and banner move, then you are merely the wind and banner. Should this not yet be so, it is neither wind nor banner, nor is it mind;

the patch-robed monks merely exert themselves in vain like driving a needle through ice. When the rain has passed over the mountain retreats, the twilight smoke clears; lie down and listen to the cool breeze."
The wind rises in the bamboo grove. Chan Master Gong of Ruiyan ascends the hall: Spring wind, willow brows; spring birds warble with a hundred tongues.
A single heart of the Patriarch—leaks forth in two places. Without moving a step, one returns home; habitual outflows are instantly extinguished. Like casting a jewel into the dark...
The awns of the grain pierce through the golden needle-holes at dawn; deep, firm, and profoundly remote, who would discern them if no one were there?
How pitiable are these living beings! Yet every single thing follows the same track. Do not think of Amitābha; *Namo Ganshijue* (Homage to the Dry Dung-Pillar)!
One must never speak of this before those who lack wisdom and are deluded.
Chan Master Yunmen Wenyan ascended the hall and said: "I have no choice but to tell you all: 'Directly beneath, there is nothing.

This already constitutes a burying of you; yet you still wish to step forward, chasing after words and phrases, seeking understanding through a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions, setting up extensive difficulties and arguments, only to gain a slippery tongue that leads you further and further away from the Way."
When will there ever be a time of rest? If this matter were merely within the realm of words, how could the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings not themselves consist of words?
For what reason, then, is it said to be "a separate transmission outside the teachings"? If it were obtained through scholarly understanding or intellectual ingenuity—
It is simply that even when the sages of the Ten Grounds preach the Dharma like clouds and rain, they are still rebuked for their realization of nature as being "like viewing through fine gauze.
From this, one knows that all those with a mind are worlds apart from the enlightened.
Nevertheless, for one who has attained the Way, how could the fire of the path ever burn the mouth? All day long they speak of matters, yet it never once lingers upon their lips or teeth. Unfettered.
I have once spoken of a single word. Throughout the day one wears clothes and eats rice, yet one has never touched a single grain of rice nor hung a single thread of silk.
Even so, this is still merely talk regarding the gateway of the teaching. One must truly attain such realization for it to be so.
If we speak from the standpoint of the Zen monk’s school, presenting one's wit within the words is but a vain effort of lingering thought; even if one were to do so under a single phrase—
"To take it upon yourself is still to be a drowsy fellow. At that time, a monk asked, "What is the one phrase?
The Master said, "Lift [the needle]. He ascended the hall and said: "The Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings—whether explained horizontally or vertically;

the old monks of the world, whether speaking in straight lines or diagonals—bring me the principle you claim to have explained, even if it were as small as the point of a needle, and let me see it. To speak in such a manner is already to be a fabrication."
A doctor treating a dead horse. Nevertheless, how many actually reach this realm? I do not dare hope that you will have echoes within your words and conceal the blade’s edge within your phrases;
yet, in a single blink of an eye amidst a thousand differences, the wind is calm and the waves are still. I humbly pray you will partake.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "All you brothers have come from all quarters seeking out masters of learning to resolve the matter of birth and death.
Surely wherever you have been, there were no venerable elders who spoke words of compassionate skillful means? Is there any phrase that you have not yet penetrated?
Come forward and cite it, so that I, this old man, may deliberate upon it with you all. Is there such a one? Is there? At that time, a monk stepped forward, intending to speak.
Questioning him next, the Master said, "Go, go! The road to the Western Heaven is long, more than a hundred thousand miles," and he immediately descended from his seat.
Later, while ascending the hall, he heard the sound of the bell and said, "The world is so vast and wide; why does the sound of the bell wear the seven-fold robe?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "I cite one phrase to teach you how to directly take it up; that is already like spitting filth upon your head.
Even if you were to pick up a single hair and instantly illuminate the entire world with it, that would still be like gouging out flesh to create a sore."
Even so, you must truly reach this very state before it will do; if you have not yet reached it, do not engage in empty pretension.
You must instead take a step back and search within the root of your own being to see what kind of principle this is.
There is not even a hair’s breadth of anything here to provide you with intellectual understanding or to cause you doubt. Furthermore, as for you all—
Each and every one of you possesses a matter within yourselves where the great function is manifest before you;

it requires not even a hair’s breadth of effort from you, and you are no different from the Patriarchs and Buddhas. It is simply that your own root of faith is shallow and thin, while your evil karma is thick and heavy.
Suddenly, many horns have sprouted. Why do you carry your alms-bag across thousands of villages and ten thousand miles, enduring such humiliation?
Furthermore, what is lacking for all of you? What great man does not possess this share? Even if one can take it up alone, it is still insufficient;
thus, one must not allow oneself to be deceived by others or accept their directions. As soon as you see the Old Master...
If you open your mouth, I would simply take this stone and shove it into your mouth. It is like flies on excrement, competing to swarm and lick it away;
three or five of them gather their heads together to deliberate, crying out in bitter grievance.
"Brothers," the ancient masters of old could do nothing for you all, so they skillfully offered a word or a phrase as a means to provide you with a way of entry. Know this!
Set aside such matters for a moment and exert some effort yourself; is this not a point where you have a slight measure of intimacy?
Hurry, hurry! Time does not wait for man; one cannot guarantee that the next breath will follow the out-breath.
What other use have you for body and mind elsewhere? You must take heed; be careful. Adieu.

Ascending the hall, he said: "The Buddha-dharma is indeed most abundant; it is only that our tongues are too short. After a long silence, he said: "Now they are long! Ascending the hall again, he said:
"As soon as a single word is raised, a thousand carts follow the same ruts. To encompass even a mote of dust is still but a teaching of the gate of transformation."
"If one is a patch-robed monk, how should it be? "If one deliberates here upon the meaning of the Buddhas and the meaning of the Patriarchs, the single path of Caoxi will sink away.
Is there anyone who can speak of this? Come forward, whoever can speak. A monk asked, "What is the discourse that transcends the Buddhas and surpasses the Patriarchs?
The Master said, "A sesame cake. [The monk] said, "What connection is there between this and that? The Master said:
"Clearly, what connection is there? He then said: 'All of you have reached a point where there is nothing more to be done.

When you hear someone speak of the meaning of the Patriarchs, you immediately ask about talk that transcends Buddhas and Patriarchs. But tell me, what do you call a Buddha? What do you call a Patriarch?
First, explain the principle of transcending Buddhas and Patriarchs. You ask about 'exiting the three realms,' yet you yourself hold..."
Viewing it from the perspective of the three realms, where is there any hearing, sensation, or cognition that obstructs you?
What sensory objects of sound or dharmas of form are there for you to perceive? What kind of vessel are you perceiving? Why do you take that as a view of differentiation?

The ancient sages could do nothing about it; they threw themselves across for the sake of beings. To say "the entire body is the whole truth" means that in every single thing, the essence cannot be grasped.
When I tell you that there is nothing at all right here, you have already buried it.
If you truly have no point of entry, then for now, investigate and contemplate it by yourself. Aside from putting on clothes, eating food, defecating, and urinating, what else is there?
Why do you give rise to all these various kinds of deluded thoughts out of nowhere?
Furthermore, there is another type who acts as if it were a matter of casual ease, gathering together to learn the conversational paths of the ancients.
With a consciousness that clings to and records deluded thoughts and conjectures, you claim, "I have understood the Buddha-dharma.
You do nothing but talk of entanglements and pass your time according to your own whims; yet you still complain that it does not meet your expectations.

Abandoning your parents, teachers, and elders, you travel thousands of miles away. What kind of urgent necessity drives such a wild scavenger as you to wander on pilgrimage? (He strikes with his staff.)

[The Master] descended from his seat and entered the hall. He said, "One must know that the times have grown turbid and we live in an age of decline. Lately, monks go north claiming to pay homage to Mañjuśrī, and go south claiming to travel to Mount Heng.
To practice pilgrimage in such a manner is for them to be mere 'name-monks,' pointlessly consuming the offerings of the faithful."
Alas, alas! When questioned, you are like black lacquer—merely indulging your own nature as time passes by.

Even if there are three or two of you who are wild students of much learning, memorizing discursive paths and seeking out similar phrases everywhere, you seek validation from elder masters while treating those of superior caliber with contempt.
You thus create karma of meager merit. On the day Yama, King of Hell, drives his nails into you, do not say: [“I did not know!”]
No one has told you this. If you are a beginner or a junior student, you must exert your spirit; do not merely memorize what others have said.
Much emptiness is not as good as a little reality; otherwise, in the future, you will only deceive yourself. What business is there? Step forward!
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "I observe that you all cannot even grasp the meaning within two or three turns of the teaching.
What benefit is there in vainly donning the patched robe? Do you understand? I shall explain it for you.

In the future, when you travel to various regions, if you see an elder master raise a finger or hold up a whisk and say, 'This is Chan; this is the Way,' simply take your staff, break his head, and go on your way."
If it were not so, you would all fall into the retinue of the celestial Māra and destroy my school.
If you truly do not understand, then look within the thicket of entanglements. I have always told you:

within every atom of every land, the Buddhas of the three periods of time, the twenty-eight patriarchs of the Western Heaven, and the six patriarchs of the Tang lands—all are preaching the Dharma upon the tip of this staff. Divine.

Penetrating transformation and manifestation, the sound responds throughout the ten directions, freely traversing both vertically and horizontally. Do you understand? If you do not, do not attempt to deceive yourself with empty words.
Even so, have you yet seen with true and authentic clarity? Even if you reach such a state, you have not yet glimpsed it in a dream.
A monk-sandhika, amidst the Three Families Village, does not encounter a single person. Suddenly, he picks up his staff.
He drew one line and said, "All is contained right here. He drew another line and said, "All emerges from right here.
"Take care," he said. Ascending the hall, he said: "Awakening to the Way through sound; clarifying the mind through form. Thereupon, he raised his hand and said, "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva."
He paid money to buy a *hūbǐng* (crisp cake), then let go of his hand and said, "So it turns out it was just a steamed bun.

Ascending the hall, he said: "Within heaven and earth, amidst the universe, there is a treasure hidden within the mountain of form (*rūpa-śaila*). [The Master] takes the lantern and places it inside the Buddha Hall;
he brings the triple gate and puts it upon the lantern. What do you say to this? He provided his own substitute response: "Chasing after things."
The mind shifts. It is also said: "Clouds arise and thunder resounds.
He ascended the hall, held up his staff, and said: "Ordinary people, being substantialist, call it 'existent. Those of the Two Vehicles, through analytical reduction, call it 'non-existent.
Pratyekabuddhas call it 'illusory existence. Bodhisattvas realize that its very substance is emptiness. As for us monks, when we see a staff, we simply call it a staff."
[The Master] held his staff. "When walking, simply walk; when sitting, simply sit.

You must not move or touch [anything]. He ascended the hall. "The lid of the box covers heaven and earth; the eyes weigh every ounce and grain. Without involving worldly conditions, how do you take this up?
The assembly had no reply. [The Master] spoke on their behalf, saying: "A single arrowhead pierces the three barriers."
Ascending the hall, the Master said: "You sons of the Buddha, do not engage in false conceptualization. Heaven is heaven; earth is earth; mountains are mountains;
waters are waters; monks are monks; laypeople are laypeople. After a long silence, he said: "Bring me the mountain on which the altar stands! A monk then asked:
"When a student sees mountains as mountains and waters as waters, what then? The Master replied: "Why do you ride upon the Buddha at the Main Gate?"
The attendant passed by the Hall and said, "In that case, there is no longer any deluded thought. The Master said, "Give me back the *huatou*!
He ascended the hall and said, "If you do not find resonance, first seek a point of entry. The myriad Buddhas of the fine dust are upon your own tongue."
The Three Baskets of the Holy Teachings are beneath your very heels. It would be better for you to awaken;
is there anyone who has awakened? Come forth and speak before the assembly.
Addressing the assembly: The entire world of the ten directions, the heavens and earth—[the Master] draws a circle with his staff and says: "Reduced to a hundred fragments!

As for the Three Vehicles and the Twelve Divisions of the Teaching, and the coming of Bodhidharma from the West—if you let these pass, it will not do; if you do not let them pass, they cannot withstand even a single shout.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "True emptiness does not destroy existence; true emptiness is not different from form. A monk then asked, "What is true emptiness?
The Master said, "Do you hear the sound of the bell? The monk replied, "This is the sound of the bell. The Master said, "When will you ever dream of it? (i.e., never).
Ascending the hall, the Master said: "On this level ground there are countless dead people; those who can pass through the thorn forest are true adepts.
At that time, a monk came forward and said, "If that is so, then the first seat in the hall has something superior. The Master said, "Suru suru."
Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said: "The staff has transformed into a dragon and swallowed up the universe.
From where could the mountains, rivers, and the great earth have come?"
Addressing the assembly: "When the Great Function manifests, no fixed rules remain. At that time, a monk asked, "What is the Great Function manifesting?
The Master picked up his staff and cried out in a loud voice, "Śākyamuni Buddha has arrived!"
Ascending the hall, he asked, "Do you wish to recognize the Patriarch? Pointing with his staff, he said, "The Patriarch is leaping and bounding right above your head!"
Do you wish to recognize the eyes of the Patriarchs? They are right beneath your heels. He further said:
"This is the food and drink used for sacrifices to the gods and spirits. Nevertheless, even the gods and spirits can never be satiated."

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "There are two kinds of illnesses when light does not penetrate through to liberation. First, there is the lack of clarity in all places, as if there were an object before one's face.
Second, even if one has penetrated through so that all phenomena are empty, there is still a lingering sense that something exists;

this too is light not penetrating through. Furthermore, there are two kinds of illnesses regarding the Dharma-body. Even if one attains the Dharma-body, it is because attachment to dharmas has not been forgotten."

The view of a self still persists; you remain sitting within the vicinity of the Dharma-body—this is one thing. Even if you manage to penetrate through to the Dharma-body, it must not be left as it is.
If you examine it closely, what trace of breath remains? That too is a sickness.
Cen Master Deshan Mi ascended the hall and said: "I have three phrases to show you all. One phrase covers heaven and earth;
one phrase cuts off the flow of all streams; one phrase follows the waves and rides the currents. How will you distinguish them?
If you can distinguish them, you have the capacity for study. If you cannot distinguish them, you will simply roll along the roads of Chang'an."
Ascending the hall: Those who come in this manner present a ready-made case; those who do not come in this manner merely set up a target and invite an arrow.
Those who come neither in this nor that manner are like Xu Liu carrying a single board. Even such swift and sharp brilliance still leaves one as a dullard.
Ten thousand miles of cloudless sky—the blue heavens remain.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the case where Linji addressed the assembly, saying: "Those who come this way are as if they have lost something; those who do not come this way bind themselves without a rope.
Throughout the twelve hours of the day, do not engage in random deliberation. Whether you understand or do not understand, it is all entirely wrong.
I speak clearly and plainly like this, leaving it to everyone under heaven to criticize and disparage me. The Master said: "The ancient mirror is one zhang wide."
The rafter of the hall is three feet long. How wide is your small alms bowl?
Master Dongshan Chanshi ascended the hall and said: "Words do not unfold the matter; speech does not meet the occasion. Those who rely on words perish;
those who linger in phrases are deluded. Can you still attain it? Within the domain of you monks, reaching this point, you must possess the eye that discerns the Dharma."
[The Master] said, "Indeed. Yet, even for Dongshan to speak in such a manner, there is a fault. Tell me, where does the fault lie? Chan Master Nantai Zun ascended the hall and said:
"Regarding the ancestral vehicle from of old, how should its guiding principles be upheld?
How should it be discussed? Are the two words 'Buddha-dharma' sufficient? Are 'True Suchness' and 'Liberation' sufficient? Nevertheless, as it is..."

It is so. It is narrow and does not allow the wind to pass, yet it allows great passage for carts and horses. If one speaks from the perspective of the gate of principle and phenomena, the moment a single word is uttered, heaven and earth tremble;
mountains, rivers, and the great earth become tranquil, the seas are calm and the rivers clear, and the preaching of all Buddhas of the three periods of time is manifest before one.
If you understand this clearly, you shall ascend together to the other shore before the Hall of the Ancient Buddhas. There is nothing more to do; take care.
Chan Master Juehua Zhao ascended the hall and said: "If everyone were like today, the Old Barbarian (the Buddha) would have cause for hope; yet Dīpaṃkara Buddha was not as good as you, O Gaṇin.
If everyone were like today, the Old Barbarian would be utterly hopeless; yet you, O Gaṇin, are not as good as Dīpaṃkara Buddha.

If you understand this clearly, then the Buddhas of the great earth and its motes of dust, the twenty-eight patriarchs of the Western Heaven, the six patriarchs of the Tang land, and all the elders throughout the world [are one]."
Last night, at one moment, I took up my staff and turned the wondrous Wheel of Dharma upon its tip.
If you cannot see clearly here, then hundreds of thousands of Buddhas have passed through your nostrils, and the twenty-eight patriarchs of the West have pierced through your skull.
Do you know this? If you do not, I shall point it out for you. After a long silence, he said: "What is there in the mountains, rivers, and the great earth?"
[This is] no fault. Long standing, take care.

Zen Master Wuzu Jie ascended the hall and said: "The sickness of the Buddhas and the sickness of the Patriarchs—let us all, together with you venerable Chan practitioners, cast them outside the triple gate.
Venerable Chan practitioners, have you yet been able to cast out my own sickness? If you can cast out my sickness, then..."
Do not let this obstruct your realization of the Buddha’s illness and the Patriarchs’ illness. Take care!
Master Chimen Zu ascended the hall and said: "If there were even a single dharma, Vairocana would fall into the rank of ordinary beings.
If there were not even a myriad dharmas, Samantabhadra would lose his realm. At this very moment, where does Mañjuśrī emerge?"
"If you cannot bring it forth, the golden-maned lion will have its waist broken. Fortunately, there is this bowl of rice; do not wait for pepper and ginger to be sprinkled upon it.
Entering the hall, the mountain monk said: "I remember a saying from within my mother’s womb; today I shall present it to the assembly."
"You all must not engage in rational deliberation. Is there anyone who can deliberate upon this?
If you cannot deliberate upon it, do not misrepresent it thirty years from now."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Xuefeng rolls a ball; Luohan writes characters; Guizong slays a snake; Daisu burns a mountain field. But tell me, what matter do they clarify?
Is there anyone who can clarify it? Try saying something! If you cannot clarify it, therefore it is said:
'To slay a snake, one must have the hand that slays a snake; to burn a mountain field, one must be the person who burns a mountain field. A single flicker of emotional dust arises—"
False views: "If there is no sinew in the eyes, one will be poor for a lifetime.
Master Cóng of Dòngshān ascended the hall and said: "What should this mountain monk say? The past is the present; the present is the past.
Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: 'Pines are straight and thorns are crooked; cranes are white and crows are black. Do you understand?"
"Mo. Although it is so, it is not necessarily the case that pines are invariably straight and thorns are invariably crooked, or that cranes are white and crows are black.
Here at Dongshan, there are also crooked pines and straight thorns;
there are also black cranes and white crows. [I have] stood for a long time."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The morning cock announces the dawn; after the gruel, it is already bright. The lanterns are still dozing, yet the pillar is wide awake.
He added, "When it is wide awake, call it wide awake; when it is clearly distinct, call it clearly distinct.
Tomorrow and the day after, do not mistake the servant for the master. Be careful!"
Cen Master Baoshan ascended the hall and said: "Everyone here is like this—such calm winds and tranquil waves; where did they come from?
Suddenly, you encounter a vast expanse of surging waters with white waves lapping the heavens. At such a time, it would be difficult even to find a single helmsman.
Is there anyone among you who can take the helm? No one in the assembly responded. The Master said, "You have brought a whole shipload of people to ruin."
Chan Master Shangfang Yue ascended the hall and said: "Gathering the yellow leaves and swirling the blue smoke; on the bamboo mat, one sleeps through the midnight hours in one's robes.
After the morning gruel, the session is dismissed at the third roll of the drum—who could possibly speak further of the Zen of the Patriarchs? He then descended from his seat.
Chan Master Yuwang Tan ascended the hall and said: "A thousand flowers vying to bloom and a hundred birds singing in spring—this is the phrase that points upward.
The Buddhas appearing in the world and the spiritual teachers giving rise to compassion—this is the phrase that points downward. What is the phrase that does not involve either of these two paths?"
If you recognize it, the breath issues from the crown of your head; if you do not recognize it, it is like a clay ox plowing a stony field.
[The Master] struck the meditation seat and descended. Master Jinshan Xin ascended the hall and said: "That which is most prized in the world is the Beryl of He Shi and the Pearl of Lord Huai."

Jinshan calls it "donkey dung and horse manure. That which is most precious in the supramundane—True Suchness, liberation, bodhi, and nirvana—Jinshan calls "boiling fat and the clanging of a bowl. But tell me, where does such talk land?
It is not that his mind of selection and rejection is heavy, nor is it a matter of believing in heterodox and inverted views. Do you all wish to know? A fierce tiger does not...
Looking at the meat upon the table, how could a great furnace cast the needle within one’s pouch?
Master Chan Shun of Yunju ascended the hall and said: "The single, firm, and dense body manifests within all dust.
The shrimp and earthworms each have their burrows; the crows, magpies, doves, and pigeons likewise have their nests. At this very moment, why is it that..."
[The Master] said, "Who is it that preaches the Dharma? After a long silence, he said: "Things are grouped by their kind;

beings are divided by their class. Ascending the hall, he said: "The Way is no different throughout the Three Gorges; morning after morning, I speak only thus. Sengyou is skilled at painting portraits; Zhenfu produces bing-iron."
Ascending the hall: Neither long nor short, neither small nor large—whose realm is this principle? *Pah!* Ascending the hall:
To hear the two words "Buddha-dharma" is already to defile one's ears and eyes. Before you have even stepped through the gate of Yunju, I would give thirty blows to the soles of your feet.
Even so, it is still for the sake of exerting my utmost effort for the sake of the assembly.
Ascending the hall, he raised the example of Jia Shan, who said: "Recognize the Son of Heaven at the gate of the bustling marketplace; realize the old monk upon the tips of the hundred grasses.
Yunju, however, was not like this: "The woman shakes the loom with a rhythmic *ya-ya*; the child plays with his mouth, making *guo-guo* sounds."

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "In other quarters, there are those who play with the heads of snakes and poke at the tails of tigers, or leap across the great ocean and hide their bodies amidst the blades of a sword.
Here at Yunju, it is like washing one's feet in hot water on a freezing day; at night, one takes off one’s socks and falls asleep, only to have them tied back with leather straps at dawn.
When the wind blows the fence down, one simply calls for laborers to split bamboo and tie it back up."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Yunju does not understand Chan; he washes his feet and goes up to bed to sleep. The winter melon is straight and blunt; the gourd is curved and winding.
Chan Master Liang of Yuyang ascended the hall and said: "Mañjuśrī’s precious sword—those who obtain it are the most honored. He then picked up his staff and said:
Today, Jingyin’s approach is such that it leaves no path for even a thousand sages to tread. Nevertheless, this is still like two swords clashing—how can one employ it without striking their blades?
After a long silence, he said: "Wild mugwort sprouts of its own accord as it stands empty before the water."
The river swallows have just returned, yet no one is to be seen.
[He] entered the hall and ascended the seat. The great sun rises in the east, piercing through the darkness of the great thousandfold world-system.

If you all stand within the light, you are still merely chasing after shadows and echoes. If you stand within the darkness, you are likewise a fellow who hides his head while exposing his shadow. Having reached this point—
"How can you express it? After a long silence, he said: "When meeting people, speak but three parts; do not yet cast out your whole heart.
[End of] Session. Entering the hall, he said:
"Within worldly dharmas, how many people have been lost? Within the Buddha-dharma, how many people have been intoxicated?"
As for this state of being neither deluded nor intoxicated—of what sort of person is this the affair?

[The Master] ascended the hall. As soon as the tips of words strike one another, the ocean of meaning becomes profoundly deep. If you would take the direct shortcut, each of you please return to your quarters.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said, "Manifesting form in response to things is like the moon in water.

He then picked up his staff and said, "This is not a 'thing,' yet it manifests its form right now. But tell me, where is the moon? After a long pause, he said, "The open sky has a path that must be penetrated;
the bottom of the abyss leaves no trace to be sought. He struck the incense stand and descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall: The white sun rises in the east; the white sun sets in the west. As swift as the tossing of a pitch-pot, it flashes through the vast void.
A divine dragon takes flight in a single leap, penetrating the boundless; yet even a tiny scale still leaps within the mud. Amidst the spiritual flame, do not settle or linger.
A three-year-old child wears a four-cornered topknot. *Can*. (Enter.)
Ascending the hall, after a long silence, he raised his fist and said: "When the fist is clenched, the Five Peaks stand upside down; when the hand is opened, the five fingers are distinct.
Sometimes he locks fast the barrier of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; sometimes he opens wide the dwelling of the thousand sages.
Today, here before you, I present this—tell me, for what purpose is it used? He struck the meditation seat and said: "The subsequent text is long; it is entrusted to those who come."
One day, Chan Master Chengtian Jian ascended the hall and said: "The realm of Vairocana is the profound gateway of myriad wonders.
Those who possess knowledge speak of it but cannot exhaust its depths; Sudhana draws from it but never finds depletion; Manjusri embodies it and remains in silent stillness. Universal...
The worthy witness this through its manifold layers. If one follows its *dharmatā*, it is like clouds gathering in the azure sky—originally there is not a single thing.
If one follows its function of wisdom, it is like flowers blooming in a spring valley—their application is boundless.
Though one may speak of [teachings] as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they all equally follow this One Way. Now I ask you all: what is this One Way? After a long silence, he said: "White."
When the clouds part, the bright moon is seen; when the yellow leaves fall, the sound of pounding clothes is heard.
*Chān*. Entering the hall: Do not leave behind your entanglements; do not seek out Buddhas or patriarchs. Having abandoned these two paths, on what shall you rely?
Jiang Yan dreamed of the writing-brush; Tianlong saw a tiger. Thus it has been handed down by the ancients: "The moon does not span five [phases]. *Chān*.
Ascending the hall, he said: "To cut through with one stroke and bury the ancestral style;

for a lion to turn over and drag through mud and water—even if you were to sit and block the ten directions so that neither ordinary nor sage can pass, I would still give you thirty blows right between your heels."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Holding up one and letting go of another—wondrous function sweeping across all directions. To eliminate the profound and gather in the mundane, to destroy the holy;

yet if measured against the fodder of the fundamental share, it is much like polishing a tile to make a mirror. How should a monk of the patch-robed lineage act? After a long silence, he said: 'Reality.'"
Chan Master Jiufeng Shao ascended the hall and said: "The mountain monk’s preaching of Chan is like a cricket spitting oil—it comes out as soon as it is squeezed;
if not squeezed, there is not even a single drop. Why is this? It is simply because I have never studied the causes and conditions of the past and present."

Furthermore, having pre-arranged and rehearsed their superior views and knowledge, they wait for the moment of ascending the hall to grind their lips and polish their beaks, using the stench of gruel and rice to suffocate the monks.
Every question and answer is merely a matter of necessity; how could it be otherwise?
Not only do I, this mountain monk, observe that the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat in silence for ten kalpas without opening his mouth, but later, because of the various devas...
Only after Brahmā and the sixteen princes had entreated him again and again did he finally speak; it was not that he was being secretive or stingy.

It was simply because he did not dare to bury the potential of others. Since this mountain monk does not bury the potential of others, one cannot say that this mountain monk has ever ascended the seat. *Chán*.
Chan Master Xita Shu ascended the hall and said: "At the seat of Huangmei, those like hemp seeds are numerous; yet to display one's wit within the words is truly lamentable.
To say 'there is fundamentally nothing at all' is like the blue sky and white sun being obscured by clouds. *Chen* (Examine!)."
Chan Master Wénlì of Huìlì ascended the hall. "The mountains are silent; I sit leaning against the city walls.
These tasteless words fall apart, scattered and fragmented. Striking the incense stand with his staff, he descended from the seat.
Master Yuyin Yi ascended the hall. As soon as Mazu had ascended the hall, Xiong峰 (Xiongpeng) immediately rolled up the mat.
A gust of spring wind arrives; flowers lie scattered across the ground. He then descended from the seat.
Chan Master Yuquan Hao addressed the assembly, saying: "One night the rain poured down in torrents, knocking down the grape arbor.

The administrators, the heads of departments, the attendants, and the laborers all propped what could be propped and braced what could be braced. Propping and bracing until daybreak, it remains as pitiful as ever."
Chan Master Tiansheng Dao ascended the hall and said: "One does not proceed from one stage to another; within the nature of quiescent extinction, how could there be stages?
Śākyamuni bowed his head and asked Dīpaṃkara: 'Virtuous One, what is meant by receiving a prediction [of enlightenment]? He then descended from his seat."
Chan Master Tianyi Huai ascended the hall and said: "At the summit of Mount Sumeru, the golden bell is not struck; within the Bimbāra Cave, no one gathers.
This mountain monk rides backward upon the Buddha Hall, while you all wear straw sandals backward.
In the morning you roam Mount Tandi; in the evening you arrive at Mount Luofu. Take back your own staff and needle-case."

Ascending the hall, the Master said: "Monks may explain things horizontally or vertically, yet they do not yet know the eye upon the crown of the head. At that time, a monk asked, "What is the eye upon the crown of the head?
The Master replied, "The robe is worn through and the bare bones are exposed; the roof is broken and one sleeps watching the stars."
Ascending the hall, when the assembly had gathered and settled, he said: "If you say 'I hope you are well' as you come up, it can exhaust ten thousand taels of gold.
If you say 'Take care' as you go down, it can likewise exhaust the offerings of the four continents. If you treat this as a matter of Buddhist Dharma, you are mistaken."
"A single drop of water is difficult to dissolve. If you deliberate upon this as if it were a matter of no concern, you are putting grit in your eyes. For now, how is it?
After a long silence, he said: "Do you understand? Be careful."
Ascending the hall, he said: "To be a master of our school, one must drive the plowman’s ox and seize the hungry man’s food.
When encountering the lowly, one makes them noble; when encountering the noble, one makes them lowly. To drive the plowman’s ox is to cause his crops to flourish.
To seize the hungry man’s food is to ensure he is forever free from hunger and thirst. To make the lowly noble is to turn earth into gold. To make the noble lowly is to..."
I transform gold into earth. This old monk neither drives the plowman’s ox nor takes away the hungry man’s food.
Why? For what use would I have for the plowman’s ox? And what would I eat of the hungry man’s food?
I do not grasp at earth to make gold, nor do I transform gold into earth. Why? Because gold is gold and earth is earth. It is jade.
This is jade; this is stone. This is the monastic; this is the layperson. The heavens and earth of past and present; the sun and moon of past and present.
The mountains and rivers of past and present; the human relations of past and present. Although it is thus, once the Great San Pass is broken through, how many will encounter Bodhidharma while lost?
Ascending the hall, he said: "A wild goose flies across the vast sky; its shadow sinks into the cold water. The goose has no intention of leaving a track; the water has no mind to retain the shadow.
If you can be thus, only then will you understand how to act within the realm of heterogeneity. There is no need to shorten the crane or lengthen the duck, nor to level mountains or fill valleys.
Let it go, and there are a hundred uglinesses and a thousand clumsinesses; bring it back, and there is only grasping and clutching. When it is employed..."
"I dare to compete with the Eight Great Dragon Kings in wealth; yet it would not be worth even half a penny in total.
[He] descended from his seat. "The skull constantly interacts with the world; the nostrils touch upon the family style. When the banana tree hears thunder, it blooms;
when the sunflower faces the sun, it turns. "O virtuous ones, when the banana tree hears thunder and blooms, does it have ears? When the sunflower follows the sun..."
It turns. Is there still an eye? If you can understand this, then the Western Heaven is this very land.
If you do not understand, it is included within "seven times nine is sixty-three."

Ascending the hall, he said: "The spiritual source is devoid of traces, yet the form-body manifests everywhere. The Dharma transcends annihilation and permanence; existence and non-existence cannot be demonstrated. Thus it is said:
'In every speck of dust one does not see the Buddha; in every world-system one does not hear the sutras.

If you wish to understand the personal transmission of the prediction at Vulture Peak, look at the sun by day and the stars by night. After a long pause, he said: "If you go to other places, do not speak of this mistakenly. Study!"
Ascending the hall, he said: "Last night the cold frost was piercing; the Yellow River froze solid, and the Iron Ox of Shanfu broke at the waist.
Everyone says that Nüwa melted stones to patch the heavens, yet how could she possibly remedy the single gap in the northwest?

Now, if I were to patch it for her, I fear there would be no place for the people of this great earth to breathe. Therefore, I shall leave this one aperture for the people of the great earth to breathe through. *Chan* (Examine!)."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Empty clarity illuminates itself without taxing the mind or strength. When those of superior capacity see this, even ghosts and spirits become mere tea and rice.
When those of middling or inferior capacity attain it, their wild minds are instantly stilled. Yet there is one more person—take care not to mention them."

Ascending the hall, he said: "Light penetrates the sun and moon; brightness and darkness cannot contain it. Wisdom transcends the holy and the ordinary, the wise and the foolish; it passes through them all without lingering. Therefore it is said:
'It cannot be attained by bowing the head or by deliberation. After a long silence, he asked: 'What is it?'"
Ascending the hall, he said: "The green vines wind their way straight up to the summit of the cold pines; the white clouds drift indistinctly, appearing and disappearing within the great void.
How does this compare to 'clouds rising on the southern mountain and rain falling on the northern mountain'? If you can understand this, the sweet melon is sweet all the way to its stem.
If you cannot, the bitter gourd is bitter down to its roots."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The realms of boundless lands are not separated by even a hair’s breadth between self and other.
But tell me, what Dharma does the Tathāgata of Immovable Light preach in the World of Wondrous Joy? The ten periods of past and present never depart from the single moment of the present thought.
As for the very first assembly of Buddha King of Majestic Sound—how many people did he deliver? If you are a master who penetrates all quarters, try to explain."
"Look at the Way. After a long silence, he said: "Difficult is the journey! Difficult is the journey! Look for yourself at the summit of the ten-thousand-fathom peak.
He ascended the hall and said: "The withered mulberry tree knows the wind of heaven; the sea water knows the cold of heaven. The golden-colored dhūta’s vision is not true."
At Mount Kukkutapāda, he watched over his robes and bowl with others; the three thousand great parables and eight hundred minor parables were much like washing clods of earth in the mud.
Throughout forty-nine years and more than three hundred and sixty assemblies, even in the kingdom of Magadha, it was still lacking something.
Though Deshan and Linji were indeed men of stature, how could they compare to the King of Kaśmīra, who [resolved matters] with a single stroke of the blade?
[The Master] said, "Segment. Suppose there were someone here now whose nostrils reach the heavens—where would this mountain monk’s life be?
After a long silence, he said, "Peace was originally brought about by the generals; yet we do not permit the generals to see that peace. He gave a shout and descended from his seat.
Chan Master Fachang Yu ascended the hall and said: "If you withdraw a thousand feet, I shall sprout right where you stand.
If you present yourself face-to-face, I shall hide my body while revealing my shadow. If you pick up pebbles from a spring pond, I shall scatter bright pearls.
Thus, it becomes like a holeless iron hammer—so that water cannot wet it and wind cannot enter."
It seems so. But tell me, does Fachang have any way of benefiting others? After a long silence, he said: "A sharp blade may cut the flesh, yet the wound eventually heals;
but harsh words wound a person, and the resentment never fades."

Ascending the hall, he said: "The spring mountains are green; the spring waters are lush. A single dream of Nanke has just reached its fulfillment. Carrying my staff, I stride out through the pine gate;
In every place, the peach blossoms are fragrant and rich. Reflecting on the old Master Lingyun of days past, For thirty years there was nowhere to be found.
Nowadays everyone vies to pluck the willow flowers; Red petals fill the ground, yet no one sweeps them up.
Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said: "If I hold it up, you call it 'first illumination, then function.
If I set it down, you call it 'first function, then illumination. If I cast it aside, you call it 'illumination and function simultaneous.
But when I suddenly neither hold it up nor set it down, where will you go to speculate? Even if you were to understand this..."
Magnanimous and discerning—if he had encountered Linji or Deshan, his forehead would have struck the ground. But tell me, what excellence did he possess?
After a long silence, he said: "Having already crossed the great ocean, one need not boast of its waters; were it not for Mount Sumeru, there would be no mountains."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "At midnight, who has snatched away the black hen? The stone woman is groundlessly subjected to pointed scrutiny.

The King of Emptiness issues a decree for an urgent search; the Mind-only immediately becomes the commander of the army. Yunmen leads the charge; the ranks of Guishan are arrayed. The five positions are set as banners and spears;
the three mysteries are deployed as halberds and crossbows. Yaoshan grasps his blade; Qingyuan bears his axe; Shigong bends his bow."
Heoshan beats the drum: the battle lines are arrayed like a long serpent on the Snowy Peaks; the troops are stationed like flying tigers at Huangbo.
The wooden horse is cooked with its fur; the clay ox is boiled with its horns. Rewards are given to the three armies to gratify the host; they beat the tangled vines and distribute the proclamations.
They cut across the sea, raising dust, and sweep across the mountains, tossing up the earth. They strike the dark gate and clear the narrow paths. How many ordinary people suffer such hardship! None.
The oceans of peripheral lands compete in their flurry; among the sages and commoners of the three realms, there is no place to be found. No place to be found—do you still know?
Last night the clouds withdrew and the heavens were vast; as before, it cried out in the high tree under the moon.
Chan Master Yunju Yuan ascended the hall and said: "How cold! How cold! The wind shakes the bamboo until its sound grows thin; the waters freeze so the fish move with difficulty;

the forest thins so the birds find it hard to roost. Already the severity of the frost is heavy; how much more so for the traveler whose robes are thin? Cease thinking of the thousand peaks of the mountains along the purple road;
instead, embrace the single cluster of flames from the red brazier. Cast down the *zhunyu*—the bamboo peg in mid-air—and overturn [the world]."
"Kāśyapa’s banner-pole in front of the gate fell straight down, yet he further said, 'I do not understand. Calculating this, it is truly groundless. *Chan* (Case closed).
Zen Master Zhihai Yi ascended the hall and said: 'I remember when I was seven years old;
at a village school, I obtained a Dharma-gate that transcends emotion and leaves behind views—most wondrous and most profound. Since it first permeated my spirit, more than sixty years have passed.'"

Today I have come forth to announce this to the great assembly. If you wish to uphold and transmit it, you should listen with careful attention. He then said: "The plowing and sowing on Cold Mountain are finished;
leading the calf and carrying firewood, we return home. This night, one brazier’s fire provides clothing for the bodies of the entire family.
O practitioners of Zen: when meeting people, do not speak of this inappropriately.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The ancients said: 'To engage with beings and benefit living things is most exquisite. Yet, you, my nephew, are ultimately unworthy. His family naturally has its own descendants;
when brought forth for application, they will be perfectly suited. O Zen practitioners, do you understand? When the vegetable garden wall falls, it is built only in the sun;
when the courtyard fence is breached, it is repaired after the rain. When the buildings leak, they are mended as best one can—by sons and grandsons, both great and small."

Exhausting all traces of worldly elegance, Zen Master Huilin Zhao ascended the hall and said: "The head is round like heaven; the feet are square like earth. With an ancient countenance of imposing majesty, he possesses the spirit of a true man.
He kicks over Mount Sumeru and tramples the waters of the sea, leaving neither Śakra nor the Dragon King any place to stand."
He then took up his staff and said, "You have come here only to try to evade me on this staff!
*Du!* No matter what supernatural powers or transformations you may employ, in the end you must return to this very place. He struck the ground once with the staff.
Chan Master Fayun Xiù ascended the hall and said: "Sailing by watching the wind is precisely following the waves;

cutting off the flow of all streams does not avoid leakage as before. Assigning duties according to talent cannot transcend the limitations of length and shortness; buying a hat to fit the head is difficult to get exactly right.
Even if you were to see neither heaven above nor earth below, and could not distinguish east from west or north from south—"
"Divided? What use is there in that? Whether forged from pure steel or cast from raw iron, one must still break out in a sweat on the forehead.
If it were not like this at all, how could one deliberate upon it? After a long silence, he said: "Who can know these pieces of sincere heart?"
It makes one laugh to death that the stone girl of Huangmei is dead.
Entering the hall, the mountain monk does not know how to speak with clever artifice; he simply responds to the occasion by calling out to you to come and drink a cup of tea.

There are also no secret instructions from the Patriarchs. If you practitioners have not yet become intimately acquainted with this, you will find yourself treading upon a scale-weight as hard as iron.
[Ascending the hall: Autumn clouds, autumn waters, and green mountains fill the eyes. If you can realize it here, you will be fully satisfied a thousandfold and ten-thousandfold.
If this is not yet the case, the Daoist rides his ox backward. *Chan*! (Examine!)
Ascending the hall, he said: "Cold rain falls fine, the north wind blows high; sand runs, stones roll, and branches creak as they snap.
All of you know this well enough, but tell me: what color is the wind? If you can recognize it, I grant that you possess the eye.
If you do not recognize it, do not blame me for deceiving you. *Chan* (Examine)."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "For nine years at Shaolin, he sat in cold meditation, yet was seen through by Shenkang. Now, jade and stone are difficult to distinguish;
one can only wrap it in hemp and paper. Do you understand? Many laugh at me; few smile at me."
Ascending the hall, he said: "For members of the monastic community, it is not considered extraordinary to bow high to Śākyamuni and not prostrate before Maitreya.
Yet, what was the purpose of sacrificing one's body for half a verse or casting oneself into fire for a single phrase? After a long silence, he said: 'Each person dwells as a mountain man.'"
"What need is there to speak further of its destruction?
Chan Master Fufu of Changlu ascended the hall and called to the assembly, saying: "The rivers and mountains wind around the balustrades, appearing as if they were an ink-and-water landscape screen.

The halls and pavilions soar into the void, as magnificent as the grotto-heavens of the immortals. The myriad phenomena of the forested universe interpenetrate like the reflections in the ocean-seal; it is a single path..."

The divine light is no longer obstructed. Do you all understand? After a long silence, he said: "In the vast and silent expanse of heaven and earth, standing alone, toward what infinite horizon do you gaze? *Chan*.
The Abbot addressed the assembly in the language of India. National Teacher Nanyang said: "If one teaches the Dharma with something to be gained, this is the howling of a jackal;
if one teaches the Dharma with nothing to be gained, this is called the lion’s roar. The Master said:

"The National Teacher speaking thus is very much like covering one's ears while stealing a bell. Why? To speak of existence or non-existence is entirely the howling of a jackal. If you all wish to recognize the lion..."
"Is this the lion's roar? "Tsk!
Chan Master Zizhi of Kaiyuan ascended the hall and said: "For the patch-robed monks, hiding one’s body within the eye of a needle is too spacious;
galloping a horse across the great ocean is far too narrow. If the General does not mount the drawbridge, the valiant warrior’s donning of armor is but a weary toil. Walking three [miles] by day..."
I do not ask about traveling eight hundred *yojanas* in a single night; how do you speak the single phrase of "not moving a step"?
If you can speak it, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra are right before your eyes.
If you cannot speak it, you must immediately pull up your skirt and tighten your straw sandals. Go! (Chán).
Ascending the hall, he said: "The cold sky is vast and empty; the great earth is boundless and wide. Clouds arise from the mouths of caves; water flows from the high plateau.
If you hold fast to it, the ten directions of the world will appear hazy and indistinct. If you let it go, east, west, south, and north will be level and serene."
Vast and boundless is the universe, with countless beings. Each and every one has nostrils reaching to the heavens.
Now I ask you all: is this holding fast, or is it letting go? Is there anyone who can decide this? If no one can decide it, outside the triple gate stand two great men:
one with brows knit and sword gripped; the other with eyes bulging and fist raised. *Chan*.

Chan Master Mingyin Yuan ascended the hall. Holding his staff horizontally across his chest, he said: "If you proceed in this manner, it will be such that there is but one sun in heaven and but one king in the land;
the old Śākyamuni will drink in his breath and swallow his voice, and the entire Great Canon of Teachings will be like wood gnawed by insects.
Even if you strive to bore into or look up toward it without success, it is precisely an unperforated iron hammer. Suppose you were to pick it up with a casual hand—"
"This too is leftover soup and stale rice. Only by spitting it all out at once can there be a slight degree of accord.
Furthermore, to fall into emptiness and oblivion is still the livelihood of the ghosts. Do you understand? Only after the rain does one know the mountains are verdant;
only when affairs are difficult does one see the heart of a true man. He struck his staff down and descended from the seat.
Chan Master Bian of Xitai ascended the hall and, citing the words of Linji regarding the "true person of no station," called to the assembly, saying:
"The old fellow Linji was usually as straight-backed as iron, yet when it came to this point, he was much like one who has lost his way at midday and sees flowers in the air.
Even if one were to say that the true person of no station is nothing but a dry piece of excrement—"
This is like a mud turtle dragging its tail; that monk of the Mahāsāṃghika school knows only the extreme heat of late summer, but he does not know the bitter cold of midwinter.
Had he been judged by the standards of that time, what words could have been used to block the tongues of all people under heaven?
Xitai simply let it rest at that, yet out of a desire for the purity of "not seeing with one's eyes," he could not avoid reaching out a hand to create a mess.
Linji’s single load, Xitai’s single heap—this load and this heap, to whom are they entrusted?
Let them be scattered throughout all quarters; it would put to shame that ancient adept of old.
Chan Master Zhongji ascended the hall and said: "Ho! Ho! Ho! What thing is that chirping at the bottom of the well?
Even if it were the three thousandfold world-system, it would still be nothing but a ghost cave. Ho!"
Ascending the hall: Last night at the fourth watch I arose; I laughed aloud and could not stop.
Fortunately, I had a sound sleep, yet the frost-bell struck me as if split in two.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Heoshan and Puhua suddenly went mad; Beating drums and shaking bells, they put on a performance.

The kalpa-fire blazes fiercely—time to brew tea; The mountain winds blow strongly—best to enjoy the cool. Four snakes in one basket, watch them play; Two mice gnawing at a vine, lacking self-awareness.
The moon shines bright over the vast ocean, where does it go? In the palace of Guanghan, there is a bed of white silver. Tut!"
Ascending the hall, he said: "The eighty-four thousand profound Dharma gates—each gate has a path that transcends heaven and earth.

Why is it that everyone fails to tread upon them? It is simply because there are too many legs on the centipedes. Not only are there many legs, there are also many mouths; these nailed beaks and iron tongues only serve to increase one's ugliness.
To brandish the mallet or raise the whisk is like washing mud with mud; to lift an eyebrow or blink an eye is but a chicken in a cage. If you wish to know..."
Where the Buddhas and Patriarchs have not reached: the door is closed against falling blossoms as spring birds cry out.
Chan Master Daizhong Long ascended the hall and said: "The Dharma is no different from the Dharma; the Way is no different from the Way. At every moment one encounters Śākyamuni;
in every place one runs into Bodhidharma. Take a step and you meet him shoulder-to-shoulder; open your mouth and he bites it to pieces. If you do not let him bite you—"
"Great and small, great.
He ascended the hall. "If you wish to achieve liberation through wisdom, you must first bring movement to stillness. He struck the meditation staff and said, "Oṃ sūru-sili svāhā.
"Return to the hall for tea."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Why is it that one who is unimpeded when encountering objects cannot lift their head?

Why is it that one whose ground is secure and firm cannot set foot down? It is like a celestial king bestowing a magnificent mansion; though one has obtained the great residence, one must enter through the gate.
He then asked, "What is the gate? Fan Kui trampled it open and the True Lord emerged; Guli raised his hand and the scaled dragon sprang forth.
Case: Zen Master Zishou Yan ascended the hall and said: "Clouds arise at the valley mouth; the moon fills the long river. The woodcutter chops deep within the clouds;
the fisherman casts his line from the sandbar. Reaching this point, even if it were Wu Daozi or Zhang Sengyou, there would be no place for you to apply your brush."
[He] remained silent for a long while, then said: "Go to the hall and ask the Holy Monk.

[The assembly] took up the theme. Ascending the hall, he said: "Heaven and earth are solemn and still; the seas are calm and the rivers clear. The wind does not rustle the branches; the rain does not break the clods of earth.
Spring brings forth and summer grows; autumn harvests and winter stores. This is the way of the world. What, then, is the Buddha-dharma? He remained silent for a long while.
He said: "If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata.
When the Chan Master Benjue ascended the hall, he said: "To split one into two and arrange them as three—everyone can say this. To set aside one and pick up seven—this too requires deliberation.
On this very day, what is it that Yunmen spoke of? Do not seek it elsewhere. How will you reveal it?"
*The News:* After a long silence, he said:
"The sun and moon flow on ever-changing. Zen Master Dizang En ascended the hall. Raising his fist, he said, "At times it is a fist. Then opening his hand, he said, "At times it is a palm.
"If you encounter a patch-robed monk who has merit, reward him accordingly," he said, and then let his hand fall. "Truly, the earth is vast and people are few."
Those who meet are few. Entering the hall:
After the rain, the cuckoo calls; before the mountains, the wheat ripens. Where is the young cowherd? Riding his ox, they laugh as they follow one another.
Furthermore, he takes up his short flute and blows it crosswise; before the wind, one or two melodies. *Chān*. Dàochǎng Yìn Chánshī ascends the hall:
"At the ferry-head of Sháo Shí, a boat floats across the wild waters; amidst the waves of Fényáng, oars stir through the solitary smoke.
Clouds and moon are impartial; streams and mountains are no different. A single word meets the track; a thousand miles share the same breeze. I dare—
He asked the assembly, "What is a phrase that accords with the wind? After a long silence, he said: "Where are the eight thousand disciples now?
Ten thousand li of mountains and rivers belong to the Imperial House."
Chan Master Fayun ascended the hall and said: "If Li Lou has intention, white waves will in vain surge to the heavens;
if Wangxiang has no mind, the bright pearl suddenly appears in the palm of his hand. He struck a circular shape with his hand and called to the assembly, saying: "Do you see it?"
After a long silence, he said, "If you look, there is a share for you.
He ascended the hall, held up his staff to show the assembly, and said, "I, this mountain monk, have held the abbot’s office for over seventy days, yet I have never once moved this [staff].
Now, I cannot help but manifest a small measure of supernatural power as an offering to you all. He then struck the ground with the staff and descended.
The Seat. Master Yuankuangman ascended the hall and said: "That which is fit to be a beam shall be a beam; that which is fit to be a pillar shall be a pillar.
A sharp-witted monk will immediately know where it falls. He suddenly took up his staff and said: "Do you know what this is fit to be?"
He struck the incense altar once and said, "Do not say it has no use. He struck it again and said, "Investigate! Chan Master Zhao Ti Zhan ascended the hall and said:
"The six sense-objects are not evil; they are identical to true awakening. On horseback, who is this fair-faced youth of noble family?
Piercing through flowers and breaking willows, his kerchief hangs down over his shoulder. Last night he was drunk at the Bright Moon Tower; calling for dice, he lost everything."
A golden mansion; falcons on arms and hounds at heel—returning or not returning. Eyebrows like silkworms, teeth as white as jade—yet anger remains powerless.
How many can truly know this mind? Yellow-haired and blue-eyed, they are not those one knows. *Lara lara*. Clapping hands once, he descends from his seat.
Chan Master Changlu He ascended the hall and said: “One, two, three, four, five, six— The blue-eyed barbarian monk cannot count them all.
A clay ox enters the sea and goes beyond Silla; A wooden horse chases the wind as far as India. India is vast and boundless; where shall one seek it?
On Mount Potalaka, one asks Avalokiteśvara. Samantabhadra claps his hands and laughs aloud: ‘Go back! Go back! It is autumn.’”
The water is deep. Zen Master Zifu Ming ascended the hall and said: "Zifu has nothing else to contribute. Once every five days he strikes the drum for an assembly;
when has he ever spoken of the subtle or discoursed on the profound? It is merely coarse speech and direct words. Licorice is naturally sweet; the yellow bitter gourd remains as it was."
Suffering! Suddenly, as if your nostrils were piercing the heavens, when you encounter people, be most careful not to misquote [the Master].

*Chan*. Master Yunfeng Xuan ascended the hall and said: "Rest! Cease! Let one thought endure for ten thousand years! Be like cold ashes or withered wood! Be like an incense burner in an ancient temple!
Be like a single length of white silk! "Great assembly, the insight of the ancients was like the radiance of the sun."

Emptiness. Not clinging to the two extremes, how could one fall into the aggregates or the realms? One can only sigh for the descendants of later generations, who mostly understand this as a mere state of uniformity.

This mountain monk is not like that. He goes on without ceasing; he goes on without resting; he goes with his karmic consciousness vast and boundless; he goes in sevenfold confusion and eightfold inversion;
he sits and lies amidst the clamor and sensory colors at the busy crossroads of the city; he goes into the three-family villages.
Filling the streets and blocking the roads, they go about playing amidst thorns and brambles;

they go to the mountains of knives and trees of swords where bellies are split and hearts are gouged out, and to the cauldrons of boiling water and furnace coals where skin is pierced and bones are rotted away. To sing such a song is much like a three-year-old child rolling an embroidered ball.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, “What is the meaning of the West? The Master said, “It strikes the forehead; it bumps the nose.

The monk asked, “What is the underlying intent? The Master said, “A donkey carries it; a horse loads it. The monk asked, “Is there anything further beyond this? The Master said, “In the morning you arrive in India;
in the evening you return to Tang. The monk said, “Thank you for answering my question. The Master said, “The Great Vehicle is being worn out by your clumsiness. The monk [departed].
[The student] withdrew. The Master then said: "When a monk asks about the meaning of the Westward Journey, he strikes his forehead and bumps his nose.
What is the underlying intent? A donkey carries it and a horse hauls it; arriving in India in the morning, returning to Tang in the evening. The Mahāyāna is just like a polished, clumsy fellow."
"Why is this? A person of immeasurable stature has been turned around within the flow of words. Thereupon, Xuedou Ning, the Zen Master, clapped his hands, laughed loudly, and descended from his seat.

Zen Master Xuedou Ning ascended the hall for a discourse: "The hundred rivers have different flows, yet the ocean is their ultimate limit. The myriad phenomena of the forest and the ten thousand images have emptiness as their ultimate limit.
The four sages and six classes of beings have the Buddha as their ultimate limit. For the clear-eyed patch-robed monk, the staff is his ultimate limit."
The ultimate. Now tell me, with what does the staff reach its ultimate? If someone can say it, I will entrust it to them with both hands.
If not, it is better to lean idly against the side of the meditation seat, leaving it for one’s descendants to point out the way.
Chan Master Kaixian Zong ascended the hall and said: "One does not do it; two does not rest. Twist the nostrils;
press down the clouds. Heyshan knows how to beat the drum of Yanguan; Wengyi Sengyao does not paint the oxen of Dai Song.
Rice from Luling; oil from Touzi. Xuefeng continues to roll his twin balls. Last night the wind brought news from Hengyang; a single cry from a cold wild goose amidst the frost."
Moonlit Seclusion.
On this day, National Teacher Suizhen ascends the hall and says:

"Today, National Teacher, atop a solitary peak and at the highest summit, has launched a single iron boat, cutting off the vital passages for all people under heaven, so that they cannot raise their oars or move their paddles. There is a silken prize."
"Son, tell me: in whose hands does it rest? He picks up his staff and says, "Look! Look! Though I told you it was a dragon, you simply did not believe me.
Only when you have snatched it away casually will you be truly amazed."
Chan Master Miaozhu ascended the hall and said: "Last year’s plum; this year’s willow. Their colors and fragrance—" he gave a shout.
After a long pause, he said: "Had I not given that one shout, I would have almost said it was just as before.
Now tell me, how is it after having spoken? The eyes pop out!"
*Record of the Essential Teachings of the Successive Patriarchs*, Volume Ten;
*Record of the Essential Teachings of the Successive Patriarchs*, Volume Eleven.
Compiled by Xingyue of Loudong, Abbot of Lian’an Chan Monastery at the Eighteen Streams in Wulin.
Master Qingliang Yi ascended the hall for the Five Visits (wǔcān) formal discourse. After the assembly had stood for a long time, he said to them:
"If you were to disperse right now just as you are, would there be any principle of the Buddha-dharma? Try to say something about it. If there is none, then why have you come here?"
"If there were [such a thing], it would also exist in the midst of a great marketplace where people are crowded together; why must one come here?
Everyone has once read various treatises such as the *Huayan yuanjue jing chao*, the *Baimen yihai*, the *Huayan lun*, and the *Nirvana Sutra*.
In which of these teachings is there such a moment? If there is, try to cite it. Is it perhaps found in such a scripture as this?"

Is this "what" the appropriate time for such talk? What connection could there possibly be? Therefore it is said: "Subtle words stagnate at the forefront of the mind, constantly becoming the field of discursive thought;
the ultimate reality resides right before one's eyes, yet it is turned into a realm of names and forms.
Furthermore, how can these be overturned? And if they are overturned, how can one attain the correct state? Do you understand?
"Do not merely recite your practice manual like that; what use is there in it? He ascended the hall and said:
"For those who have left the household life, it is enough simply to accord with the times and the seasons. When it is cold, it is cold; when it is hot, it is hot.

If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should contemplate the causes and conditions of time and season. The skillful means of the ancients and the present are not few. Have you not seen [the teaching of] Shitou?"
The Master, upon reading Zhaolun, remarked: "Only the sage is one who regards the myriad things as himself.
Other schools then say that the sage has no self, yet there is nothing that is not his self. He had a saying which he called the *Cantong qi* (Token of Accordance).
At the end, [the Master] said: "The mind of the Great Sage of India—there is nothing that surpasses these words. In the interim, he merely spoke according to the occasion, O Elder.
