Now, you wish to realize that all phenomena are for your own sake; this is because throughout the great earth, not a single dharma can be seen.
He further instructed him, saying: "Do not let your time be spent in vain. Just as I told you earlier, simply act in accordance with the moment."
This is sufficient. If you shift the time and miss the occasion, you are merely wasting your life.

To form a conceptual understanding of form within that which is not form—Venerable Sir, to form a conceptual understanding of form within that which is not form is precisely to shift the time and miss the occasion.
Now tell me: to understand form as being non-form—is that appropriate or not? Venerable Sir, if you understand it in such a way, you are entirely off the mark. This is the correct [approach].
"This is like a madman running in two directions; what use is there for it? Elder, simply maintain your station and pass the time according to the season.
Take care. He ascended the hall and said:
"Throughout the entire world of the ten directions, all is bright and clear, without so much as a single thread of hair. If there were even a single thread of hair, then..."

This is a single strand of hair. National Teacher Shao of Tiantai ascended the hall and said: "The skillful means of the ancient sages are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. The Patriarch said, 'It is not the wind or the banner that moves;
it is the mind of the wise person that moves. This is the unsurpassed Dharma-gate of the Mind-Seal. We belong to the school of the Patriarchs."
This is for an inferior guest. How do you understand the meaning of the Patriarch? Do not say that the wind and banner are unmoving while your own mind is deludedly moving.
Do not say that one does not strike at the wind and banner, but rather speaks from within the wind and banner themselves. Do not ask, "What is it when the wind and banner move?"
Some say that one should clarify the mind by means of objects and need not recognize the objects themselves; some say that form is emptiness;
others say that it is neither the wind nor the banner that moves, but rather that one must have a wondrous realization. What connection do such interpretations have with the intent of the Patriarchs?
Since such understandings are not permitted, you venerable elders should know this for yourselves: if you attain a thorough awakening here, [you will see].
What dharma-gate would not be clear? One simultaneously and thoroughly understands the skillful means of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas;
what further doubt could there be? Therefore, the ancients said: "One thing understood, a thousand things are clear; one thing deluded, ten thousand things are confused.
Elder, how could it be that you understand one koan today and do not understand it tomorrow? Is it because there is some matter of the "transcendent" (shangxiang) that is difficult to grasp?

Indeed, there are some inferior ordinary beings who do not understand such a view; even if they were to pass through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, it would merely cause them to exhaust their spirits and deplete their thoughts—there is no other possibility.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "A hair swallows the vast ocean, yet the nature of the ocean remains undiminished; a tiny speck of dust is cast upon a sharp blade, yet the keenness of the blade remains unmoved.

Whether one sees or does not see, whether one understands or does not understand—only I know this. Thereupon, he spoke a verse: "Having momentarily descended from the high peak, it has already been proclaimed:

The perfect penetration of Prajñā pervades the ten directions. In the vast expanse of humans and devas there is no distinction; Throughout the dharma-realm, whether horizontal or vertical, it dwells everywhere."
[The Master] entered the hall and ascended the seat.
A monk asked, "I have heard it said in the past: 'If a person sees Prajñā, they are bound by Prajñā;
if a person does not see Prajñā, they are also bound by Prajñā. Since they see Prajñā, why are they nevertheless bound? The Master [replied]:
[The Master] asked, "Tell me, what does Prajñā see? [The monk] replied, "If one does not see Prajñā, why is one still bound?
The Master said, "Tell me, where does Prajñā not see? He then said, "If one sees Prajñā, it is no longer called Prajñā."
If one does not see Prajñā, it is not named Prajñā. For now, how can one speak of seeing or not seeing? Therefore, the ancients said:
"If there is even one dharma lacking, it does not constitute the Dharmakāya; if there is even one dharma in excess, it does not constitute the Dharmakāya;
if there is even one dharma present, it does not constitute the Dharmakāya; if there is not even one dharma present, it does not constitute the Dharmakāya. This is the true nature of Prajñā.
This is the core principle. May all the senior elders join together in providing witness, so that the Dharma may endure for a long time and the land may remain peaceful.
Take care. [Ascending the hall: An ancient said, "What is Chan? The three realms are continuous. What is the Way? The ten directions are vast.
Why does he say the three realms are continuous? Where is the principle of the ten directions being vast? You must...

Do you understand? Eyes are blocked; ears are blocked; tongue, body, and mind are blocked. There is no place for vacancy, and there is no place for movement. How do you, Venerable One, understand this?
It cannot be grasped horizontally, nor can it be grasped vertically; it cannot be extended, nor can it be seized.
There is no place for the application of mind, nor is there any place for contrivance. If you can understand in this way, only then will you understand the Dharma.
The gate is cut off from discrimination; all speech is free from leakage. Once, a monk asked, "What is the speech that is free from leakage?
I told him, "It is like the nostrils—excellent. Elder, if you understand it in this way, naturally there will be no passing of wind.
If you can recognize that the entirety of the ten directions is the golden eye of the true eye, you will be a treasure of non-action.
[The Master] ascends the hall. A monk asks, "The world is at peace; may Your Majesty live long. What is the King? The Master says, "The sun rises and the moon is bright.
[The monk] asks, "How should one comprehend this? The Master says, "Who is the student? He then says, "The world is at peace..."

"May the King have long life; may the land be prosperous and joyful, free from all calamities and hardships. These are the words of the Buddha. What was ancient does not change, and what is now does not shift.
One word can settle both past and present—understand this well. O Venerable Elders, the Dharma of the Buddha is not such a principle.
Do you wish to understand? When speech is uttered, it is not sound; before form appears, there is no object. Only then will you realize that all under heaven is at peace."
"May Your Majesty live long! Please remain standing for a moment;
we are deeply honored by your presence. Master Qingliang Qin ascends the hall. Stay a while, sirs. We have stood here for a long time, honored officials and great assembly.
Today’s invitation has been most diligent and earnest. How can this extraordinary merit be compared to anything else? Therefore it is said: For those who have not yet attained realization..."
"Listen to a single word. Right now, who is it that moves their mouth? He then descended from his seat, stood up, leaned on his staff, and addressed the assembly, saying:
"Do you understand? The devas and nāgas listen in silence as flowers rain down. Do not take this as a painted image of Subhūti to carry away.
For now, simply believe, accept, and practice accordingly."
Ascending the hall, the Master said: "I originally intended to dwell in the mountains to hide my ineptitude and nurse my illness until the time passed.
However, because my late teacher has a case that remains unresolved, I have come forth to settle it for him. At that time, a monk asked, "What is this unresolved case of the late teacher?
The Master struck him and said, "The ancestors did not resolve it; the calamity now reaches their descendants. The monk asked, "Where does the fault lie?"
"Where? The Master said, "The fault lies with me; the calamity reaches you.
Chan Master Baizhang Heng ascended the hall and said: "Ride this precious vehicle straight to the site of enlightenment. Every day you trouble yourselves, venerable elders, by visiting me;
there is nothing for me to offer in reception. The weather is cold, so do not stand for long. Please turn your carriages back; take care."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Venerable elders, just now you came out from the Sangha Hall; had you turned back before even crossing the threshold, you would have already been repeating the verse.
It is not fitting that we should continue to hammer this point over and over again here.
An ancient said, 'Studying others is not as good as studying oneself. Therefore it is said: the myriad phenomena of the forested universe are Sudhana."
The patriarchs and masters [taught that] karma, afflictions, and worldly toil are the very realm of Samantabhadra.

If you can investigate in this manner, you will be a fellow student with Sudhana. If you are unwilling to investigate in this way, then return to the hall and warm yourself by the fire while investigating the Brahmin Jvalamitra. Take care.
Chan Master Yongming Qian ascended the hall and said: "The Buddha-dharma is manifest; why then do you not understand it?
You venerable ones, if you wish to understand the Buddha-dharma, simply ask Zhang San and Li Si. If you wish to understand worldly dharmas, then study the ancient Buddhas."
"The monastic community has been at peace for a long time;
I have stood here for a while. Baoci said: 'When a traveling monk visits a spiritual teacher and arrives at a monastery, he sets down his water flask and bowl;
this can be called the completion of the essential task of practicing the Bodhisattva path. Why must he come here again to raise [this matter]? "
To discuss True Suchness and Nirvana at this time is an untimely discourse. Nevertheless, there is an ancient saying: "It is like sifting through sand to recognize treasure;
once the grit and gravel are removed, the pure gold reveals itself. This is then called the Sangha Jewel, eternally abiding in the world and fully endowed with all qualities.

It is also like a rain of a single flavor falling upon lands of various types, where the myriad things grow, differing in size yet sharing a common essence. Their sweetness varies according to their nature.
The difference lies in the occasion; it cannot be said that the ground and the rain possess names such as "large" or "small.
This is because when the square is spoken of, the square appears, and when the circle is spoken of, the circle appears. Why is this so? Because phenomena have neither partiality nor correctness;
they appear in accordance with the conditions. This is called the "manifestation of the form-body in response. Do you see it yet? If you do not see it, do not remain sitting idly.
Master Ren Chan of Lohan ascended the hall and said: "At Baoen, we have never before selected sayings for others.
Today, I shall select one or two sayings for you, venerable seniors. Do you take pleasure in this? Venerable seniors, the crane’s legs are long and the duck’s legs are short;
licorice is sweet and Huangbo is bitter. Is such selection and discernment to your satisfaction? Venerable seniors, do not..."
"Is it that the channels of blood and energy are blocked, or that mud and water create a barrier? Do not misunderstand this; take care.
This was the instruction given by Chan Master Baoen as he ascended the hall. "All you venerable seniors possess the ever-perfect moon; each harbors a priceless treasure.
Therefore, though the moon is within the clouds, it is bright yet does not illuminate; though wisdom is hidden within delusion, it is true yet [does not manifest]."
[The Master] did not respond. [The assembly] stood for a long time without purpose.
Zen Master Zongzhen ascended the hall and said: "The seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing of you venerable elders can only occur once.

As for that which is realized—*is it seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, or is it not seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing?* Do you wish to understand? I shall explain it for you, venerable elders."
It has been explained thoroughly. You must wait until you attain awakening before it is realized. I have stood here for a long time; take care.
Chan Master Xiqian Yuan ascended the hall and said: "Upon exiting the Sangha Hall door and seeing Mount Wulao, the task of a lifetime of study is finished.
What need is there to come here again? Nevertheless, even so, this has caused you, the Venerable One, some weariness."
Take care. Master Wuyun Feng ascends the hall and says:
"All you venerable seniors, you abandon one teacher to seek out another teacher;
you all follow the example of Sudhana’s journey to the south. Now I ask you, venerable seniors: when Sudhana took his leave of Mañjuśrī, he intended—"
Ascending Mount Miaofeng to pay homage to the Bhikṣu Dechen. Upon arriving at his location, why was it that Dechen met him on a separate peak?
Now, the intent of the Teachings and the intent of the Patriarchs share the same expedient means; ultimately, there is no separate principle.
If he has clearly realized this, then for you as well, it will be manifest. Venerable Elders, is the fact that you are currently gathered around this old monk a meeting or a non-meeting? This—
This place is the Wondrous Peak; it is also the Separate Peak. If you can let go from this point, you may be said not to have brought shame upon this old monk.
You will then constantly see the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī, never for a single moment being separated from him. Do you believe this is possible?
Master Rui Lu Xian ascended the hall and said: "In general, regarding the study of the Way, it is not necessarily the case that studying 'talking about the matter' constitutes studying the Way;
it is not necessarily the case that studying 'discerning the matter' constitutes studying the Way; it is not necessarily the case that studying 'substituting words' constitutes studying the Way;

it is not necessarily the case that studying 'alternative words' constitutes studying the Way; it is not necessarily the case that studying the extraordinary and marvelous phrases within the sutras and treatises by twisting them apart constitutes studying the Way."
To tear apart the extraordinary words of the patriarchs is the study of the Way.
Even if you achieve mastery—penetrating them in every way through such study—if you still lack a place of realization within the Buddha-dharma, you are called a follower of "dry wisdom.
Have you not heard the ancient masters say: "Cleverness cannot withstand birth and death; those of dry wisdom cannot escape the wheel of suffering"? If you people...
Regarding the study of the Way: one must engage in genuine study before it can be attained. When walking, take up the inquiry while walking; when standing, take up the inquiry while standing;
when sitting, take up the inquiry while sitting; when sleeping, take up the inquiry while sleeping; and when speaking, take up the inquiry while speaking.
Investigate while silent; investigate during every moment of labor. Since you investigate during such times as these, tell me:
whom are you investigating? What words are you investigating? At this point, you must reach a state of clarity within yourself before it will suffice.
If it is not like this, you are called a person of mere haste; thus, there is no [attainment].
The Essential Meaning of Thorough Investigation.
Chan Master Baoming Cheng ascended the hall: "As it is for one person, so it is for many.
Take care! Chan Master Yaofeng Xian ascended the hall: "Winter departs and spring arrives; the gates of the multi-storied pavilion open. If you can enter..."
I have wandered about for a while. Have you venerable elders been able to enter back into this very place?
If you have entered, then as the ancients said: "Every place is Maitreya; there is no gate and no Sudhana.
If you have not yet entered, it is simply because you, venerable elders, have been wandering in vain. I shall say no more. Long standing, take care.
Chan Master Ruchen ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying: "Do you know that the Holy Monk has come here together with all of you?
Since you have condescended to honor us with your presence, how could I dare detain you? Please take care, as I stand before you for long."

In the evening session, Master Baizhang Hai’s general outline for the discourse was as follows: Whenever the Master ascended the hall, there was always an old man who followed the assembly to listen to the Dharma.
One day, when the assembly had withdrawn, the old man alone did not leave. The Master asked him, "Who are you? The old man replied, "I am not a human being."
In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he once dwelt on this mountain.

When a student asked whether those who practice the Great Way still fall within the realm of cause and effect, he replied, "They do not fall within cause and effect. Consequently, he fell into the body of a wild fox for five hundred lifetimes.
"I now request that you, Preceptor, provide a turning phrase on my behalf, so that I may escape this wild fox body. The Master said, "Ask me.

The old man asked, "Does a great practitioner of the Way still fall within the realm of cause and effect? The Master replied, "He is not ignorant of cause and effect. At these words, the old man attained great enlightenment.
He prostrated himself and said, "I have already escaped the wild fox body. I dwell behind the mountain; I venture to ask that you follow the funeral rites for the deceased."
When it was time to escort the deceased monk, the Master ordered the *karmadāna* to strike the gavel and announce to the assembly that they were to escort the deceased after the meal.
The great assembly gathered for discussion; everyone was at peace, and there was no one ill in the Nirvāṇa Hall. "For what reason is this? they wondered.

After the meal, the Master led the assembly to the base of a cliff behind the mountain. With his staff, he pried out a dead wild fox and performed its cremation according to the Dharma. When the Master arrived—
In the evening, during the formal session, the Master recounted the preceding circumstances.

Huangbo then asked, "The ancients fell into the body of a wild fox for five hundred lifetimes because they gave one wrong answer. If they had not made even a single mistake, what would they have become?

The Master said, "Come closer, and I will tell you. Huangbo stepped forward and struck the Master with his palm. The Master clapped his hands and laughed, saying, "I thought the beard was red; it turns out the chin is red too!"
Furthermore, there was the Red-Bearded Barbarian.

One evening, when Master Yaoshan Yan was ascending the hall for the late evening assembly, the congregation had gathered. The Master said, "Today I have been asked to resolve a doubt; where is the Senior Monk?
A monk stepped forward from the assembly and stood there. The Master descended from his meditation seat, seized him by the collar, and said, "O Great Assembly, this..."
The monk was hesitant; the Master gave him a shove and returned to his quarters.
When Chan Master Zhaozhou Shen held the evening assembly, he said, "Tonight I shall answer questions. Anyone who can ask a question, please come forward.
At that moment, a monk stepped out and bowed. The Master said, "I have been casting a brick to draw forth a jade, yet all I have drawn forth is a mere brick."
One day, Zen Master Linji Xuan said to the two senior monks Puhua and Kefu, "I wish to establish the school of Huangbo here;
you two assist me. The two took their leave respectfully and departed.
Three days later, Puhua came back up and asked, "What did the Master say three days ago? The Master struck him. Three days later...

Ke Fu asked as he had done before: "Why did the Master strike the assembly leader the other day? The Master struck him as well. That evening, during the *xiaocan* (informal discourse), the Master said:
"Sometimes one takes away the person but not the environment; sometimes one takes away the environment but not the person; sometimes both person and environment are taken away;
and sometimes neither person nor environment is taken away."
Cen Master Deshan Jian held an evening assembly and addressed the community, saying: "Tonight I shall not answer questions; anyone who asks a question will receive thirty blows of the staff.
At that time, a monk came forward and bowed. The Master struck him immediately. The monk said, "I have not even asked a question;
for what reason does the Master strike me? The Master said, "Where are you from? The monk replied, "A man from Silla. The Master said—
"Before you have even stepped onto the boat's railing, you deserve thirty blows.
The Venerable Master Muzhou, during his evening instruction, said to the assembly: "Have you all yet attained a point of entry?
If you have not yet attained a point of entry, you must seek one. If you do attain a point of entry..."
"Once you have gone, you must not let me down. At that time, a monk came forward and bowed, saying, "I, [Name], shall never dare to let the Master down.
The Master said, "You have already let me down. He spoke again, "When I speak clearly to you, you still do not understand;
how much less could you grasp it if I were to conceal it? He spoke yet again, "The old monk has been staying here to maintain this monastery..."
"I once saw a man who had nothing to do come here. Why do you not approach him? At that time, one monk stepped forward.
The Master said, "The rector is not here. Take him yourself outside the main gate and give him twenty blows.
The monk asked, "In what way have I erred? The Master replied, "To add a twist to a neck-shackle."
Cen Yang Zhao Chan Master, because of the bitter cold in Bing and Fen, had suspended the evening *zana*.

A strange bhikṣu arrived, shaking his monk’s staff, and said to the Master, "There are six great beings (*mahāsattva*) within this assembly; why do you not preach the Dharma? Having spoken, he departed.
The Master secretly recorded this in a verse: "The foreign monk with the golden staff's radiance Came to Fenyang for the sake of the Dharma. Six persons shall attain [realization]..."
A man of great capacity. [The Master] exhorted him to propagate [the teaching].
Chan Master Bian of the Immortal School had not ascended the hall for a long time. When the assembly entered the abbot’s quarters to pay their respects, the Master said:
"Tonight, I am taking leave together with the assembly. I wonder, will leave be granted? If leave has not yet been heard granted, then speak first."
This is a failure. Take care.
This was the evening *chan* assembly of Master Shouren of Luohan Monastery in Zhangzhou. The Master said: "Every thing originally has no fixed location;
a single bright moon is reflected in the pond of the mind. Having said this, he returned to his quarters.
Zen Master Wuzu Yan held an evening *can* (general assembly). He cited Deshan’s words: "Tonight I will not answer questions.
Anyone who asks a question shall receive thirty blows. Many among the assembly have raised this case, and few have failed to understand it. But tell me, where do you see Deshan?
If there is anyone who does not care for their life or limb, please come forward and speak.
If there is none, I, this mountain monk, shall go to meet the old man Deshan on behalf of the assembly. When Deshan says, "Tonight I will not answer questions;
those who ask shall receive thirty blows," you should simply say to him, "I do not even ask a question, nor do I take a blow. Tell me, does this accord with the truth?
What about that old man Deshan? To reach this point, one must truly be a man of substance.

Furthermore, for over ten years I have traveled the seas in search of the Way; I met several venerable masters who considered themselves fully realized, yet when I arrived at Fushan’s assembly, I was utterly unable to open my mouth.
Later, under Baoyun, I bit through a single iron sour plum.
"Directly, one attains the perfection of a hundred flavors. Now tell me, how would you express this in a single phrase regarding the *gāṅ-zǐ* (a type of bean curd)?

He then said: 'The cockscomb flower blooms, enchanting the early autumn; who can dye its purple silk head? Sometimes the wind stirs and they lean against each other repeatedly, as if vying incessantly before the steps.
(There are many such words from ancient times for the opening of the evening assembly; here I have cited the general outline of the former patriarchs' teachings. The rest has not been recorded.)
Small Assembly Outline (Four Sections), by Chan Master Zhenjing Wen.
At the summer retreat assembly at Mount Yangshan, the Master held up his whisk and said, "Ya! Ya!
Throughout the entire ten directions of the world—whether sages or ordinary beings, monks or laypeople, grasses or trees—all are fully realized beneath this whisk."

The Buddha acts as the patriarch; there is neither before nor after, for liberation occurs all at once. Is there anyone who has not yet attained liberation? If there were, their life would hang by a thread.
Again, he claps his hands and says: "Those who truly understand are few. Therefore, this matter concerns reality and not fiction.
One must investigate with reality and awaken to reality. If even a hair’s breadth remains unexhausted, one falls entirely into the realm of demons. How could this be...?
One does not see the Way of the ancients: "On level ground there are countless dead; to pass through the thornbush forest is to be a true adept.
Nowadays, most people merely attain a state where body and mind are stilled and the past and future are severed, thinking, "In a single thought-moment, ten thousand years have passed."
"Rest! Cease! Be like an incense burner in an ancient temple; be cold and indifferent—this is the ultimate.
Little do they realize that they are instead obstructed by this sublime state, such that right knowledge and vision cannot manifest before them and spiritual powers and radiance cannot be revealed.
Or again, they cling to the notion that "the ordinary, everyday mind is the Way."
They take this to be the ultimate: heaven is heaven, earth is earth, mountains are mountains, waters are waters, monks are monks, and laypeople are laypeople.
They follow the thirty days of the long month and twenty-nine days of the short month; clinging to the grass and leaning on the wood, they wander blindly in a state of unconsciousness.
Suddenly, if one asks them, "How is my hand like the Buddha’s hand? they immediately say, "It is the same."
"Venerable sir, my feet are like what? Donkeys' feet! [The Master] then said, "These are the feet of the Venerable. [Dongshan asked,] "Everyone has a place of birth affinity (*jìngyuán*);
where is the place of birth affinity for you, Elder? [Dongshan] then said, "I am a person of such-and-such a province. [The Master] said, "What kind of talk is that?"
Do not misunderstand this. In all your actions, you must take the ordinary path as your foundation for stability. Resolve upon it and align yourself with it;
do not dare to move even a single step further, fearing you might fall into a pit or a ditch.
For a long time, act like a person with both eyes blind walking along a road: you cannot let go of your staff for a single pace, holding it firmly.
Relying upon it, you follow it step by step. One day, if your eye of the Way suddenly opens and you realize what was previously wrong, you will cast away the staff and open both hands.
The ten directions will be vast and empty; you will move freely in all eight directions, east, west, south, and north, with nothing that is acceptable or unacceptable.
How could you possibly rely exclusively on another’s gateway or follow along as a mere traveling companion? What joy would there be in such a self?
Ultimately, how is it so? Have you not seen Yunmen say: "Nowadays, most of the old monks in the world rely on their lineages, academic learning, and the entanglements of formal proclamations;
they are merely cast from printing blocks and molded from molds.
If a person were to understand clearly, why not deal with everything as it arises in the moment? Furthermore, have you not seen Linji say: "In my place, this is the living Patriarch"?
The Master’s intent in coming from the West: take it up and use it; wherever you stand, all is true. He does not say, "How was it in the past? How is it now?
Is this word obtainable, or is it unobtainable? Where is the false? Where is the real?
Bring forth even a hair’s breadth of a truly real principle and show it to me! This is simply because the person's own eyes are not open. By themselves—
There is no place for views; one simply receives the void and follows the echoes. With all manner of taboos, one entangles and binds oneself.
Even if one speaks in this way, were one suddenly to see things clearly and distinctly at that very moment, it would still be like staring with wide eyes inside a coffin.

Even now, there is still that man of blazing brilliance—the one with teacherless wisdom and spontaneous wisdom who does not consort with the myriad dharmas—who grinds his teeth and manifests a thousand transformations.

Upon seeing me speaking such nonsensical words, he should have stepped forward and struck me across the mouth, dragged away my chair and flung it outside the triple gate, and shouted the assembly into dispersal. How could...?
"How vexing! Is there anything more? After a long silence, he said, "If there is nothing, then watch this old monk ride the mountain behind the hall and leap into all of your eyes.
I shall go about acting in a topsy-turvy manner, reviling the Buddhas and cursing the Patriarchs! With a shout, he descended from his seat.
Chan Master Chushi Qi’s Small General Talk for the Summer Retreat: To blink one's eyebrows is already to have missed it;
once the mouth opens, one has already fallen into verbal error. Few people know the pivot of the Patriarch’s gate; the entire world is vast and empty, yet everyone treads upon fire.

To unfold the teaching before the sound deceives the *śrāmaṇera*; to deliberate on the words after the phrase merely turns them into a track. With a single kick, he overturns the waters of the great ocean.
A single blow knocks down Mount Sumeru—yet even this is not yet the mark of one who is impulsive by nature;

how much less so for those who imitate patterns and forms, feigning muteness and deafness, severing false攀缘 (pān-yuan) to seek true liberation? This is much like mistaking a skull for water, or buying cinnabar to paint the moon.
When, in the year of the donkey, will you ever find rest? Longshou Mountain does not begrudge its verbal karma for your sakes.
He punctures [the delusion] by holding up his whisk and saying, "Do you see it? This is the gate of Mañjuśrī.

If one enters through the gate of Mañjuśrī, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, walls, and rubble will cause you to turn your back on the dust of the senses and unite with awakening. He strikes the whisk.

Do you hear it? This is the gate of Avalokiteśvara. If one enters through the gate of Avalokiteśvara, the sound of pines and wind, the echoes from mountain streams, and the cawing of crows and chirping of magpies will teach you to return to the root and restore the source.
Upon reaching this state, you realize the Immovable Honored One and achieve supreme awakening.

Yet you must further know that there is a single aperture at the crown of the head. Do you understand this thoroughly? In the morning air of the wheat harvest season, the summer days of the *huai* tree...

The afternoon shadows were clear and cool. Again, [the Master] raised the case of Layman Pang’s visit to Great Master Ma. Pang asked, “Who is the one who does not take companionship with the myriad dharmas?
The Master replied, “Wait until you can suck up all the waters of the West River in a single mouth, and then I will tell you.
The Master [Zhaozhou] offered this verse: “A phrase that covers heaven and earth— Master Ma could not lift it even with all his might. How amusing that Qingyuan received it!”
Stonehead. Whenever you meet someone, simply ask about the rice of Luling.
A small *paramārtha* (private) discourse for the summer retreat: there are some who have a sandalwood grove surrounded by sandalwood;
there are some who have a thornbush grove surrounded by thorns; there are some who have a sandalwood grove surrounded by thorns; and there are some who have a thornbush grove.
Surrounded by sandalwood trees, you people carry staffs slung across your shoulders and wear tightly laced straw sandals, wandering here and there, east and west.

In which grove do you dwell? If it be a grove of sandalwood, then you are a golden-maned lion, capable of both yielding and seizing, capable of killing and bringing back to life. If it be a grove of thorns, then you are but a fox or a wolf.
The wild jackal cannot grant life, cannot take it away, cannot kill, and cannot bring it back to life.
Following the herd and chasing the pack, fearing death and craving life—if one beats and kills thousands or tens of thousands of them, what crime or transgression is there?

Furthermore, when surrounded by the five kinds of forest dwellers, if one calls it a golden-maned lion, it is still a fox, a wolf, or a wild jackal; if one calls it a fox, a wolf, or a wild jackal, it remains so.
A wild jackal is also a golden-haired lion. Ultimately, what shall it be called? Can it let go or cannot let go?
Can it seize or cannot seize? Can it kill or cannot kill? Can it bring to life or cannot bring to life? How can this be determined?
If you can determine it, I grant you the freedom to roam the world at will; if you cannot determine it, there shall be no liberation for ninety days.
For such a period, they undergo the suffering of sinking and wandering for a hundred kalpas. Again, a monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is the man-eating lion?
Zhaozhou said, "Take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, take refuge in the Sangha; do not bite the old monk.
The Master said, "That monk was merely a dung-eating dog. Why was it that as soon as Zhaozhou saw him, he immediately discharged his excrement and urine?"
The colorful [deceptions] rush toward the petty household.
A summer retreat small discourse: In the kingdom of Magadha, this command was personally enacted; one must risk death to know it, for it replaces one’s very life-force.
Even if one lets go with both hands from a precipice and is willing to accept it oneself—reviving after being cut off—it cannot deceive the Sovereign. This too is so.
Staring with eyes wide open inside a coffin—here in Fengshan, there are no such complications. Usually, we simply count ninety days as one summer retreat.
We eat yellow rice and Chen-rice, seasoned with bitter vegetables and soup. Before Zunseng Temple, the green mountains stretch on and on without end;
at the Westxing Ferry, the white waves roll vast and infinite. If you wish to walk, let it be; if you wish to sit, let it be.
"Sitting. Whether coming out, it is up to you; whether entering, it is up to you. Unfolding and rolling up with ease—why be constrained by this or that?
Yet, one must not allow oneself to be buried within a heap of sounds and forms, nor must one allow oneself to depart from those sounds and forms.
When neither of these is the case, what then? "The noble son in brocade robes; the recluse beneath the forest trees is lofty. Furthermore, there is a verse which says: "Set aside the East..."
Walking upon the mountains and waters; a fragrant breeze brings a subtle coolness to the halls and pavilions. To dwell in the mountains costs not the slightest effort;
there is someone naturally carrying the broken-legged cauldron.
Chan Master Zhuang of Da’ān gives a small *can* (sermon) for the summer retreat: "When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault. You all..."
For a person to resolve to practice Zen is already to miss the point;

how much more so to listen to those old masters on their meditation platforms as they speak of the profound and the subtle, citing ancient precedents and modern examples to represent the school's transmission. This is to be far removed from it indeed.

If you wish now to accord with the original ground, you must simply let go of everything that came before—knowing nothing and understanding nothing—and turn toward the time prior to the existence of both sentient beings and Buddhas.

Fix your gaze with single-minded focus to see what is there. Suddenly, you will burst through empty space and perceive that the worlds of the ten directions are entirely the monastery of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*).
Where else could there be mountains, rivers, or the great earth? When I, this mountain monk, speak thus, it is because of this.
This is like applying medicine to a dead horse. If one were a monk who transcends the lineage and defies conventional categories, every step would have a path for self-expression.
[The Master] picks up his staff and asks, "Among this great assembly, is there any monk who transcends the lineage and defies conventional categories?
He strikes the ground with the staff: "The clay ox suffered distress last night; even until now, no trace of it is seen."
Small Assembly Sermon for the Retreat: The mind is like the realm of empty space; it reveals dharmas equal to empty space. When one realizes this emptiness, there is neither "is" nor "is not.
From the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity down to the present, all have transmitted this mind-dharma to future generations to perform the great work of Buddha.
Today, Jing Mountain takes this very mind-dharma as its great monastery. Throughout the ten directions of the Dharma-realm, whether they be sages...
If ordinary people were all equally enlightened in the wisdom of equality, [the Master] would suddenly pick up his staff, strike once, and say:
"The Tathāgatas of the past have already accomplished this gate; the Bodhisattvas of the present each now enter perfect clarity;
those who practice and study in the future should abide according to this. When Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva went to buy a sesame cake with money, he let go of his hand."
It is, however, a steamed bun. [The Master] strikes the meditation desk once with his staff. He then raises the story of Zhaozhou’s examination of the old woman, offering this verse:
"On the road to Mount Tiantai, the old woman was exposed; It took Zhaozhou to do it— I say there is no basis for it at all.
People say there is a reason for it."

Chan Master Shuzhong Yun’s Small General Introduction for the Summer Retreat: Those who are sharp and quick-witted lift their robes and go immediately; they are like a hawk snatching up a pigeon—thirty blows to the heels would be well-deserved.
Those who are dull and muddled do not turn back after three attempts; they are like fish lingering in a stagnant pond—a single needle-point on the crown of their heads would suffice.
The heavens and earth of antiquity and today, the sun and moon of antiquity and today, the human relations of antiquity and today: good does not increase.

A single hair’s breadth of ugliness does not diminish by even a hair’s breadth. To take Great Perfect Enlightenment as one's monastery and yet draw lines on the ground to create a prison—this is how the labels of "punishment" and "name" become manifest.
While the body and mind dwell in the wisdom of equanimity, one remains buried in a ghost cave where worldly anxieties abound.

At Lingyan Temple tomorrow, the summer retreat begins; tonight’s informal discourse (*xiaocan*) will neither speak of the marvelous nor discuss the profound, nor will any [elaborate] arrangements be made.

Set a time limit: beneath three rafters and before a seven-foot mat, let everyone sleep crosswise or lie prostrate as they please, drinking when thirsty and eating when hungry; you will surely find the flower of the mind blooming and illuminating the lands of the ten directions. If, however, you harbor thoughts of limitation and fall into the trap of views and hearing, then on a future day someone will come to demand the price of your meal—do not say I did not warn you. Again, he raised an ancient precedent: The World-Honored One once said: "If one can see the Buddha-nature within this very body, then even if one does not practice the Way, one will naturally attain it. If you do not see the Buddha-nature within this very body, then even if you practice the Way for a hundred thousand kalpas, you will never attain it. Do not say that the Buddha-nature is something external. It is precisely because you do not see the Buddha-nature within this very body that you seek it elsewhere. If you truly see the Buddha-nature within this very body, then even if you do not practice the Way, you will naturally attain it. What is this Buddha-nature? It is the very thing that, from morning until night, you cannot avoid. You have been wearing it on your head for eighty years; you have been carrying it on your back for sixty years. It is not something you can cast away, nor is it something you can discard. It is not something you can grasp, nor is it something you can let go. It is not something you can see with your eyes, nor is it something you can hear with your ears. It is not something you can speak with your mouth, nor is it something you can think with your mind. It is not something you can know through consciousness, nor is it something you can perceive through the senses. It is not something you can reach with your hands, nor is it something you can touch with your body. It is not something you can obtain through effort, nor is it something you can lose through negligence. It is not something you can gain through merit, nor is it something you can lose through demerit. It is not something you can increase through good deeds, nor is it something you can decrease through evil deeds. It is not something you can brighten through wisdom, nor is it something you can darken through ignorance. It is not something you can purify through meditation, nor is it something you can defile through distraction. It is not something you can cultivate through the path, nor is it something you can abandon through the non-path. The World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma in the kingdom of Magadha during the summer retreat. At that time, he said to Ānanda:
"Among my great disciples and the fourfold assembly of devas and humans, they do not give rise to reverence when I constantly preach the Dharma.

I shall now enter the chamber of the *iṃśa* mortar and sit for the ninety-day summer retreat. Should anyone suddenly come to inquire about the Dharma, you must speak on my behalf, saying: 'All dharmas are non-arising.'"

"All phenomena are without cessation. Having spoken thus, he closed his room and sat. He then offered this verse: The summer retreat is drawing near; Extend your compassion and encourage our cultivation.
If humans and devas do not hold us in reverence, Time will simply continue its flow. Every dharma is without arising or ceasing; In every instance, there is releasing and gathering.
For these ninety days, I have briefly closed my room; This great kindness is truly difficult to repay.

Within the sphere of the patch-robed monk, there is no need for contrived arrangement. Have you not heard it said that the entirety of heaven and earth is the single eye of the śramaṇa?

Whenever I see a virtuous teacher giving a small lecture or a general discourse, they all speak with the elegance of gathered flowers and clustered brocade, their words interlaced like lattice patterns, so thorough that not even a drop of water can leak through.
Or they employ great capacities and great functions, driving the oxen of the plowmen and snatching the food from the mouths of the hungry, scolding and rebuking those who stand in line."
The Patriarch jostles and pushes aside the former sages like wind, thunder, and rolling lightning; those who watch cannot even blink.
To uphold the teaching in this manner tonight is utterly without a handle and utterly without flavor—like a mosquito on an iron ox, there is truly no place for the mouth to bite.
It leaves people in a state of doubt. When one arrives here, how can one respond? Bring forth the staff!
Can you take it away? Can you take it away by shouting? Is it not possible to leap down from the meditation seat and return to the abbot’s quarters?
Or otherwise, can you provide two fresh turns of phrase as an answer? Such theoretical discussions are all merely medicinal prescriptions used by others in various quarters;
they not only fail to cure the chronic ailments of the vital organs, but only serve to further increase them.

A grave illness! Since it is not like this at all, how can it be so? Now, regarding that place where even Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot reach, he answers with that which the old monks of the world have cast aside as useless.

Not only does he answer them, but he intends for those who hear and see him to completely wash away from their chests all notions of Chan, the Way, Buddha-dharma, and intellectual views, so that everyone becomes like the lion king Kṣāntivādin.
