"Where does the fault lie? Yunmen said, "Return to me the payment for ninety days' worth of meals. The Master said, "Level as a mirror's surface, yet treacherous as a mountain of blades.
This monk possessed the strategic ingenuity to break through the sturdy barrier;
Yunmen skillfully employed the tactic of subduing an enemy's army without fighting. Nevertheless, the nostrils remain in Lingyin’s hands.
Chan Master Xueyan Qin’s Small General Talk at the Close of the Summer Retreat: "No liberation and no bondage is still like driving a stake into empty space;
having cultivation and realization is no different from chasing the wind or grasping the moon.

Therefore, during this summer retreat of one hundred and twenty days at Longxing, I have done nothing but sleep early and rise late with the pure assembly before me, eating plain rice and coarse tea, like a rustic farmer in a village of three households."
This old man, hurriedly and laboriously, passes his days just like this. I do not dare to bind you all with even a single thread of monastic regulations.

If you, sirs, can simply let go of your hands and feet and trample over them, then throughout the twelve hours of the day, you will be free to pierce through every hole and fall eastward or westward as you please;
whether moving against or with the current, rolling up or unfolding, you will be sovereign in every direction.
[The Master] strikes the whisk and says: "White clouds lie even beyond the green mountains. He then raises the case of Muzhou asking Yangshan:
"For an entire summer you have not come up here. Yangshan replies: "I have cleared a patch of fallow land and planted a basketful of millet.
Muzhou says: "Then you have not spent the summer in vain. Yangshan asks: "How about you, Master? Muzhou replies: "One meal at midday, and one sleep after nightfall."
Yangshan said, "Master Yunmen has not spent his time in vain. Having finished speaking, he stuck out his tongue.
Guishan said, "Jizi, why do you wound your own life? The Master (Zhaozhou) commented: "Guishan and Yangshan were such that the son transmitted the father’s vocation;
it was truly worth admiring. Yet, as time passed, they ended up contradicting one another. One might say: 'The father is no father, and the son is no son.'"
This summer, Longxing has done nothing, yet it was not in vain. Tell me, is he the same as the ancients, or is he different?
The toad at the bottom of the well swallows the moon.

A Small Sermon upon the Conclusion of the Summer Retreat. During the ninety days of the *kṣetra-pāda* (the summer retreat), from the eastern corridor to the western corridor, one does not move even a single step.
Upon concluding the summer and performing the *pravāraṇā* (the ceremony of self-examination), one sits in this hall upon this seat and may travel across the entire world without hindrance.
Even seeing it thus is still a mere proclamation or a tangle of vines; you have not yet possessed the eye that penetrates the barrier. But what, then, is the eye that penetrates the barrier?
Is there anyone who, having lived before the heavens and earth were yet formed and after the Buddha had already appeared, knows where to find their place of rest?
If there is such a person, Dao Lin’s three hundred and sixty joints—from the crown of the head to the heels—have been seen through by them all at once.
If this is not yet so, go to various places after five days and stay outside the gates for a time.
Regarding the Small Sermon on the End of the Summer Retreat: for ninety days one restrains the feet and for three months one protects life.

When the practice is perfected and the merit fulfilled, it is as before—at noon or at the third watch of the night—the waters of the Dragon Spring are calm and the waves are still; the mist locks the path of the otters and clouds stretch across the bridge. As for those who depart...
Those who go depart on their own; those who stay remain on their own. Those who sit sit on their own; those who walk walk on their own. Why is this so?
"Though there may be a path through the night atop the staff’s tip, let us for now support one another with our broken-legged cauldron. Again, Master Jia Shan addressed the assembly, saying:
"Recognize the Son of Heaven at the gate of the bustling marketplace; realize the old monk upon the tips of the hundred grasses. To speak in such a manner—

"Such talk is precisely to falsely recognize the shadows of discrimination within the sensory realms. If you were to sit with hands folded and robes hanging loose, or dwell alone on a solitary peak, you would not have even dreamed of it.
Do you all wish to see Jia Shan? Do you recognize Yang Shan?
He held up his whisk and said, "One verdict settles everything."

Chan Master Chushi Qi’s Small General Discourse upon the End of the Summer Retreat: "O worthy ones! To have 'a hundred things settled and a thousand matters resolved' is what defines a person of no affairs (*wushiren*).
If you reach the various quarters, they will surely take you and arrange you beneath a bright window. However, here at Yongzuo, we cannot let such a thing pass. Why is this so?
Even one who has 'a hundred things settled and a thousand matters resolved' is still only halfway there. Have you not seen how Master Yuanwu..."
Shangdao: To engage people through the dharmas of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is to cause them to fall within the dharmas of conventional truth;

to engage people through the spiritual capacity (mārga) of the patriarchs and Buddhas is to cause them to fall within the spiritual capacity of the patriarchs and Buddhas; to engage people through the "upward" picking up and holding forth is to cause them to fall within that upward picking up and holding forth;
to engage people through "thus and thus" is to cause them to fall within "thus and thus. To [engage people] through non-...
To receive people with "thus" or "not thus" is to fall into the midst of "not thus, not thus.
To receive people with "neither thus nor not thus" in every case is to fall into the midst of "neither thus nor not thus" in every case.
"Even if there is not a single cloud ten thousand miles away, the blue sky must still receive a blow of the staff. You should know that this matter does not come from elsewhere:
'In the treasury of our King, there is no such sword; yet this sword never leaves the King’s treasury. The final phrase finally reaches the secure barrier;
it blocks the vital ford, allowing passage to neither ordinary person nor sage. This was the final phrase for the ninety-day period.
"How would you say it? [The Master said: "In the summer months, fiery clouds scorch the azure caves; in the clear autumn, perilous dewdrops fall upon the golden platter. Again, he raised a case:
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is it like when the trees wither and the leaves fall? Yunmen said, "The body is exposed in the golden wind. The Master said:
"If that monk had said, 'Thank you for answering my question,' Master Yunmen would have found it difficult to justify his position. As for this mountain monk..."

"Not so. What about when the tree withers and the leaves fall? He raised his staff; as soon as [the monk] hesitated, he struck him down from the Dharma hall to avoid being scrutinized by those from all quarters.

Small-scale Sermon for the End of the Summer Retreat: The golden wind fans the wilds; the pale moon flows across the heavens. Distant waters spread out flat; fine clouds are all unrolled. Everywhere, cicadas chirp at evening;
on the continuous mountains, tree leaves startle with the onset of autumn. It is luminously without concealment; it is clearly manifest, utterly free of leakage.
Height does not reside in the highest peak; wealth does not reside in Fuyan; joy does not reside in heaven; suffering does not reside in [hell].

"O virtuous ones of the various hells! Just as life and death alternate and cold and heat shift in succession, as the unraveling of knots follows one after another and time flies like an arrow—where, ultimately, shall the True Man of No-Rank (wuwei zhenren) be placed?
'Donning the straw raincoat and tilting the bamboo hat beyond the thousand peaks;
drawing water from a different stream to irrigate the vegetables before the Five Elders. Again, he raised the case where Cuiyan addressed the assembly at the end of summer, saying: 'One summer...'"
I have already spoken for the sake of you brothers. Look: are the eyebrows of Cuiyan still there? Baofu said, "The heart of a thief is always apprehensive.
Changqing said, "He is born! Yunmen said, "The barrier. The Master’s verse says: "Prominently emerging from the forest is Cuiyan;
His tongue never moved—for whom did he speak? Now, fortunately, his eyebrows remain; Even those with iron brows and copper heads [cannot steal them]."
I am not yet familiar with it.

Regarding the small *sīmā* (summer retreat) *pratyavekṣaṇā*: what was spoken by the one at Baoen during this summer retreat, and what was investigated by you all during this summer retreat—you must know that what was spoken did not convey a single word, and what was investigated did not rely upon a single dharma.
Not conveying a single word, though spoken, there is no speaking; not relying [upon a single dharma]...
To investigate one dharma and find no dharma to investigate—this is true investigation. To speak and find nothing to say—this is true speaking.
Therefore it is said: "The ten directions gather together; each and every one studies non-action. This is the field for selecting Buddhas;

with an empty mind, they return as top graduates. A great man must not accept being directed by others. With an empty mind as a top graduate, one suppresses the worthy to become base. Thus it is accomplished.
The Buddha acts as the patriarch; he loves the holy and hates the common—yet it is not like this at all.
To have no rope yet bind oneself is to be like a lion cub letting out a single roar, causing foxes, wolves, and jackals to vanish in an instant.
It is like a drum smeared with poison: those who hear it, whether far or near, all perish. When the ninety-day retreat is complete, what then? Ordinarily, it is just like the autumn wind blowing in.
When one does not intend to cool others, people cool themselves of their own accord. Again, it is related that Dongshan and his senior teacher Mi were visiting Chan Master Zhe of Ezhou.
Zhe asked, "Where have you recently come from, Reverend? Dongshan said, "Hunan. Zhe asked, "What is the surname of the Military Governor (Guancha Shi)?
Dongshan said, "I do not take his surname. Zhe asked, "What is his name? Dongshan said, "I am not informed of his name."

Zhaozhou asked, "Do you still attend to administrative affairs? Dongshan said, "There is naturally a hall and a curtain. Zhaozhou asked, "Do you still come and go? Dongshan said, "I do not come and go.
Zhaozhou said, "How can it be that you do not come and go? Dongshan shook his sleeves and departed.
The next day, Zhaozhou entered the Sangha Hall and said, "Yesterday, I did not find one turn of phrase satisfactory when I spoke with the two *jiaoluo*. I now ask the two *jiaoluo* to speak it."
"If you can speak, we will open the gruel and wait for you to pass the summer. Speak quickly, speak quickly! Shanshan said, "One born of great nobility.
The Master said, "If you wish to understand this nobility, do not rely on these two flaps of skin [the mouth]. Where would all of you go to grope for it?"
A Small *Can* on the Conclusion of the Summer Retreat: To stumble upon a flat plain is no small matter; one’s heels have slipped away, bringing laughter to the bystanders.
"This very mind is Buddha," "neither this mind nor that Buddha"—this place has not even two taels of silver, yet the common folk sell three sheng of wine.
Furthermore, there are those who are utterly witless, brooding over and over again before the wind and under the moon, from the furthest corners of the earth to the ends of the heavens.
A lifetime of wandering. In the West (India), they used a wax man as a test; here, I use a bamboo stick as a test. To call it a "bamboo stick" is to offend;
not to call it a "bamboo stick" is to turn one's back on it. Speak quickly! Speak quickly!

If you hesitate even for a moment, I shall strike you across the spine with this very staff. Again, Changqing said: "It has been thoroughly cleaned and swept away. Yet you still come forward to approach me."
"Seeking! I shall strike you across the spine with a blow of my staff. If there is a blow that reaches you, you must feel shame and remorse;
if not a single blow reaches you, where then will you find understanding? Xuedou said: "Xuedou does not say it this way.
Having already swept everything clean and put it away, you must come forward. I shall strike you across the spine with a blow of my staff. If there is a blow that reaches you..."
"You will then be subjected to humiliation. Not a single blow shall reach you; I shall treat you with impartiality. Simply understand it in this way.
The Master said, "Among the assembly, they deliberate and say: 'One must clear away [impurities] while sitting on clean ground.
To come forward seeking a blow is to have a share in receiving one. Seeking is the disease; the blow is the medicine. Therefore, Xuedou said: 'There is a blow that reaches you.'"
"You are immediately subjected to humiliation. Not a single blow reaches you; I grant you an equal exit.

Zen practitioners fabricate their own doctrines like hemp and millet, yet they fail to realize that these two great elders—one digging a pit in the earth, the other leveling a well and blocking a stove—both intended to bring about a state of Great Peace through effortless means.
Alas, they instead invited ridicule. Vipaśyin Buddha set his mind upon this long ago, continuing until—

Now, not obtaining the subtle, he gave this small *shanshan* (summer retreat) discourse. In the Linji school’s style, one must discern the host; if one does not discern the host, having eyes is like being blind.
Thus it is said: "Without allowing for deliberation, he cuts through the entire body; only then is he named the 'Host among Hosts,' the sharp-edged precious blade."
The sword is always manifest before one; were it to be aimed at an offender, its blade would leave corpses strewn for ten thousand li.

All you who carry staffs and travel as pilgrims—have you yet discerned the Master? If you can discern him, then upon seeing that old fellow on the meditation seat just opening his mouth and moving his tongue, you would turn your back on the Dharma Hall and put on your straw sandals to depart;
only then would you possess even a modicum of the true spirit of a patch-robed monk.

But you are just like this—so soft and yielding, as if you have no backbone. When you hear someone say "existence," you cling to existence; when you hear them say "non-existence," you cling to non-existence.
Throughout the twelve periods of the day, you lack any true mastery. With what will you confront birth-and-death and repay the offerings of the faithful?
To bury yourself and bring shame upon the ancestral lineage, none surpasses such a person. Hardly has the retreat begun when...
Look at the summer retreat: day after day, year after year, one waits for Old Man Yan to collect his bill for the meal.
It is already late; why not turn back early? Reflect carefully and see what the principle is. "The skull-bone constantly interacts with the world; the nostrils touch upon the family style.
The divine light of ten thousand miles is the mark behind the crown. If you can realize this directly, you will turn [the wheel].
The attainment of sainthood lies in but a moment. Should this not yet be so, you will end up beating your breast with your hands.
Again, he raised the kōan of the outsider who asked the Buddha, "What Dharma did you preach yesterday? The Master offered this verse: "Having traveled dozens of stages throughout Jiangnan,"
The morning breeze and waning moon enter Huacheng; on Chaoyuan Pavilion, the west wind blows fiercely. All together they enter the Changyang grove as the sound of rain.
Master Shuzhong Yun’s *Xiaoxi* (Small General Address) for the end of the summer retreat: Bodhidharma did not come to the Eastern Land, and the Second Patriarch did not go to the West.
"Sky! Water grows, the boat rises; when the mud is deep, the Buddha is great. At Ch'oeam, we spent an entire summer with our brothers chatting here and there, wasting our time in vain.
At Noryang, I simply observed the ninety days of a single summer retreat. "The snow on the swan's neck," "the wax man," and "the ice."
An iron ball. This single fire-bracelet—take it all up and throw it behind you.
The sun does not wait for fire to be hot; the moon does not wait for wind to be cool. The foul old woman in the village of three houses has no skill at all;
the tipsy old man at the crossroads is far too full of gallantry. For one who discerns the subtlest measure of a grain, what number can there be? It clings to the teeth and adheres...
There are many things beneath the teeth.

A small *can* (private instruction) upon the conclusion of the summer retreat: when the rules of the *an-gu* (summer retreat) are fulfilled, a single thought spans ten thousand years; when the mouth of the "cloth bag" is opened, everything is resolved and all matters are settled.

From the south of heaven to the north of earth, there is nothing that is not the wondrous field of *yuanjue* (perfect enlightenment); from the east of the stream to the west of the stream, it is all the king’s water and grass.
Just so, just so. One can clear a patch of fallow land and plant a basketful of millet.
Not so, not so. One meal at midday and one sleep after nightfall. Not so, not so, yet not so—then it is just so.

Drawing forth the long sword that leans against the heavens, one cuts through the entanglements of superficial discourse; thus, above there is nothing to grasp at, and below there is no self to be found.
The Master’s own radiance was ever manifest before him, standing firm like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high. At such a time as this, do you all still know this news?
If you do not yet know it, you will inevitably continue to scatter sand and dirt upon the pure ground.
When the World-Honored One was first born, he pointed with one hand toward heaven and with the other toward earth, walked seven steps, and his eyes—
Looking around the four quarters, he then said: "In the heavens above and on the earth below, I alone am honored. Is this not that very message?

In the West, the Seven Buddhas and Sixteen Patriarchs; in the East, the Two and Three [Patriarchs]—some administering blows, some shouting "Ho!", some rolling a ball before the hall, some placing water in the room—is this not that very message?
As for the rest—the three pounds of flax, the dried dung, the cypress tree in the courtyard...

The story of Mazu and the cypress tree, the story of the donkey eating grass in the back garden, the dialogue of Zhaozhou examining the old woman, and the story of Baizhang and the wild duck—though these may present three sides or two faces, and differ in a myriad ways, are they not all, after all, this very same message?

To engage in such theoretical discussion merely to accommodate various capacities is nothing but idle chatter before those with the clear eye. Have you not seen it said: "The one path that points upward"?
Not transmitted by a thousand sages, students exhaust their bodies like monkeys grasping at reflections. [The Master] suddenly seizes his staff, strikes it once, and says:

"Shattered to pieces! No old nest or track. Having grasped the nostrils, one loses the mouth. If you intend to hide your body within the Big Dipper," [he continues: "You will find yourself in the midst of the Southern Cross."
One should join one’s palms toward the Southern Dipper (the constellation of the Great Bear) and then recite this verse: The summer retreat has ended; where will you go to unpack your bedding?
I urge you to temporarily still the mind for a moment. In all directions, the furnaces have cooled like ashes; At Shaoshi, the gate and courtyard are as deep as the sea.
If you wish to awaken and transcend Buddhas and patriarchs, Do not take intellectual understanding as your inner core. Beside the Stone of Awakened Clarity, one may find true delight.
Together we listen as the pines and winds perform the sublime music.

Chan Master Zhuang Da’an’s Small General Address upon the End of the Summer Retreat: At the absolute summit all is vast and silent; amidst the towering, rugged mountains, not to depart from this very place is itself the *dharma-śālā*.
Why wait for a formal proclamation to call it a Buddhist service? Furthermore, what need is there to speak of long or short periods?

One must establish and maintain mindfulness. The kingdom of Magadha has already been burdened with excessive verbiage; the city of Vaiśālī has become nothing but redundant words. Consider, for instance, when Guishan asked Yangshan, "What have you accomplished during this summer retreat?

Yangshan replied, "I have cleared a patch of fallow land and sown a basketful of millet. What common ground is there for conversation? Guishan said, "A shrimp is bent for your sake. Yangshan said, "I have cleared a patch of fallow land and sown a basketful of millet.

What common ground is there for conversation? Guishan said, "A shrimp is bent for your sake. Yangshan said, "I have cleared a patch of fallow land and sown a basketful of millet. What common ground is there for conversation? Guishan— [The text ends here].
Yangshan said, "Master Yunzi, this summer can truly be called not spent in vain. Why did you not give him his own portion of fodder?

He then looked up and asked Baizhang, "What have you accomplished during this summer retreat, Reverend? This was quite a clever retort. Baizhang replied, "During the day, one meal; at night, one sleep.
Yangshan followed up with a search for flaws, saying, "Reverend, this summer can truly be called not spent in vain. They exchanged [these words].
"You deceive one another! Tonight, if someone were suddenly to ask me, 'What have you done at Jingshan during this summer retreat?
I would simply tell him: 'Step by step, I tread upon solid ground. Now tell me, was it spent in vain, or was it not? [He] takes up his staff, draws a line, and says:
'The crane has nine mounds, yet its wings find it hard to soar; the horse lacks the thousand-li stride, so its pursuit of the wind is in vain.'"

Small-scale *chanshi* for the end of the summer retreat: Within the present moment there is no dharma; outside the dharma there is no mind. When both mind and dharma are forgotten, principle and phenomena penetrate one another.
Above, there is nothing to grasp or look up to; below, the self is utterly cut off. Every single thing reveals the true mechanism; every single object fully manifests wondrous function.
"When I press my finger, the Sea-Seal (Sāgaramudrā) emits light; when you briefly raise your mind, the dust of affliction (*kleśa*) first arises.
Old Śākyamuni is filled with shame on his face. You need only externally cease all conditions and internally have no gasping of the mind;

when the mind is like a wall, only then can you enter the Way. This was a moment of exposure by Master Bodhidharma. Generally, in the monasteries, the small formal discourse (*xiao-chan*) is taken as the family teaching."

"What fault is there in all of you putting on your robes and eating your meals every day? When the summer retreat is completed at the end of seventy days, it will not hinder your freedom to come and go.
This old monk’s affairs as abbot are many; I shall no longer speak at length or drone on. He struck his whisk. "Those who recognize gratitude are few; those who betray it are many.
He then raised another instance, citing Cuiyan’s address to the assembly at the end of the summer: "For one summer, I have been with my elder brother..."
The younger brother speaks of the east and the west; look, are the eyebrows of Cuiyan still there? The Master said: "All summer long he spoke of the east and again of the west;
Cuiyan’s skillful means were truly meager. That his eyebrows were struck away is but a trivial matter; how could one avoid entering the thicket with one's whole body?"
Record of the Essential Teachings of the Successive Patriarchs,
Scroll Eleven Record of the Essential Teachings of the Successive Patriarchs,
Scroll Twelve Compiled by Xing Yue of Lou Dong, Abbot of Lian’an Chan Monastery at the Eighteen Streams in Wulin.
Chan Master Liaoyuan Yu’s Small Lecture on the Dissolution of the Summer Retreat: In the past, there was never anything to bind; now, what need is there to unbind?
Since binding and unbinding are fundamentally without mind, for one who is neither bound nor liberated—thus, thus! The myriad phenomena of the universe are, to the very bottom, solitary.
Dangerous! The great earth, mountains, and rivers are all steep and perilous above. It is not so, it is not so. Beneath the gate of the great sun, every day is autumn;
before the hall of the bright moon, every moment is summer. Within "it is so" there is "it is not so," and within "it is not so" there is yet "it is so.
All-encompassing wisdom penetrates without obstruction. Take the lantern and bring it into the Buddha Hall. Bring...
[The Master] places the lantern atop the mountain gate and asks the assembly: "Within these ninety days, have you attained resonance with the Way yet?
If not, I, this mountain monk, have a skillful means. He suddenly takes up his staff, strikes it once, and says:
"A gust of west wind comes; two or three leaves fall. He then cites the story of Mingzhao when he was traveling as a pilgrim and arrived at Xinghua Temple in Quanzhou.
At the place of Master Jiaotan, Jiaotan said, "A high-ranking traveler-monk must reach the place where one person is, and must also reach the place where half a person is.
Mingzhao then asked, "I do not ask about the place where one person is; what is the place where half a person is?
Jiaotan was speechless. Later, he instead had his junior disciple ask Mingzhao, "What is the place where half [a person] is?"
"Regarding 'the place where a person is': [Zhaozhou] said, 'Do you want to know where the half-person is? He is merely a fellow who plays with mud balls.
Master Ying'an commented: 'I have heard of the One-Eyed Dragon; indeed, he possesses only one eye. If today a monk were to suddenly ask, "What is the place where the half-person is?
I would strike him across the spine with my staff immediately. If he asked again..."* *(Note: The source text ends mid-sentence regarding the hypothetical follow-up question.)*
"What is the place where this one person resides? Drive him out immediately! Why? Because 'once you have started, do not stop.
The Master said, "They are all fellows playing with lumps of mud; Old Man Ying’an was slightly superior. He then composed a verse and presented it to the assembly:
"Xingjiao upheld [the truth] and was not deceived; Mingzhao followed the example and played with lumps of mud. Within the blow of the staff there is an eye—clear!"
Like the sun; one must recognize true gold by looking within the fire.
Small Assembly: "Ten thousand miles, not a blade of grass; once you step out the door, it is all grass. The Great Elephant of Jiazhou suddenly turns over;
the Iron Ox of Shanyu is startled into a collapse. Not appearing before people—selling a dog while hanging up a sheep. When the mirror is shattered, heaven is desolate.

If it is the ground, then gold and sand are mixed; if it is not, then jade and stone are burned together. Without the hammer and tongs of one’s own true portion, it is difficult to clarify the single aperture above.
Holding up his staff, he said: "A single tune on the unperforated flute of Shaolin has, from the beginning, mostly been blown against the wind."

Small Assembly: The autumn wind is cool; the autumn night is long. The three-month period has already concluded. How shall we deliberate? It is not the character "yi" (以), nor is it the character "ba" (八).
The horns of the yellow ox point toward heaven, while its four legs hang down past its nose. My Head Seat has entered the world.
"My head seat is tending the ox; my head seat is traveling on pilgrimage; my head seat has arrived. This Dharma abides in its own place;
the characteristics of the world are eternally present. That which was spoken before the time of Vimalacitra is precisely the second phrase.
Bring me back the first phrase! [The Master] strikes the whisk and says: "The seal of the three essentials opens; the vermilion dot is narrow. There is no room for hesitation; the host..."

The Guest’s Portion. Again, [the Master] raised a case where a monk asked Yunmen: "At the end of autumn and the beginning of summer, if someone suddenly asks you about your future path, how will you respond?
Yunmen said, "Everyone, step back. The monk asked, "Where does the fault lie? Yunmen said, "Give me back my ninety days' worth of rice money!
The Master said: "This monk was too eager to reach his destination; Yunmen pierced through the thinnest spot first. There is [a lesson here].
Questioning Original Enlightenment: "If you simply point toward it, saying 'Ten li of long pavilions, five li of short watchtowers,' where does the error lie?
'I urge you to drink one more cup; once you go west out of Yangguan Pass, there will be no old friend.'"
A Small Sermon: Long-term or short-term, the face of the sun or the face of the moon—the universe unfolds upon the tip of a single hair;
it flashes like lightning within a spark struck from stone. If you have a staff, I give you a staff; if you have no staff, I take away your staff.
When the water is level, it makes no sound; when the mountain is still, it does not move. Thirty years ago, this mountain monk went forth to seek the Way upon the sea.
Upon reflection, it is simply this: meeting tea, one drinks tea; meeting rice, one eats rice. Cold, one turns toward the fire; hot, one seeks the cool.
Leisurely in the morning, leisurely in the evening—unaware that the hair on one's youthful head has turned entirely white.

By the time one reaches the point where others push one out to dwell in the mountains and hand over the handle of the ladle for others, how can one avoid being crude and muddled? Sometimes at midnight one pierces a needle; sometimes in mid-air...

Seeking a seam [of opportunity]. Were it not for the present assembly of venerable ones exerting their strength to support one another, we would soon see east made into west and south turned into north;
the Dharma hall would be overgrown with weeds and the ancient buildings sealed with moss.
Therefore, although the brothers in the hall this summer are not many, they are all men whom no one elsewhere can ensnare or call back from their resolve—men who have swept away all heterodox views.
The Dense Forest. Setting aside the sicknesses of the Buddhas and the Patriarchs, how much more so Master Yongfu, who stands here like the jaw supporting the lips?
He strikes his staff and says: "A single melody on the unperforated flute of Shaolin—blown against the wind, then blown with the wind."

Master Gulinmao’s Small General Address at the Conclusion of the Summer Retreat: In early autumn, at the end of summer, one goes east or west—to a place ten thousand miles away where there is not a single blade of grass.
Yet, as soon as you step out the door, it is already grass. Where do you intend to go?
Out of necessity, the ancients opened up the great road that penetrates heaven; they also called it the pure, great ocean of quiescent extinction. It is shared by all of you.
Coming out is the same as entering; from the very beginning, there has never been even a hair’s breadth of distinction between the signs of self and other.
If you can realize this directly, then within ninety days your effort will not have been in vain. On the morning of the day of *pravāraṇā*, you may go east or west as you please;
you simply must not go to that place where there are ten thousand miles of land yet not a single blade of grass. Why? It is because you all have never yet set foot upon this One.
This is the path. Therefore, there is a great matter ahead. Xuefeng said, "The entire earth is the gate of liberation;
yet people take it by the hand and refuse to enter. Yunmen said, "The entire earth is the gate of liberation;

yet they mistakenly treat it as a matter of Buddha-dharma. If one point is not penetrated, two points fail; if two points are not penetrated, every encounter results in stagnation. I, this mountain monk, say:
The entire earth is the gate of liberation. All Buddhas of the past, future, and present are contained within it;
you all are also contained within it. [The Master] picks up his staff and says: "This staff, too, is contained within it.
Tell me, is there anything that is not contained within it? After a long pause, he lets out a shout and says: "In vain, with the intent of not yet returning..."
This is spoken for those who aspire toward the Way.
An informal discourse to mark the conclusion of the summer retreat: the ninety-day long period has reached its full term; the ancient tale of two thousand years is once again brought to completion.
Thus, cultivation and realization depend upon the person and have no fixed location; there is neither bondage nor liberation, neither identity nor separation. Within this realization—
Ultimately there is no realization; killing and living both belong entirely to Bodhi. Birth and non-birth are both termed Prajñā.
From South India to North Wutai, the Wisdom of All-Wisdom is pure, non-dual, and indivisible, for it is without distinction and without interruption.
To lift Mount Sumeru and weigh it at twelve *liang*—the Sea God knows its nobility but not its price. Dragging the *zhan*.
The kingdoms of Ba and Silla fought a head-to-head clash; the Queen Mother descended from the clouds by day to look on.

Looking at the ancient shore, who is there holding a fishing rod? Again, a man of old said: "During the ninety days of *jinzu*, the fish swim within the net; during the three months of summer retreat, the birds enter the cage.
When life and death are exhausted, the silkworm makes its cocoon. How can one penetrate these three layers? The Master struck his staff.
It is said: "When one is about to complete a mountain nine *zhang* high, yet fails to advance even a single basket of earth.
This is the small *śamatha-vipaśyanā* instruction for the end of the summer retreat. Of the ninety days of this summer, tomorrow marks the completion of the task.

Since there is no merit in cultivation or realization, all this time has been spent in vain. Nevertheless, even if you proceed in just this way, you will not have failed those who rely on you. Is it not so?
It is said that in the past there was an elder who did not speak with his fellow monks for an entire summer.
A monk said to him, "I do not dare hope for the Master to preach the Buddha-dharma; even if I might hear two characters of the 'True Cause' (zhengyin), that would suffice.

The elder replied, "As for the True Cause, there is not even a single character. Having said this, he tapped his teeth and remarked, "Just now, I spoke without reason. An elder in the next room heard this.
He said, "What a fine pot of soup, ruined by two mouse droppings! The old master held fast his secure barrier, blocking all passage so that not even a drop could leak through.
This monk did not understand the mechanism of the situation and was caught on his hook.

Had it not been for the old master across the wall who provided him with an annotation, he would have almost wasted his entire life. Nevertheless, tell me: did this monk finally consent? Afterwards...
When Master Xuedou brought this up, he said: "In whose household is there not one or two grains? Only upon entering the water does one see the tall man.
My mountain monk’s announcement in this manner is like selling private salt on the public highway.
You all must have blood beneath your skin before you can succeed. After all, how is it so? Were it not for the wild geese last night, who would have seen the sea gate?
In the autumn, [Dongshan] again raised the previous case regarding King Yama’s night assembly, saying: "The Shaoshi mountain has no doors or gates; how can one pass through?
Standing patiently at night deep, listen as I speak of the east and west. The Master called to the assembly, saying: "There is the provisional and there is the real;
there is the illumination and there is the function. It is simply that you must not understand it in such a way. Be careful!"
A small *can* (private instruction) for the end of the summer retreat. Master Wuzu said: "One is three, three is one. A *nüzhēn* flower by the seashore;
a stone of a woman waiting for her husband by the Ju-ma River. The stone strikes the red earth, drawing a winnowing basket. Let the eyes be allowed to grow with rheum.
Although Old Man Wuzu thus grandly opened the mysterious gate, there is nonetheless no principle of Buddha-dharma here. Bao...
It would be better to spend a single summer with your brothers chatting here and there, where every sentence and every word is nothing but the ultimate cream of enlightenment.
At the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, as you go east and west, do not fail this old monk. Why? Because of the thousand-year field.
The Lord of Eight Hundred: the sweet melon is sweet; the bitter gourd is bitter. Having cut off the ultimate barrier, one transcends both Buddhas and Patriarchs.

Again, regarding Mañjuśrī’s three instances of spending the summer retreat: when Kāśyapa struck the gavel intending to expel him, he immediately saw immeasurable worlds, and in each world there was a single Buddha, a single Mañjuśrī, and a single Kāśyapa. The World-Honored One asked:
Kāśyapa said, "Which Mañjuśrī do you wish to expel? Kāśyapa was left speechless. The Master said, "Great Kāśyapa, you have a head but no tail.
Ultimately, how is it? The imperial decree from the Western Heaven is strict; I have stood for a long time."
A Small Sermon upon the Dissolution of the Retreat: Time is easily lost, and now the summer retreat has come to its end. Crickets chirp by the steps; cicadas buzz among the trees.
The golden wind fans the wilds, and yellow leaves drift through the air. Within this very seeing and hearing, there is nothing else.

Thus, it must be that within these ninety days not a single thread of effort was wasted; the ignorance of kalpas shall, in this very moment, melt away like ice and crumble like a fortress. Turn toward—
There is yet more to this matter. The lion’s claws and fangs are bared; within this, there is another reckoning.
One cannot help but brandish a sword at the gate. Thus the ancients said: "It is like a wild goose passing through the vast sky, its shadow sinking into the cold water.
The goose has no intention of leaving a trace; the water has no mind to retain the shadow. Who dares to confront this wondrous blade? The Great Sun.
"Under the gate, day after day, it is already three autumns. If you all can investigate and examine this well, you will surely achieve the fruit of fulfillment.
At such a time as this, what is it like? All myriad activities have ceased and the tortoise hides its six limbs; the single nature is perfectly luminous and the crane has flown out of its cage."
A Small Session for the End of the Summer Retreat. During the three months of *an-guo* (summer retreat), one must realize the goal within the fixed period.
Before the arising of a single thought, cast off the sickness of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Have you all, during the twenty-four hours of each day, attained such resonance?
If you have not yet attained such resonance, I shall let you off the hook regarding the ninety days’ worth of rice money; however, you must not say that you have seen Baoning.
Have you not seen how Master Yunmen said: "Even to reach the point where the entire expanse of heaven and earth is free of even the slightest flaw is still a 'turning phrase.
Only when you do not see a single form is this the 'half-extraction. You must further know that there is a time for the 'full extraction.'"
Both Master Daoyuan and Yunmen failed to resolve this koan. Linji said: "There is one person who is always on the road, yet never leaves home;
there is another person who is always at home, yet never leaves the road. Which of these two is worthy of receiving the offerings of devas and humans?
To speak in such a manner is still to remain halfway there. Since he is already on the road, what need is there to speak of home?
Once you have reached home, you must forget the journey; as it is said, "The path of the practitioner is like hot water melting ice.
Once an arrow has left the bowstring, it has no power to return. Some say that the journey is the home, and the home is the journey.
Such a view has not even dreamed of the stench of Linji’s sweat. It is not as good as his.
Xinghua said: "I traveled throughout the South once as a wandering monk. With my staff, I never once struck upon anyone who truly understood the Buddha-dharma;
yet, there were those who possessed the 'breath' of a true monk. This matter is like the spark from striking flint or a flash of lightning:
whether you grasp it or fail to grasp it, you cannot avoid losing your life. Among them, here and there, one or two were able to turn their bodies and bring forth [their realization]."

One attains the vital breath (*qi*). When sitting directly facing it, one cuts it off and does not accept its arrangement. Yet, when scrutinizing beneath the heels of one's feet, one cannot avoid being in a pitch-black void.
After a long while, he said: "Enough, enough! For what reason do you persist? Spring ends and summer begins; summer ends and autumn begins;
autumn ends and winter begins. With nothing to do, look out over the river at evening: here and there, two or three old fishermen cast their lines."
Master Nanxiu’s Small Assembly Lecture upon the Conclusion of the Retreat: In the various quarters of our tradition, the essence of formal proclamation lies in transcending the ordinary.

As soon as one ascends the hall for a small assembly lecture, there is a tendency to immediately raise such cases as: "The moment he entered the gate, [Linji] struck him," or "The moment he entered the gate, [Linji] shouted.

Or the saying, "At the Wangzhou Pavilion, I met you," or "Waving the hand across the river," or "Upon seeing the monk, he turned his back to the wall. This is done so that even those with the eyes of a dragon or a falcon cannot perceive it.
One might be able to catch a glimpse [of it], but how could Śāriputra or Maudgalyāyana ever hope to reach its depths? It is said that this master has a skillful hand;

his methods are indeed lofty and his subtleties are indeed wondrous. Yet, alas, the Way of the Dharma has declined and those of sharp faculties are few. It is just like trying to fit a square block into a round hole—how can they ever be made to harmonize?
At Jingshan, we sit together on the same mat and play the tune, watching the wind to set our sails, not sparing ourselves even a drop of water.
Dragging through the mud—let the various quarters of the world laugh and marvel as they will. For those of long-standing practice and superior capacity, much talk is unnecessary;
for those who are latecomers and beginners, do not resent this bitter medicine. Having left home, to abandon one’s parents and disregard their care is already an act of unfilial piety;
such a person is a transgressor against the teachings of the sages. One's aim must be to awaken to the nature of mind, to continue the Buddha’s life of wisdom, and to deliver all sentient beings.
If it were merely this, it would not be a timely repayment for the upbringing of one's parents in this life, nor would it constitute great filial piety.

Rather, it shall cause the parents and kinsmen—both those who have been enemies and those who have been kin—throughout successive lifetimes to all attain liberation; how could this be considered a small matter?

If one remains narrow-minded and mediocre, thinking only of today as the third day and tomorrow as the fourth, one will be unable to uphold the precepts and unable to practice meditative concentration, eventually even coming to harm social customs and moral integrity.
This defiles the ancestral altars; one is not merely a transgressor against the teachings of name and ritual, but also a transgressor against the Dharma-gate.
When the moment of birth and death arrives, how shall one resist it? If one abandons this retribution-body, it will be difficult to escape falling into ruin.
As the ancients said: "Prison is not yet suffering; hell is not yet suffering. To lose the human body beneath the *kāṣāya* is what is truly suffering."
These words of medicinal stone must be engraved upon your hearts and worn as amulets.

Suddenly, if one person were to come forth from among the assembly and say, "Venerable sir, Venerable sir, you had better shut that foul mouth," this mountain monk would have no choice but to set up his station beneath a bright window. Why?
Because in recent times throughout the Three Wu and Hundred Yue regions, such a strategic approach is rare to behold. Again, he raised the case of Chan Master Jianguan of Jiufeng. Because...
A monk asked, "In India at the end of the summer retreat, there were those who attained the Way. Is there anyone here who has attained the Way at the end of the summer retreat?
Jiufeng said, "There is. The monk asked, "Who is it? Jiufeng said, "One whose head bears the midnight moon and whose feet tread upon the golden earth.
Suppose someone were to ask Jingshan today, "Is there anyone here who has attained the Way at the end of the summer retreat? Jingshan—
He simply replied, "There is none. When the questioner suddenly asked further, "What do you mean by 'there is none'? he said to him, "Every single one has eyebrows arching over their eyes;
everyone’s nostrils are large and their heads hang down. Then he added, "Tell me, is Jiufeng the same as Jingshan, or not? Having said this, he descended from his seat.
Chan Master Xiaoyin Yun’s Small Lecture upon the Conclusion of the Summer Retreat: The myriad functions do not reach it; a hundred turns and a thousand layers.
A single phrase is fully raised, penetrating in every direction. Ten thousand miles without a blade of grass—yet as soon as one steps out the door, it is all grass.
At Liu-yang and Dong-shan, there is no village ahead and no inn behind. Zhongfeng concludes the retreat tomorrow night; tonight, let us cast the die and see who wins.
He held up his staff and drew a line, saying: "Having passed through the Single Word Barrier, the Three Mysterious Essentials are shattered to pieces.
The stray cat and the white ox laugh without ceasing; the pillar and the lantern both leap about. Why is this so? When one house has trouble, a hundred houses are busy.
He then cited an instance where Guishan addressed the assembly, saying: "A high-minded traveler must, directly within sound and form..."
As for sleep: it is only when one sits or lies down amidst sounds and forms that it truly occurs. Shushan came out and asked, "What is the phrase that does not fall into sounds and forms?
Guishan held up his whisk. Shushan said, "This is a phrase that falls into sounds and forms. Guishan then returned to his quarters.
Since Shushan did not find resonance there, he took leave of Xiangyan. Xiangyan said, "Why do you not stay for a while? Shushan replied:
"Venerable Master, I have no affinity with you. Xiangyan said, "What causes and conditions prevent your accord?
Try citing one for me. Shushan then recounted their previous conversation. Xiangyan said, "I have a saying of my own. Shushan asked, "What is it?
Xiangyan said, "When words are uttered, they are not sounds; before form appears, there is no object. Shushan said, "So there is someone within this! He then entrusted him to Xiangyan.
[Shengshan] said, "Brother, you will have a place to stay hereafter; I shall come to see you.

Later that evening, Guishan asked Xiangyan, "Is that short monk who asked about the dialogue on sound and form still here? Xiangyan replied, "He has already left. Guishan asked, "What did you say to him?
Xiangyan said, "I also gave him an answer. Guishan said, "Try to repeat it for me. Xiangyan—
Yunyan said, "Speech issues from that which is not sound; form precedes that which is not an object. Guishan asked, "What did he say?
Xiangyan replied, "He deeply approved of it. Guishan laughed and said, "I thought this short fellow had some merit, but it turns out he was just stuck here all along.
If this fellow has a dwelling place in the future, he will have no firewood to burn when near the mountains, and no water to drink when near the streams."
The Master said: "Everyone in the assembly has debated this, saying that it was Guishan who employed his 'claws and fangs' of the higher realm.
It is a pity," he said, "that Shushan lost one eye. But they do not realize that it was actually Guishan who lost one eye, having been seen through by Shushan.
Zhongfeng speaks thus; do you all agree?"

This was used to manifest Master Jun’s *xiaoxian* (small formal address) upon the conclusion of the summer retreat. When the autumn river is clear and shallow, the white heron blends with the misty isle.

Fundamentally, there is no person who is deluded or awakened; it simply requires that you realize it this very day. Since there is fundamentally no delusion or awakening, what else is there to realize?

Well said, all you virtuous Chan practitioners! With the true eye atop your heads, you illuminate the past and the present; with the divine light behind your skulls, there is neither inside nor outside.
Externally, although this is inherently possessed by every person and manifests before each individual, alas, due to deluded thoughts and attachments, one cannot realize it.
Now that the period of the holy retreat (varṣā) is about to conclude and the monks wish to perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, let us go forth from today;

it will not hinder you from piercing through in seven ways, boring through in eight, or traversing in ten directions. If you do not go forth to realize it, thirty years from now you will be changing hands and shifting your chest [in the hells].
Do not say that I have not spoken.
This is the small *sǎn* (private instruction) for the end of the summer retreat. Untie the mouth of the sack; pull out the root of the staff.

In the morning you roam Mount Tiantai; in the evening you go to Mount Nanyue. This is the matter concerning each of you: where there is a Buddha, do not dwell; where there is no Buddha, run away quickly.
It is so. This is also a matter concerning each of you. Mountains and rivers present no obstruction; light penetrates everywhere.
The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, riding upon this light, manifests a hundred transformations of supernatural power, entering through the elephant’s mouth and emerging from its trunk.
Entering through the elephant’s ear and exiting through the elephant’s eye—do you people still know this? If you do, the imperial grace and the Buddha’s grace shall be repaid all at once.
If you do not know, then please return the ninety days’ worth of food money for the monastery. Tsk!
Chan Master Ermi Fu gave a small public address (*xiaochan*). Dongshan said: "At the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, each of you goes east or west;
you must go where there are ten thousand miles without a single blade of grass. One [master] said: "As soon as you step out the door, it is already grass. Another said:
"Even if you do not step out the door, it is still grass. The ancient ancestor Dongshan and these two venerable masters have forgotten their own four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*).

The five viscera exert all their strength to support [the body], fearing that one might enter the weeds. Today, at Dongshan, the retreat is concluded; the winter solstice has just arrived and the spring breath has not yet come.
It is precisely a time when the scars of burning cover the land. Brothers, you must reach out with your hands from within the thicket of dry reeds;
every inch is a jade branch, every thread a jade leaf. It does not hinder you to lie down with your whole body amidst the thorns.
In the forest, he rolled along the ground seventeen or eighteen times. When he rose up, his entire body was covered in thorns.
Not only is it difficult for Buddhas and Patriarchs to approach him, but even if the Śūnyatā-deva were to touch him, blood would flow profusely.
Even on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, when creditors swarm one's door, he is impossible to draw near. Dongshan’s announcement of this matter is very much like a guest departing in a frenzy.
Mad! He reveals his own entire body as ugly and evil. Nevertheless, it is not a poor presentation.

On a winter night, Master Xueyan Qin gave a small public address (xiaochan) on the essential principles (tigan), thanking Head Seat Meijian. At the beginning of the month of the winter solstice, he sold [the goods].

The National Teacher said, "Now, since you say there is no mind, how can the Buddha’s appearance in the world and his preaching of so many traces of the teachings be mere empty words?

The monk said, "If the Buddha’s preaching of the teachings is also without mind, then preaching the Dharma must be without speech. The National Teacher said, "Speaking is itself non-existence, and non-existence is itself speaking. The monk said, "If preaching the Dharma is without..."
The monk asked, "If karma is created by the mind, does the mind exist? The National Teacher said, "If there were no mind, there would be no karma.

Since there is now karma, the mind is subject to arising and ceasing; how could it be without mind? The monk asked, "If one is without mind, one attains Buddhahood. Has the Master already attained Buddhahood now?"
The National Teacher said, "If the mind itself does not exist, who is it that says one attains Buddhahood? If there were a Buddha to be attained, there would still be a mind;

if there is a mind, there is outflow (āsrava). Where could such a mindless state be found? The monk asked, "Since there is no Buddha to be attained, does the Master yourself still make use of a Buddha?
The National Teacher said, "If the mind itself does not exist, from where could its use arise? The monk said, "I am utterly bewildered."
[The monk] said, "There is none. Do you not fall into the view of annihilationism? The National Teacher said, "From the very beginning there has been no view; who says it is annihilated?

The monk said, "If from the very beginning there has been no view, do you not fall into emptiness? The National Teacher said, "There is no emptiness into which one could fall. The monk said, "Is there anything that can fall?"
The National Teacher said, "Since emptiness is non-existent, from where could falling [into states] arise? The monk said, "Both subject and object are non-existent.
Suppose someone were to come with a sword to take one's life—would that be existent or non-existent? The National Teacher said, "It is non-existent. The monk asked, "Is there pain?
The National Teacher said, "Pain, too, is non-existent. The monk asked, "If there is no pain, to which realm would one be reborn after death? The National Teacher said, "There is no death."
“There is neither birth nor the Way. The monk said, “Since you have attained mastery over nothingness, how do you apply your mind when pressed by hunger and cold?
The National Teacher said, “When hungry, eat; when cold, put on clothes. The monk said, “To know hunger and to know cold must be due to having a mind.
The National Teacher said, “I ask you: what is the physical form of this mind? The monk hesitated for a long time.
He searched for the substance of the mind and its physical form, but it was utterly unfindable. He then submitted a truthful report, saying, "The mind has no substance or form.
The National Teacher said, "Since you know it has no substance or form, this is precisely the primordial absence of mind; how can you say it exists?"
The monk asked, "If one encounters tigers or wolves while in the mountains, how should one apply the mind? The National Teacher said, "Seeing is as if not seeing; coming is as if not coming.
When the other has no mind, the wild beasts cannot inflict harm. The monk asked, "That which is silent, without affairs, solitary, detached, and without mind—what is it called?
The National Teacher said, "It is called the Vajra Mahāsattva. The Master gave a shout and said:
A good person is unwilling to do it; instead, they would rather lie in excrement. The monk asked, "What kind of physical form does the Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva have?

The Master said, "What meritorious virtues does the Great Being Vajra possess?

It is like empty space manifesting forms in response to objects, like the moon reflected in water. If the yellow flowers were Prajñā, then Prajñā would be identical to insentient matter.
If the green bamboo were the Dharmakāya, then the green bamboo would still be capable of responsive function. Do you understand, Master of the Seat?
The Master said, "I do not understand this meaning. Baoshu replied, "For one who has realized their nature, to say 'it is' is permissible; to say 'it is not' is also permissible.
One speaks according to function without being obstructed by right or wrong. For one who has not realized their nature, speaking of the emerald bamboo is to become attached to the emerald bamboo."
To speak of yellow flowers while being attached to yellow flowers; to speak of the Dharma-body while being obstructed by the Dharma-body;

to speak of Prajñā while failing to recognize Prajñā—for these reasons, all have resulted in contentious debate. The Master said: "The National Teacher advocated that 'the green, green bamboo is entirely the Dharma-body,' maintaining this position to the very end.
Dazhu refuted that 'the green, green bamboo is not the Dharma-body,' likewise refuting it to the very end. The Old... [text ends]

He pointed his finger and asked the Buddha, who was transforming a single finger, saying, "Since Gautama is here, I hope you will grant me one of your fingers to fulfill my wish.
As soon as he raised his sword, the World-Honored One pulled it away and departed. The World-Honored One walked slowly.
Aṅgulimāla hurried after him but could not catch up. He called out in a loud voice, "Stop! Stop! The World-Honored One said, "I have long since stopped; it is you who do not stop.
Aṅgulimāla was suddenly enlightened and went forth as a monk under the Buddha. The Buddha then had him take his alms bowl to the door of a certain elder's house.
At that moment, the woman of the household was in the throes of a difficult labor. The elder said, "Disciple of Gautama, you..."

Can one catch the black hen at midnight? He asked this because he had requested instruction from Master Zhantang; as soon as he brought up this story...
Zantang said, "You are scratching where I itch. This saying is a "golden excrement" teaching. If you do not understand it, it is like gold;
if you do understand it, it is like excrement. [The student] asked, "Is there no skillful means? Zhantang said, "I have a skillful means, but you simply do not understand.
[The student] said, "I hope the Master will show me compassion. Zhantang said, "Yanguo said: 'I have only recently entered the Way and am not yet...'"
Knowing this matter, he waited to consult the World-Honored One. Before he had even reached the Buddha’s seat, the son of another family was born.

"Since I followed the noble and holy Dharma, I have never killed a living being. While Aṅgulimāla was still carrying these words with him before reaching that other household, the son of yet another family was already born.

At Tiger Hill, while reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, I reached the passage concerning the Bodhisattva’s attainment of the Dharma-patience of non-arising upon ascending to the seventh stage, which states:
"O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva achieves this patience, they immediately enter the eighth Bodhisattva stage, the Immovable (*acalā*).
They become a Bodhisattva of profound practice, difficult to fathom, indistinguishable from [the Buddhas], and free from all marks, all conceptualizations, and all attachments."
It is immeasurable and boundless, beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Free from all clamor and contention, quiescence is manifested before them.

It is, for example, like a bhikṣu who is fully endowed with supernormal powers and has attained mastery over the mind, proceeding through the stages until he enters the samādhi of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), wherein all movement of the mind, recollections, thoughts, and discriminations are entirely stilled. This bodhisattva-mahāsattva...

The Bodhisattva likewise abides in the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*). He immediately relinquishes all effortful application (*abhisamskāra*) and attains the practice of effortless dharma (*anabhisaṃskāra-dharma*).
The mental engagements of his bodily, vocal, and mental karma all cease, and he dwells in fruition-based conduct (*vipākacaryā*).
It is, for example, as if a person in a dream sees himself fallen into a great river; desiring to cross it, he exerts great heroism and employs great skillful means with that great heroism.
Because he exerts fierce skillful means, he immediately awakens; having awakened, all that was to be done comes to rest. The Bodhisattva is likewise:
seeing sentient beings within the four currents, for the sake of rescuing and delivering them, he gives rise to great valor and great diligence.
By means of this valorous diligence, he reaches this Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*). Having reached it, by means of all functional effort...
There is nothing that does not come to rest. The two modes of activity—subjective and objective—no longer manifest before him.
For this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, even the bodhisattva-mind, the Buddha-mind, the bodhi-mind, and the nirvana-mind do not arise; how much less would he give rise to a worldly mind?
The Master said: "At this point, one loses the sack. Suddenly, the expedient means taught by Master Zhantang [appeared].
Only when it manifests before you will you know that the true spiritual friend has not deceived you; it is truly a diamond circle (*vajrapāśa*).

One must possess clarity within the store-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) to be able to penetrate it. Furthermore, there was a venerable elder called Master Luopu, who served as Linji’s attendant for a long time.
Linji frequently praised him, saying, "He is an arrow among the disciples of Linji. This is precisely it.
He deceived people. Having finished his travels, he went straight to the summit of Jia Shan and pitched a hermitage there, remaining for a year.
When Jia Shan learned of this, he wrote a letter and dispatched a monk to deliver it. Upon receiving it, Lu Pu sat down and held it back;

when the monk extended his hand to request it again, Lu Pu struck him and said, "Go back and report this to the Master. The monk returned and reported it to Jia Shan, who said, "That monk has insight."
"The letter says that he will certainly arrive within three days. If you do not see him, this man cannot be saved. The Master said, "The ancients called such a person 'one who drags others down.
I do not know what idle talk or long-winded words there are in that letter; Luopo has instead swallowed his hook and line. Indeed, within three days he arrived.
Jia Shan had previously sent someone to watch for him as he left the hermitage and then set fire to his dwelling. The Master—
Yun-zhi said, "This is precisely the 'vajra-ring' (diamond circle). Pu did not look back. The Master said, "To become a Buddha or a Patriarch, one must be such a person.
Pu went straight to Jia-shan’s quarters; instead of bowing, he stood facing him with his hands crossed at his chest.
Jia-shan said, "A rooster nesting in a phoenix's den—it is not its kind. Get out! Pu said, "I have come from afar to seek the Way; I beg the Master for a reception."
Mount San said, "Before your eyes there is no Acharya; here there is no old monk. Lu then shouted.
Mount San said, "Stop, stop! Do not be so hasty and reckless. The clouds and moon are the same, yet the streams and mountains are each different.

It may be that you, Acharya, can cut off the tongues of all people under heaven, but how will you make a tongueless person understand speech? The Master said, "Lu, however, lowered his head and reflected."
As for "measure," it refers to the single path of the mantra. Unable to comprehend its principle, he was struck across the spine by Jia Shan, who thereby pierced his nostrils.
He subsequently became a successor to Jia Shan. Later, he addressed the assembly, saying: "The final word is where one first reaches the secure barrier;
it blocks the vital ford, allowing passage neither to the profane nor to the sages. One must know that a man of the highest stream does not apply the views of Buddhas and patriarchs as mere labels."
It is right before one's eyes. It is like the numinous tortoise bearing the celestial chart, yet taking its own destruction as the very root of the matter. The Master said:
"Once he has attained enlightenment, he will understand that which clarifies this single path of true mantra—this small medicinal head.
Whether one belongs to the Yunmen, Linji, Caodong, Fayan, or Guiyang lineages, if the Great Dharma is not clarified, each will merely adhere to their own particular school."
Each takes his own teacher as his teacher, each takes his own father as his father, and each takes his own son as his son;

they merely manage to understand the essential meaning, yet they are neither fervent nor earnest. When I was among the assembly, I once requested instruction from a venerable elder regarding the Chan tradition’s teaching that "there is speech within silence, and silence within speech.
The elder cited a scriptural authority for me, saying: "Within speech there is silence."
When you encounter a dead snake on the road, do not strike it; take it home in a bottomless basket.
This is called "having words within the wordless," and it is also called "the wordless containing words. What is meant by "having words within the wordless"? It is:
"When you encounter a dead snake on the road, do not strike it. What is meant by "the wordless containing words"? It is: "Take it home in a bottomless basket."
"Return. This single phrase encompasses both meanings. "Encountering a dead snake on the road, do not strike it" is speech within silence.
"Carrying it back home in a bottomless basket" is silence within speech. It means that since it is already a dead snake, there is no further need to strike it.
Furthermore, how is it that there is difference within sameness? A heron standing in the snow.
It is not the same color. How can there be sameness within difference? The bright moon and the reed flowers are not like others.
When I speak thus, you may understand it immediately; yet what benefit does that bring? Do not seek to learn from those of such a sort.
After the great Dharma-illumination, raising even a single hair or a speck of dust allows one to understand everything at once.
It is just like the story of Aṅgulimāla; it is the skillful means spoken by Zhantang. When I first entered the Way, I could not employ it;
even the Buddha’s supernatural powers could not employ it. Since they could not employ it, why was a son born to him? If you can see into this matter here—
Śākyamuni is precisely Aṅgulimāla; Aṅgulimāla is precisely Śākyamuni.
