And it is because of great causal conditions. Why is this? Have you not seen how, in the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, the Bodhisattva Jñānaśrī asked the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī:
"O Son of the Buddha, how does a bodhisattva attain such matters as bodily, verbal, and mental actions that are free from fault?
Mañjuśrī replied: "By skillfully employing the mind, one attains all supreme and wondrous merits. For this reason...

He spoke of one hundred and forty great vows within the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—which are called the Great Merit of Pure Conduct Free from Turbulence and Confusion.

Since all these merits arise from the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), Mañjuśrī acted as an uninvited friend for those who had already developed faith, and addressed Bhadrapāla Bodhisattva in verse, saying: "I have now..."
For the sake of the bodhisattvas, he spoke of the pure practices cultivated by the Buddha in his past lives.
"You, O Benevolent One, should likewise expound upon the supreme merits of practice within this assembly. The Bodhisattva Bhadramukha replied with a verse, which said:
"By the power of the Dharma, one manifests in the world and attains the ten stages and the ten masteries. This also speaks of the initial arousal of the mind, arising from the stage of faith.

Regarding this meaning: at the very end, when Sudhana arrives before the Vairocana Pavilion, Maitreya explains for him one hundred and twenty kinds of bodhicitta, which also share this same significance.
Among them is a simile that says: "It is like the roar of the lion king;
upon hearing it, all the lion cubs increase in courage and vigor, while other beasts immediately crouch down like mice. This refers to the Buddha-lion.

O King, the roar of the bodhicitta should be understood in the same way. Just as it causes the merit of all bodhisattvas who hear it to increase, while those who cling to acquisitions all retreat and scatter upon hearing it—this is the same meaning.
Since the faculty of faith already exists, it is the very foundation for attaining Buddhahood;
when it suddenly becomes associated with active manifestation, one realizes *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, just as Śākyamuni did.
When Laozi was first at Mount Zhengjue, he raised his head and saw the morning star appear; suddenly he attained enlightenment.
He then sighed and said: "How marvelous! All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of a Tathāgata.
Yet, because of deluded thoughts and attachments, they do not realize it—this applies from the Buddhas of the ten directions above down to the six realms and four modes of birth below."
Including all wriggling and crawling creatures, within the place of my awakening, they are sealed with the single seal of equality;
there is no further distinction. Look at the Yellow-Faced Old Man: as soon as he attained awakening, he perceived this vastness. Thereafter, he gave rise to kindness and exercised compassion;
within the sea of birth and death, he did not cling to this shore, nor did he cling to the other shore, nor did he dwell in the middle current. And yet, he was able to...
To ferry sentient beings from this shore to the other shore, so that they do not dwell within the middle stream of birth and death—this principle does not transcend the seed of one's own faith.
Therefore, when the Layman Wujin inscribed the title of the *Haiyan Jing*, he spoke of the Buddha’s accomplishment, saying:
"The union of initial awakening with the fundamental is called Buddhahood. Although he was but a layman, he nonetheless perceived this.
Thoroughly realize the fundamental source. This means that at the moment of initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*), one gives rise to faith from the appearance of the morning star;
suddenly, one awakens to the fact that one’s own nature has always been Buddha. Sentient beings throughout the great earth are no longer differentiated.

This inexhaustible process is called the union of initial awakening with original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), only then attaining Buddhahood. If a practitioner of Zen can discern this clearly, they may thereafter find rest.

When body, mind, and consciousness grasp their original face, do not be coarse-minded. Once the ancient sages attained this, they extinguished the mind of arising and ceasing at that very point of attainment;

yet they did not abide in a state of quiescent extinction. This is called "quiescent extinction manifesting before one. Within this ground of quiescent extinction, two kinds of excellence are obtained:
first, they harmonize upward with the Buddhas of the ten directions, becoming one and the same as the Tathāgatas.
The power of compassion. Second, [the practitioner] below unites with the sentient beings of the six realms, sharing the same sorrow and longing as all beings.

This refers to what was previously mentioned: "arousing compassion and exercising pity to rescue and deliver those in the evil paths. Sentient beings revolve through birth and death because they lack awakening;
if those who have first attained awakening lacked compassion, how could the realm of sentient beings ever be emptied? Thus one knows, with certainty, the Buddha’s grace.
It is difficult to repay [this kindness]. Today, at the request of my fellow practitioner Jinggan, I shall deliver this general discourse on Wondrous Joy (*Miaoxi*).
It is not merely for the sake of performing posthumous rites for my late father, the attendant; rather, I intend to speak somewhat of the "diseases of Chan" for the assembly gathered here now.
Thus, Liu Zhitou took the teachings of Tiantai as his compass, saying that the diseases of Chan are most numerous. How true these words are! Such is the teaching of the Tiantai Master Zhiyi.
By means of the three contemplations of emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way, one encompasses all dharmas and teaches people to grasp the root for their practice.

Zen is devoid of words and letters; it must be realized through awakening before it can be attained. Since the age of seventeen, Miaoxi has harbored doubts regarding this matter. It was exactly after seventeen years of inquiry that he finally found rest.
Before attaining it, he constantly reflected to himself: "How many years have I already lived now? He did not [let the time pass in vain].
I know that when I was not yet conceived and before coming to this Jambudvīpa, from what place did I come?
My mind was as black as lacquer, and I knew nothing of my point of origin. Since I knew nothing of my origin, it was a state of great birth.
When I die a hundred years hence, where will I go? My mind will remain dark and vast, and I shall know nothing of my destination. Since—
Not knowing where one goes is the "great death. This is called the "great matter" of impermanence and the swiftness of birth and death.
Have you all ever doubted it in this way? Right now, as you sit and stand solemnly, your solitary clarity is vivid and distinct.
You preach the Dharma and listen to the Dharma; guest and host intersect. Miaoxi flaps his two pieces of skin, his teeth clattering together. Below the navel wheel—
Swelling with the air of gruel and rice, you speak here with a constant clamor in your mouth. This speaking is sound;
this sound is universally present within the skulls of all people. All these skulls likewise abide within the sound of Wondrous Joy (Sukhāvatī).
When you die one day, where will this realm be placed? Since you do not know where it is placed, you will collide [with it].
One does not even know when entering the womb of a donkey or the belly of a horse; nor does one know when being born into a blissful celestial palace.
A Chan practitioner who has habitually gathered insights from the sutras and treatises will have nothing they do not know when questioned.
A scholar-official who has studied the Nine Classics and Seventeen Histories likewise will have nothing they do not know when questioned. Yet, apart from these texts—
When words are cut off and thought is extinguished, one asks about the affairs within one's own house; yet of ten people, five or six do not know them.
Yet they know the affairs of others' houses with such clarity! If this is so, one has merely come into this world to make one futile round.
In the future, as one undergoes retribution according to karma, one will ultimately not know where one’s own original life-spirit (mìngběnyuánchén) has settled.

Is this not tragic? Therefore, when the ancients reached this point, they acted as if their hair were on fire, seeking out teachers to resolve their doubts and ensure their minds were opened so that they would have no uncertainty regarding birth and death.
Among them, there were those who learned through study and those who knew through innate nature.
As for that, who is the one who "learns and thereby knows"? It is like the monk who asked Zhaozhou, "A student has newly entered the forest;
I beg the Master for instruction. Zhaozhou said, "Have you finished eating your congee? The monk replied, "I have finished eating. Zhaozhou said, "Go wash your bowl.
At these words, the monk suddenly attained great enlightenment. He immediately found rest and thus understood the matter of birth and death.
In this matter, Miaoxi often said that those who find it difficult are monks of great capability.

Zhaozhou took a carrying pole weighing one hundred and twenty catties and placed it upon the monk’s shoulder; the monk bore it. Without pausing for breath, he ran one hundred and twenty li without looking back.
It was as if the rank of a Buddha were bestowed directly upon an ordinary person; his heart became steady and firm, and his spirit flourished.
To attain the power of loving-kindness and thereby mobilize the vow of compassion—this is one who knows through learning. Who, then, is one who knows through birth?
For example, when Zhaozhou was a novice śrāmaṇera, he traveled on pilgrimage with his preceptor to Nanquan.
It happened that Nanquan was lying down; after the preceptor had finished bowing, Zhaozhou then bowed. Nanquan asked him, "Where have you recently come from?"
Zhaozhou said, "I have recently left the Auspicious Image. Nanquan asked, "Do you still see the Auspicious Image?
Zhaozhou replied, "I do not see the Auspicious Image; I see only a reclining Tathāgata right before me. Nanquan then stood up and asked, "Are you a novice with a master, or a novice without a master?
Zhaozhou said, "I am a novice with a master. Nanquan asked, "Who is that master of yours? If it were as it is now..."

The Chan practitioner then stepped forward, snapped his fingers, drew a circle in the air, gave a shout, clapped his hands once, and swept his sleeves to depart—releasing such foul breath as this. Look at Zhaozhou, who calmly approached and said:
"It is still cold in the first month of spring. I humbly wish that the Master’s health and well-being are in every respect auspicious.
Nanquan then called for the *karmadāna* and said, "This novice shall be assigned elsewhere. On the following day, [the monk] came again to ask, "What is the Way?
Nanquan neither struck him with his staff nor shouted at him; he did not discuss the profound, nor speak of the subtle; he did not cite the sutras, nor quote the treatises.
He neither raised an ancient *kōan*, nor spoke of phenomena, nor spoke of principle; he simply told him directly, "The ordinary mind is the Way.
This was because Zhaozhou had already mastered the ordinary mind, and thus he asked, "Is it still necessary to have a direction toward it?
Nanquan said, "To intend to direct oneself is already to deviate. Zhaozhou said, "If one does not intend, how can one know it is?"
Nanquan said, "The Way does not belong to knowledge, nor does it belong to non-knowledge. Knowledge is deluded awareness; non-knowledge is indeterminate.
If one truly penetrates the Way that is free from doubt, it is like the great void—vast, open, and expansive.
How could one forcibly impose right and wrong within it? At these words, Zhaozhou attained complete and thorough understanding. Nanquan said, "The Way does not belong to knowledge."
It simply belongs to the realm of the unknowable. Guifeng calls it "numinous awareness" (lingzhi); Heze calls this single word "awareness" the gate to all wonders.
Huanglong Sixin says that this single word "awareness" is the gate to all calamities.
To see what Guifeng and Heze meant is easy; to see what Sixin meant is difficult. Reaching this point, one must possess the eye that transcends the ordinary to explain it to others.
It cannot be obtained. It cannot be transmitted to others. This is why our late master Yuanwu said: "Zhaozhou’s Chan resides merely upon the lips; there is no way to deal with him.
He is like a skilled general who does not carry provisions when marching; even if you provide him with water, grass, and food, he will still destroy you.
A certain scholar asked: "Is it true that the Buddha does not go against the vows of sentient beings? Zhaozhou—
Baizhang said, "It is so. Baicai said, "I, your disciple, wish to beg for the staff from the Master’s hand;
may I have it? Baizhang said, "A gentleman does not take away what another cherishes. Baicai said, "I am no gentleman. Baizhang said, "Neither am I a Buddha.
Another monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarchs? Baizhang then struck the leg of his meditation seat. The monk—
Yunmo asked, "Is this it? Zhaozhou said, "If it is, then take it away. Another monk asked, "Everywhere else people speak from their mouths;
how do you, Master, instruct people? Zhaozhou pointed to the brazier with his heel.
A monk asked, "Is it not this very thing? Zhaozhou said, "I have just recognized the old monk's heels.
Another monk asked, "What is Zhaozhou? Zhaozhou said, "The East Gate, the South Gate, the West Gate, the North Gate.
The monk said, "I am not asking about those. Zhaozhou said, "Then what are you asking me? What is Zhaozhou? Another monk asked, "What is the Way? Zhaozhou said, "The wall."
The monk asked, "What about the Way outside? Zhaozhou said, "I am not asking about that Way. The monk asked, "Then which Way are you asking about?
Zhaozhou said, "I am asking about the Great Way. Zhaozhou said, "The Great Way leads to Chang'an.
You must not understand it as 'nothingness,' nor as 'mysterious and wondrous,' nor as 'extraordinary,' nor as 'ordinary. Zhaozhou did not...

It is not in the realm of non-action; it is not in the realm of the profound and mysterious; it is not in the realm of the extraordinary; it is not in the realm of the ordinary. Ultimately, where does it reside?
Those with eyes must discern this for themselves. This old monk has sometimes said: "Before leaving home, one was driven by Bodhi;
after leaving home, Bodhi was driven by one. You all, however, are driven by the twelve hours of the day. I, this old monk—
He caused [the days] to consist of twelve periods. Furthermore, he said, "I do not like to hear the single word 'Buddha.
Since I do not even like to hear the single word 'Buddha,' Dharma is clearly nothing but a very old barbarian. A Bodhisattva of the Ten Stages is merely a man carrying dung."
The two types of awakening—the equal and the wondrous—are for breaking through the ordinary person; bodhi and nirvana are tethering stakes for donkeys.

The twelve divisions of the teachings are registers of ghosts and spirits, or paper for wiping away pus from sores. The four fruits, the three stages of worthiness, the initial mind, and the ten stages are ghosts guarding ancient tombs.
Since you have not reached this field, you will be unable to comprehend matters and principles; you students are merely running about in a coarse manner.

Taking a great stride, he would immediately respond to people with a single phrase of Chan essentials. Yet, this was not the ultimate principle. Therefore, in the quarters of Miaoxi, he would constantly question his Chan practitioners:
"If you call it a bamboo stick, you commit the fault of 'contact' (touching); if you do not call it a bamboo stick, you commit the fault of 'aversion' (turning your back).
You must not utter a word; you must not remain silent; you must not engage in deliberation; you must not engage in conceptual calculation."
"You might as well wave your sleeves and leave; you cannot have anything at all. You then snatch away the bamboo staff.
"I will allow you to snatch it for now. If I call it a fist, that is 'contact' (touching); if I do not call it a fist, that is 'contradiction' (turning one's back).
How then can you snatch it? Even if you were to say, 'Please, Master, let go,' I would simply let go. If I call it—"
If you call it a "dew-pillar," you are touching upon it; if you do not call it a dew-pillar, you are turning your back on it. How then would you take it away?

When I call it the "mountains, rivers, and great earth," I am touching upon it; when I do not call it the mountains, rivers, and great earth, I am turning my back on it. How then would you take it away?
There was an elder named Zhufeng who said, "I have been looking at the Master’s 'cane' koan as if someone were confiscating a person's entire household."
"Furthermore, regarding property, one must cause others to deliver goods. Miaoxi said, 'Your analogy is most excellent.
I truly do require you to deliver goods. Since you have no source from which to produce them, you will surely seek a path to death.
You might throw yourself into a river or leap into fire, sacrificing your life before you can truly die. Once dead, you will then slowly return to life again.'"
If you are called a Bodhisattva, you are delighted; if you are called a thief, you become enraged. As before, you remain simply the person you always were. Therefore, the ancients said:
"Letting go at the precipice, one accepts it of one's own accord. Only after death and subsequent resurrection can one not deceive the world.
It is only upon reaching this point that one finally realizes the meaning of the bamboo stick koan. He then spoke a verse: The Buddha’s...

I do not take pleasure even in a single word; what birth and death could possibly be relevant? When the opportunity arises, face-to-face, there is no room for evasion—how can one speak of the eight returns in the meaning of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra?
The Chan practitioner Yue invited a general discourse. A monk asked, "Linji addressed the assembly, saying: 'Sometimes the person is taken away but not the environment;
sometimes the environment is taken away but not the person; sometimes both person and environment are taken away; sometimes neither person nor environment is taken away.
What is "taking away the person but not the environment'? The Master said, "Three thousand miles away, all confusion and error are cut off. The monk stepped forward and asked:"
"What is 'seizing the object but not seizing the person'? The Master said, "Pulling out the wedge from the eye. The student asked, "Linji said:

'The warm sun brings life forth, spreading a carpet of brocade; the infant’s hair hangs down, white as silk. I do not know whether this is the same as or different from what you, Master, have answered.
The Master said, "A dog that bites on a dung-stick is no good dog. The student said, "The King's command has already been issued..."
"Traveling throughout the world, everywhere the general has cut off smoke and dust beyond the frontier; what is it like at such a time?
The Master said, "Just now it was still tolerable, but now it is even more reckless. [The student] asked, "The Blessed Ones of the ten directions share one path to the gate of Nirvana.
I wonder, Master Wang, is he alive today or is he dead? The Master said, "Alive? Dead? [The student] pressed on, "Throughout ancient and modern times..."
"No falling away. It is clearly present before you. The Master said, "Draw out the arrow from behind your head.

The student asked, "If someone comes who, throughout the twelve periods of the day, does not rely upon a single thing, will you still receive them? The Master said, "What do you call 'a single thing'?
The student said, "One must not repeat the verse. The Master said, "This would be a hindrance that kills people. He then said, "Life? Death?"
It is neither attainment nor loss; it is neither the Way nor non-Way. It possesses both principle and phenomena.
If you find an entrance at the place where there is principle and phenomena, you will merely be bobbing up and down within the teachings.

If you find an entrance at the place where there is neither attainment nor loss, I can guarantee that throughout your twelve periods of the day, you will still have no place to settle your body or establish your life. Since...
If you have not yet found a place to settle your body and establish your life, you will not know where Master Wang has gone.
If you can know where Master Wang has gone, then you will know the place where you yourself settle your body and establish your life. Now tell me: is Master Wang alive now, or is he dead?
Is he unborn, or is he undying? If you say he is unborn, how can you account for his death? If you say...
"Not dying"? How can one contend with birth? If you say it is both born and dies, that is again a discourse of frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).

If you say it is neither born nor dies, that is again a contradictory statement. Even if one were to transcend the four propositions and sever the hundred negations—directly, like a bright mirror facing its stand or a luminous pearl held in the palm, where a barbarian appears as a barbarian and a Han person appears as a Han person—each person must still take their own steps.
Following this, one attains a state of utter purity and vivid clarity. Birth and death are like dreams, illusions, or flowers in the sky;
coming and going are like floating clouds or the moon reflected in water. Yet even this is not yet the point of ultimate penetration.

Even if one perceives reality as it is—seeing that birth in the past was never truly born and death today was never truly extinguished—it is still merely speaking of a dream while in a dream. Why? Because birth...
It does not arise; it is like a form in a mirror. It does not perish; it is like the moon in water.
At this very moment, where is the place of origin for Wangshi?

If you can understand this thoroughly, Wangshi is right now walking hand-in-hand with all of you, entering together the Great Ocean of Tathāgata-nirvāṇa. If this is not yet so, there are cold and heat.
"May it prolong your life! There are spirits and ghosts who envy your blessings. He further said:
"This is the intent behind the Venerable Jinyue’s request for Old Man Miaoxi to preach the Dharma on behalf of his mother, Lady Wang. But how is the Dharma preached?
Have you not heard it said that the Dharma cannot be seen, heard, sensed, or known? If one acts through seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, that is precisely seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing."

"Knowing is not seeking the Dharma. Since seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing cannot be used to enter the Way, is it then the case that not seeing, not hearing, not perceiving, and not knowing is it?
After a long silence, he cried out in a loud voice: 'What else is it?
Miaoxi has exhausted his efforts in explaining, yet he can only explain up to this point. This matter is definitively not within the realm of words. Therefore..."

The successive sages of antiquity appeared in the world one after another, each employing skillful means (*upāya*) to speak repeatedly and at length, fearing only that people might become mired in words.

If they had remained within the realm of words, how could the entire Tripitaka—its five thousand and forty-eight volumes—have spoken of the provisional and the real, of existence and non-existence, and of the sudden and the gradual?
How could it be that there was no verbal teaching? It is precisely because of this [miring in words] that they spoke.

Why did Bodhidharma come from the West, yet speak of the "single transmission of the mind-seal" (*cittamudrā*) without establishing words or language, pointing directly at the human mind so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha?
Why did he not speak of transmitting the mysterious, transmitting the wondrous, or transmitting words and phrases?
It was simply because he wished for each person to directly realize their own fundamental mind and see their own original nature. Having no other choice, he spoke this:
I have already spoken of "nature," which has already become quite a mess. If you wish to uproot the very roots of birth and death, you must by all means not rely on what I have said.
Even if you can recite the entire Tripitaka as effortlessly as water pouring from one jar into another, this is called "carrying manure in";
it is not called "carrying manure out. You will instead be obstructed by these few fragments, which block your own true awareness.
One cannot see it manifest before oneself; one's own spiritual powers are unable to bring it forth.

One merely dabbles with the shadows and glimmers of the present moment, preoccupied with interpreting the principles of Chan, interpreting the mind, interpreting the nature, interpreting what is extraordinary, and interpreting what is mysterious and sublime.
It is like using a swinging club to strike at the moon—exhausting one’s mind and spirit in vain. The Tathāgata calls such people objects of pity.
Whenever the ancients spoke even a single word or half-phrase, they would set forth a *vajra-ring* and a *thorn-bush*, commanding others to swallow it or pass through it.
If there is one who is heroic, solitary, and detached—one who transcends the dust of emotions and surpasses the realm of principle—then as for that *vajra-ring* and *thorn-bush*:
This "fuzz" is merely the equipment for a monkey’s antics—a meal for offering to ghosts and spirits.

It is because you are unable to realize that a single thought-moment arises without inherent existence; instead, you merely continue to make your living within the realm of mind, intellect, and consciousness.
As soon as you see a master open his mouth, you immediately seek out the mysterious and the sublime within that master's words, only to be thrown headlong by the master like an overturned somersault.
One still does not know where one’s own original life-spirit (benming yuanchen) resides; beneath one's heels it is pitch black, and as before, one remains nothing more than a lacquer bucket.
Take, for instance, the passage concerning "taking the person but not the environment" that the Venerable One just asked about.
They only know how to recite from their books; when asked to answer according to the Dharma, they do not understand it at all.
Before one question is finished, they ask another, much like country folk playing the game of "passing the word.
Now, without sparing my verbal karma, I shall untangle this web of complications for you all and explain it once through. One day, Linji addressed the assembly, saying: "There is..."
"Sometimes the person is taken away but not the object; sometimes the object is taken away but not the person; sometimes both the person and the object are taken away;
and sometimes neither the person nor the object is taken away. Do you understand? After a long silence, he looked to his left and right and then descended from his seat.
"This very thing is the Vajra King’s Precious Sword. What I spoke of yesterday—the centipedes, venomous snakes, and scorpions—"
"Various poisons are stored within a single jar. Try reaching your hand into it and see if you can pull out even one thing that is not poisonous.
If you can pull one out, then you will have some slight correspondence with this matter.
If you cannot pull one out, it is simply because your faculties are dull and you lacked the spiritual bone from former lives; it is not to be blamed on Miaoxi."—Linji.
At that time, the Master’s several casual phrases and long remarks were his very face and form manifest before you; it was simply that you did not know how to see them.
If you can grasp this meaning, then from this point forward, for thirty years, there will never be a shortage of salt and sauce.
Reciting hymns atop a bell tower, or growing vegetables beneath the legs of a meditation seat—such things do not require asking others; one knows their true nature for oneself.
When the ancients provided these skillful means, how could they have been merely opening their mouths idly? You must know that there are thorns within the soft mud.
At that time, there was a practitioner named Ke-fu who understood Linji’s meaning. He came forward and asked, "What is 'taking away the person but not the environment'?
At that moment, Linji did not know where he had obtained so much idle talk and long-winded speech to compose such a perfect response, and he said:
"The warm sun brings forth life, spreading a carpet of brocade; the infant’s hair hangs down, yet it is white."
"Like silk. Do you all understand? 'The sun’s warmth brings forth life, spreading a carpet of brocade'—this is the environment.
'The infant’s hanging hair is white as silk'—this is the person. Of these two lines, one preserves the environment and one seizes the person.
Ke Fu then offered a verse: "Seizing the person, not seizing the environment: The conditions themselves bring confusion. The Master said: 'What confusion is there? [He] attempted..."
Seeking the profound essence, you turn your thoughts inward and question me. The Master said, "To attribute a crime to another. The pearl of the black dragon shines brilliantly;
the shadow of the moon on the cassia tree sways gently. The Master said, "Why did you not speak thus sooner? Face-to-face, there is no discrepancy; yet one still remains caught in the net.
The Master said, "Vaguely resembling a melody, it is barely worth listening to, when suddenly the wind blows it into a different tune. This.
The general purport of the verse lies within the brilliant, sparkling luster of the dragon’s pearls and the swaying shadows of the moon and cassia trees;

these two lines constitute the objective realm (*viṣaya*). A student may ask: "If one does not seize upon the realm, yet seeks to grasp the profound essence (*paramārtha*), will such deliberation not lead to self-reproach?
The essential meaning is simply that it is beyond thought or deliberation. Those who deliberate and deliberate are people who miss the mark; it must be encountered face-to-face.

To present even a single point is to be immediately ensnared by the net of words. This verse by Kefu specifically clarifies how the warm sun brings forth life, spreading a carpet of brocade across the earth;
hence there are lines such as "the light of the dragon's pearl is brilliant" and "the shadow of the moon on the cassia tree sways.

These are instances of preserving the objective realm while seizing the person. Therefore it is said: "To meet face-to-face without discrepancy, one would still be caught in the net. This is seizing the person.
...the meaning of this. The finest essence (amṛta) and poison proceed along one and the same path; only those with the eye of wisdom can distinguish between them. Again he asked:
"What is meant by 'taking away the object, but not taking away the person'? He replied: "The King’s decree has already been issued and extends throughout the world;

the General is beyond the frontier, where smoke and dust have ceased. The Master said: "'The King’s decree has already been issued and extends throughout the world'—this takes away the object. 'The General is beyond the frontier'..."
To cut off smoke and dust is to preserve the person without seizing it. The verse says: "Seizing the object but not the person—searching for words, where is the truth?
The Master said: "One must also establish defenses in moments of leisure. Question: "Seeking Chan, Chan is delusion; investigating principle, the principle is not intimate."
The Master said, "Better that good things not exist at all. The sun shines upon the pale light; the distant mountains show fresh green hues.
The Master said, "A poor child thinks of old debts. Even if one attains profound realization, it is still but dust in the eyes. The Master said, "One raises oneself up only to knock oneself down."
"Do you understand: 'The sunlight shines upon the cold light, and the distant mountains reveal their fresh verdant hues'? These two lines refer to the objective realm (*viṣaya*).

Even if you were to grasp them through a profound, mystical realization, it would still be but dust in your eyes; they have already been snatched away. As for others, both the person and the realm are snatched away.
"Neither person nor environment are taken away. This is entirely answering according to the words used when questioning those who have reached the stage of learning.
Again, he asked: "What is 'both person and environment taken away'? He replied: "In Ping-chen, all communication has ceased; one dwells alone in a single place.

At these words, there is the very face of both person and environment being taken away. The verse says: "Both person and environment taken away; from the beginning, the true command has been exercised. The Master said: "Already fallen."

Generally, regarding the perverse Chan of silent illumination (*mozhao*), when one sees a scholar-official whose mind is unsettled and troubled by the defilements of worldly toil, they immediately instruct him to become like cold ashes or withered wood, to become a single length of white silk, to become a fragrant incense burner in an ancient temple, or to become a cold, stagnant pool.

They tell such a person to find rest in this state. Do you think he can truly find rest? Little do they realize that this— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the fragmentary nature of the source.)
How can this monkey-child find rest if it does not die? How can that which comes as the vanguard and goes as the rearguard find rest if it does not die?
This wind was extremely prevalent in the Fujian region in years past.

When Miaoxi first entered Min in the early Shaoxing era and resided in a hermitage, he forcefully rejected it, calling it "severing the life-force of the Buddha's wisdom. Even if a thousand Buddhas were to appear in the world...
He did not permit [the monk] to repent. Among them was a scholar named Zheng Shangming, who was extremely intelligent;

he understood the Buddhist scriptures (*jiao-cheng*), he understood the Daoist canon (*dao-zang*), and he was naturally well-versed in Confucianism. One day, he brought a piece of incense into Miaoxi’s quarters.
His anger was palpable, and his voice and expression were both fierce as he said, "I have a piece of incense that has not yet—"
I am burning with anxiety. I wish to discuss one matter with the Upādhyāya. It is that remaining silent and speechless is the foremost place of rest within the Dharma-gate.
Yet the Upādhyāya has freely reviled it. My mind is filled with doubt because I feel the Upādhyāya has not yet reached this state, and thus I cannot believe it.
Furthermore, consider how the Elder Śākyamuni was in the kingdom of Magadha for three...
For seven days he remained in seclusion, making no sound; was this not the Buddha’s silence?
In the city of Vaiśālī, thirty-two bodhisattvas each expounded the gate of the non-dual Dharma, and at the end, Vimalakīrti remained silent, while Mañjuśrī praised his excellence.
Is this not the silence of the Bodhisattva? Subhūti sat in meditative seclusion within the mountain crags, without speech or discourse;

is this not the silence of the Śrāvaka? When Śakra, Lord of Devas, saw Subhūti sitting in meditative seclusion within the crags, he rained down flowers as an offering, likewise without speech or discourse;
is this not the silence of the ordinary person? Thus did Bodhidharma travel through Liang and visit Wei.
Shao-lin sat in cold meditation for nine years; was this not the Patriarch’s silence? Lu-tsu saw a monk and simply faced the wall; was this not the Master’s silence?
Why, then, do you, O Monk, so strenuously reject "silent illumination" as being heterodox and wrong?
Miaoxi said: "Shangming, you have asked well; I am like that too. Wait while I tell you. If I were to speak—"
"It will not do. Instead, burn a stick of incense and pay me three prostrations; if you can speak so as to be put into practice, then I will accept your incense and prostrations.
Furthermore, I shall not speak of the words and phrases of Old Śākyamuni or the former worthies to you.
I will speak right here in your room—what we call 'borrowing the mother-in-law’s shawl to bow for New Year’s. Then he asked you, 'Have you ever read the *Zhuangzi*?'"
The Master said, "What is it that you do not read? Miaoxi replied, "Zhuangzi says: 'If words are sufficient, one may speak all day long and exhaust the Way;
if words are insufficient, one may speak all day long and exhaust only phenomena. This is the ultimate limit of the Way and phenomena, which cannot be carried by either speech or silence.
Yet, there is an ultimate meaning that exists beyond both speech and silence. I have never read Guo Xiang’s commentary nor those of the other scholars.
[The Master] says: "This commentary of mine is merely based on my own fabrications. As for those who would refute me, they remain silent.
Have you not seen how Confucius one day, with great alarm and wonder, said: 'Zhan, my Way is unified by a single thread'? Zengzi replied, 'Yes.
You scholars of the common class, upon hearing that single word 'Yes,' immediately come here to speak abusively, yet you say this single 'Yes' is [merely conventional]..."

Heaven and earth share the same root; all things are one body. To bring a ruler to the heights of Yao and Shun, to establish a family and found a state, to go forth as a general or enter as a minister—even unto the moment of laying hands and feet—there is not a single word that does not suffice. Yet, how joyful it is that there is no further involvement!
One must simply realize that this principle is precisely what was sufficient for Zengzi to speak of, and sufficient for Confucius to speak of, such that his disciples [need look no further].
"No," he replied, yet he asked, "What do you mean? Seeing that the other could not grasp the principle, Zengzi answered from a secondary perspective, saying:
"The Way of the Master cannot be without words; therefore it is said, 'The Way of the Master is simply loyalty and reciprocity (zhong-shu).
Yet, one must understand that the ultimate point where the Way and all things meet does not reside in words, nor does it reside [in the literal meaning]."
"In the state of silence, words cannot carry it; even silence cannot carry it.
What you have said does not yet accord with the meaning of Zhuangzi, let alone accord with the meaning of Śākyamuni Buddha and Master Bodhidharma.
Do you wish to understand the ultimate point of Zhuangzi’s "neither speech nor silence"? It is precisely as Master Yunmen brought it up.
He raises his fan and says: "The fan leaps up to the Thirty-three Heavens and strikes Śakra on the tip of his nose.
A carp from the Eastern Sea receives a blow of the staff, and the rain pours down like an overturned basin. If you can understand this speech of Yunmen—"
"This is exactly what Zhuangzi said, what Zengzi said, and what Confucius said—all are one and the same.
The monk remained silent. Miaoxi said, "Though you do not speak, your mind has not yet submitted. It is clear that the ancients certainly did not sit in mere silence.
Consider this: when you previously cited Śākyamuni’s 'closing the room' and Vimalakīrti’s silence, look now—"
In the past, there was a presiding master known as Dharma Master Zhao. He brought forth that which is beyond words and speech, saying to others:
"Śākyamuni closed his chamber in Magadha; Vimalakīrti remained silent in Vaiśālī; Subhūti proclaimed 'no-speech' to manifest the Way;
and Śakra and Brahmā ceased their listening as flowers rained down. All of these instances were governed by the spiritual power of the Principle (Li). Therefore...
The mouth remains silent because of this; how can it be said that there is no eloquence? It is that there is something which eloquence cannot express.
This is when principle and spirit suddenly collide, such that one unconsciously arrives at a point where speech is impossible. Although there is no speaking, its resonance is like thunder;
therefore it is said, "How can it be said that there is no eloquence? For it is precisely that which eloquence cannot express. Herein lies the worldly intelligence.
There is not even a single point of eloquence to be used. Only when one reaches such a field is it truly a place where one may cast off the body and abandon life.
Such a state must be personally realized and awakened to by the individual themselves.

Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The palaces of the Tathāgatas are boundless; those who have attained spontaneous awakening dwell within them. This refers to all the [patriarchs] of antiquity...
This is the Noble Great Dharma Gate of Liberation: boundless and immeasurable, without gain and without loss; without silence and without speech, without going and without coming.
It is thus in every atom, thus in every land, thus in every thought-moment, and thus in every dharma.

It is only because the faculties and natures of sentient beings are narrow and inferior that they fail to reach the realm of the sages of the Three Teachings, and thus distinguish between "that" and "this. Little do they realize that this is merely the realm [of delusion].
Although the Dharma-realm is as vast as this, you instead sit in silence within a ghost cave beneath Black Mountain.
Therefore, the former sages condemned it as a deep pit of liberation—a place to be feared.

When viewed with the divine eye of the Way, one is sitting amidst mountains of knives and trees of swords, or within boiling cauldrons and glowing embers. Even a typical master of the lecture hall would not linger there.
"In a place of silence, how much more so for a guest under the gate of our Patriarchs? Yet you say that as soon as one opens the mouth, one falls into 'this age.
For now, let us rejoice that there is no connection [between words and reality]. Shangming, unaware of this, prostrated himself.

Miaoxi said, 'Although you have prostrated yourself, there is still something further to attend to. That evening, he came to enter the room and asked him, 'How old are you this year? He replied, 'Sixty-four.'"
He asked him, "From where did you come sixty-four years ago? The man was unable to open his mouth.
I took my bamboo staff and struck him on the back, sending him out. The next day he came into the room again and said, "Sixty-four years ago, I had not yet even been born;
how could the Master ask where I came from? Miaoxi said, "You..."
Sixty-four years ago, it was not originally in the Zheng family in Fuzhou.

Right now, as for this segment of listening to the Dharma and expounding the Dharma—this vivid, solitary luminosity—before it had even arisen, where exactly did it ultimately reside? He said, "I do not know."
Miaoxi said: "If you do not know this, you are truly born great. For now, your life is limited to a hundred years.
After those hundred years, even if you wished to fly out beyond the three-thousandfold world system, you would still have to enter a coffin.
At that moment, the four elements and five aggregates will all dissolve at once; though you have eyes, you will see no objects, and though you have ears—"
He does not hear sounds. There is a lump of flesh—the mind—whose discriminations no longer function. There is a body that, even when burned by fire or hacked with a blade, feels no pain.
When one reaches this state where everything is vividly and solitary clear, where does it go?
[The master] said: "Even Anguo did not know. Miaoxi said: "Since you do not know, you are truly dead. Therefore it is said: 'Impermanence is swift; life is fleeting.'"
The matter of death is great; it is precisely this principle. Here, one cannot employ cleverness, nor can one rely on memorization.
Let me ask you further: throughout your life you have produced so much of this "zhi-hu-ye-zhe" (scholarly pedantry);
on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, with which single phrase will you confront birth and death? You must first understand clearly the point of where life comes from and where death goes.
"It is attained. If one does not know this, one is a fool. Only then did he submit in his heart.

From that point on, he proceeded to save others, no longer remaining in a state of silence and non-speaking. Those who were willing came to apply themselves to practice. Today, this assembly likewise listens to the Dharma together.
One must know that every person possesses this great matter of karmic connection, which remains unchanging and unmoving from antiquity to the present.
It is neither a state of forgetfulness nor a state of deliberate intent; simply remind yourself of it from time to time.

When deluded thoughts arise, you must not attempt to suppress them with the mind, for to stop movement by means of stopping is only to stir it further. One should simply attend to the very point where movement and stillness occur.
Look at this critical phrase (*huatou*). Even if Śākyamuni Buddha or Master Bodhidharma were to appear, it would still be just this.
When a monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou said, "No.
You scholars love to engage in intellectual fabrication, saying that this "no" is not the negation of existence and non-existence, but rather the negation of true non-existence.
It does not belong to the world’s empty voidness. When speaking in this way, can you still withstand birth and death?
Since you cannot withstand birth and death, it is not yet so. Since it is not yet so, you must maintain mindfulness while walking and maintain mindfulness while sitting;
whether in times of joy, anger, sorrow, or pleasure, or when responding and interacting with others, it is always a time for maintaining mindfulness.
Section. Bring it up! Bring it up! When there is no flavor left and the heart feels as if a ball of red-hot iron has been suddenly thrust into it—at that moment, this is the true state;
do not let go. Suddenly, the flower of the mind will blossom forth, illuminating the lands of the ten directions.
Then you will be able to manifest a Jewel-King Land upon the tip of a single hair and turn the Great Dharma Wheel while sitting within a mote of dust. You...
When people like these hear such talk, they often think to themselves, "The old fellow Miaoxi flaps his lips and rattles his tongue;
he speaks as if it were so, but we do not know what is truly in his belly. You must know that what Miaoxi can speak, he can also practice;
there are no two different things. This is why the thirteenth patriarch of India, Kāṇhamuni...

Venerable Luo wished to find a disciple to succeed him in the ancestral seat. He thought that there must be high-minded people dwelling in deep mountains and remote valleys, so he went there to seek them.
Thus one knows that it is not only disciples who earnestly seek a teacher; teachers also earnestly seek disciples.
He then entered the mountains and indeed saw a man coming out to meet him, saying, "This deep mountain is solitary and desolate, a place where dragons and serpents dwell."

The Master said, "I am here, Great Virtue. Why have you deigned to trouble your divine feet? The Patriarch replied, "I am not one who has attained the state of Supreme Honored One; I have come to visit a worthy man.
The Master thought silently to himself, "Has this master attained the nature of certainty and clarified the eye of the Way? Is he a great sage who continues the True Vehicle?"
The Patriarch said, "Although you spoke with your mind, I already knew it by my own mind. Simply prepare for the life of renunciation; what need is there to worry that I am not a sage?
Having heard this, he repented and apologized. Thereupon, he joined the Patriarch and left the household life; he was none other than the fourteenth patriarch, Nāgārjuna.
Nowadays, those who study the Way often do not doubt themselves but instead doubt others. Thus it is said: "Under great doubt, there will surely be great awakening.
But tell me, what is it that one awakens to? After a long silence, he said: "I do not dare to treat you lightly;
you shall all become Buddhas. He then descended from his seat.
The attendant, having completed the seven-day period of mourning, requested a general discourse. A monk asked: "In the Master’s room, you said: 'To call it a bamboo stick is to encounter obstruction;
not to call it a bamboo stick is to turn one's back. One must not offer words, nor must one remain silent.
Then you struck the ground once with your sitting mat and said: 'The student is adding legs to a snake; I instead request the Master to place a head upon its head. The Master [responded].
Xuefeng said, "Clouds arise by themselves and fall by themselves; they incur the resentment of others. Jian said, "I also wish for the Master to grant me full understanding.
The Master said, "Above all, do not move your fingers within the leather boot. Jian said, "Is there still a way to benefit others? The Master said, "No. Jian said, "That is quite a bit better.
The Master said, "It would have changed your very eyes. He then said, "To call it a bamboo stick is to be obstructed. Not to call it..."
To call it a "bamboo pointer" is to turn one's back on it. One must not utter a word; one must not remain silent; one must not engage in deliberation; one must not hesitate.
At such a moment, even Śākyamuni the Elder and Master Bodhidharma, though they possess nostrils, find themselves utterly without a place to breathe.
Do you understand this? When encountering the noble, it becomes base; when encountering the base, it becomes noble. If you direct yourself toward this nobility or baseness—
Having arrived at this point, you must further purchase straw sandals to travel on foot before you can succeed. Therefore it is said:

it cannot be sought with a mind of intention, nor can it be attained by a mind of non-intention; it cannot be constructed through words and language, nor can it be communicated through silent stillness.
Even so, it is like the sky universally covering all, or like the earth universally supporting all—it is total release and total gathering, total killing and total giving life. Sublime!
Xī delights in speaking thus, for it does not depart from this very message. It is just as that Zen guest struck the ground with his sitting cloth earlier.
[The Master] then struck the meditation seat once and said: "Tell me, what matter on which side has he clarified?
On this day, the Bhikṣu Liaoxian, acting as the attendant Jìnli, is conducting an auction of clothing and goods sent from a lay family; I request that you all attend.
Han Juyang proclaimed the fundamental tenets to adorn the ground of retribution. It is a pity that these brothers have only now begun to find a point of illumination regarding the "cane" koan;
by now, they are already speaking of last year’s talk. One day he asked him: "If you call it a cane, you contradict [the truth];
if you do not call it a cane, you turn your back on it. How about this? He was unable to answer, and instead said, "I look forward to..."
"Please, Preceptor, provide a skillful means to instruct me. The mountain monk said to him, "You are a man from Fuzhou.
I shall give you a parable: it is like taking a choice variety of lychee and peeling away the skin and shell all at once."
He brought it to her mouth with his hand, but she did not know how to swallow it. Upon hearing this, he could not help but laugh and said, "If the Master swallows it, there will be trouble.
After some time had passed, he asked her again, "As for that lychee you swallowed the other day, you simply do not know its flavor.
She replied, "If I were to know its flavor, I would see even more trouble. I— [The text ends here].

For those who love others, there are two turning words: namely, "That which enters through the gate is not the family treasure. One should know with certainty that in the house of a true master, there is no substantial dharma to give to others.
For instance, in the mundane world, when it comes to crafts and technical skills, one can produce them provided there is a model.
If this is so, a single understanding must first be attained through self-awakening; it must be realized in the mind and manifested in the hand.

If you have not yet found a place of peace and ease, but instead pursue knowledge, views, and intellectual comprehension, such poisonous mixtures will enter the mind like oil into flour, from which they can never be extracted.
Even if they were somehow removed, it would require great effort to manage them. This matter is like...
The blue sky and white sun are forever without obstruction; yet they are blocked by these various poisons. For this reason, one cannot attain mastery over the Dharma.
This old man has always admired Master Zhenjing’s saying: "Nowadays, most people merely attain a state where body and mind are extinguished and the past and future are severed.
They think, 'I have rested; I have ceased; in a single thought-moment, ten thousand years pass. They are like an ancient temple."
To go behind the incense burner, to go where it is cold and still—this is taken as the ultimate. Little do they realize that they are instead obstructed by such superior and wondrous states;
thus, their own correct knowledge and vision cannot manifest, and their spiritual powers and radiance cannot be revealed.
Or again, some cling to the notion that "the ordinary mind is the Way" as the ultimate limit, thinking, "Heaven is heaven."
Earth is earth, mountains are mountains, water is water, monastics are monastics, and laypeople are laypeople. A full month has thirty days;

a short month has twenty-nine. In all one's activities, it is necessary to follow the ordinary path as one's steady and settled course, proceeding in accordance with it and never daring to take another step, for fear of falling into pits or ravines for a long time.
It is just like two blind people walking along a path; they cannot let go of their single staff for even a single step.
They must grasp it tightly and rely upon it, following it step by step. One day, if the eye of insight suddenly opens, one will realize one’s former errors.
One then casts away the staff and lets go of both hands; the ten directions are vast and open, moving freely in all eight directions, with no fixed east, west, south, or north.
It is not so. Only upon reaching this point does one attain true mastery. How many people nowadays are able to cast aside their staffs and let go of their hands?
Formerly, when Master Zhenjing’s newly compiled *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings) was being circulated, my late Master was serving as the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) in the hall at Wuzu.
One day, while on the corridor, Wuzu saw a monk holding a volume of text. Wuzu...
He asked, "What text is that in your hand? The monk replied, "It is the recorded sayings of Master Zhenjing.
The Patriarch then took it and read it, whereupon he praised it, saying, "How shameful! That in the final age there should be such a venerable elder. He then called for the Head Seat.
At that time, the old master [Zhenjing] was washing his socks in the back room; hearing the call, he hurried out in great haste. The Patriarch said, "I have attained [the Dharma]."
The text of this one volume is inconceivable; it is what is called "skillfully expounding the essential Dharma. You should try to see it for yourself: "Rest! Cease!
In a single thought, ten thousand years pass; the past and future limits are severed.
How many people nowadays have reached such a state? Yet they call it a "supremely wondrous realm. Formerly, there was a man named Guǎngdào at Bǎofēng; he was indeed—
Such people have an entire being that pays no heed to anything; they do not perceive any worldly affairs at all.
The dust and toil of the world cannot obscure them. Even so, they are nonetheless hindered by this sublime and wondrous state from seeing the Way-eye.

You must know that when one reaches the point where not a single thought arises and the boundaries of past and future are severed, it is precisely at such times that one requires a venerable master—just like Shuilao.
While gathering rattan, the Master asked Mazu, “What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
Mazu said, “Come closer and I will tell you. As Shuilao approached, Mazu gave him a kick straight in the chest, knocking him down.
Suddenly, Shuilao attained great enlightenment; he rose up unawares and laughed heartily. Mazu asked, “What have you seen?”
Liaozhi said, "The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates and their immeasurable, wondrous meanings can all be recognized as to their very source upon a single hair-tip.
In this teaching, it is called 'entering the stream while losing the object. Once that which is entered is stilled, the two characteristics of motion and stillness clearly do not arise.
As soon as one finds such a point of entry, fixed characteristics are lost; once fixed characteristics are lost—"
Falling neither into the conditioned nor into the unconditioned, the two characteristics of motion and stillness are clearly seen as non-arising;
this is precisely the gateway through which Avalokiteśvara enters the principle. Having attained awakening, he opened his own treasury and brought forth his family treasures, saying:
"The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates and their immeasurable wondrous meanings are all recognized within the tip of a single hair."
He departed, laughing loudly again and again. Mazu knew that he had already reached this stage;
he paid him no further mind and offered no subsequent words. Later, when he resided at Shuilao Hermitage, hundreds of monastics came to study with him.
As soon as he began to teach, he would flaunt that single kick, saying: "Ever since I took that one kick from Master Ma, straight..."
Even now, he laughs without ceasing. But when did he ever have peaks where the crags are layered with emerald green and mountain streams flow with murmuring clarity?
When did the willows along the banks hold mist or the flowers in the courtyard smile at the sun? When did the orioles sing in the lofty trees or the butterflies dance among the fragrant thickets?
What kind of talk is this? He simply says: "Ever since I took that one blow from Master Ma, I have laughed without ceasing until this very day. This is precisely what it means.
This is the very model of one who has "entered the stream and lost the object," wherein the two marks of movement and stillness are clearly seen as not arising.
Furthermore, it is like when Yunmen asked Dongshan, "Where have you recently come from? Dongshan said, "From Chadu. Yunmen said, "Where did you spend the summer?
Dongshan said, "At Baoci in Hunan. Yunmen said, "When did you leave there? Dongshan said, "On the twenty-fifth of the eighth month. Yunmen said—
"I grant you three blows of the staff. The ancients were simple and honest, responding according to the facts; he himself said, "This time I have truly come from Chadu.
What fault is there that you say, 'I grant you three blows of the staff'? A man of great character must settle this matter with this old fellow before it is finished.
On the following day, he went and asked him, saying, "Yesterday I received the Master’s grace in being granted—"
"Three blows of the staff—where exactly does the fault lie? The Gatekeeper said, "You rice-bag! You go off to Jiangxi and Hunan acting just like this.
At these words, Dongshan suddenly attained great enlightenment; there was no longer any message to be conveyed, nor any principle to be brought forth, and he could do nothing but prostrate himself.
Having thus awakened, he opened the treasury of his own being and drew forth from it.
Regarding his own family treasure, he said: "In the future, I shall dwell in a thatched hut in a place where no human smoke rises.

I will not store a single grain of rice nor plant a single stalk of vegetable. I will receive those coming and going from the ten directions, and for all of them, I will drive out the nails and pull out the wedges;
I will strip off their greasy hats and cast off their foul-smelling cloth robes, teaching them to become free and easy."
"Is a patch-robed monk not indeed brilliant? Yunmen said, "Your body is as large as a coconut, yet you have opened such a wide mouth.
This is the appearance of the second type of person who has entered the stream and lost all objects of perception, wherein both the signs of movement and stillness are clearly seen as non-arising.
Furthermore, National Teacher Yan of Gushan stayed at Xuefeng for many years; one day, Xuefeng knew that his karmic conditions were ripe.
Suddenly, [Zhao] Feng rose and grabbed him, saying, "What is this? Yan was instantly enlightened; he did nothing but raise his hand and wave it back and forth.
Feng said, "Are you applying intellectual reasoning? Yan replied, "What reasoning could there be?

Later, Yang Dain included this in the *Transmission of the Lamp* (*Chuan Deng Lu*), calling it "losing the mind of realization. This is the third instance of "entering the stream and losing the object."
This is the manner in which the two characteristics of movement and stillness are clearly seen as non-arising. Furthermore, one day Master Guankui saw Linji.
As soon as Linji stepped down from his meditation seat and seized him, Guankui said, "Understood, understood.

This is the fourth instance of entering the stream and losing all objects of perception—the manner in which the two characteristics of movement and stillness are clearly seen as non-arising. This cannot be explained to others.

I have attained it, yet the person who transmitted it to me has not. For seventeen years I have been a monk, and though I have attained various fragments of realization, I have gained some understanding under the Yunmen lineage and some understanding under the Caodong lineage;
however, I was unable to sever the continuity of past and future. Later, while in the capital at Tianning Monastery, I saw the Old Monk ascend the hall.
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the place where all Buddhas emerge? Yunmen said, "On the water above the Eastern Mountain.
If it were Tianning, it would not be so. What is the place where all Buddhas emerge? A fragrant breeze comes from the south.
"A slight coolness arises in the halls and pavilions. At that moment, the past and future suddenly severed;
it was like taking a tangled skein of thread and cutting it all at once with a knife. At that time, my whole body broke into a sweat.
Although the movement of mental phenomena did not arise, I remained sitting in a state of pure nakedness. One day, I entered the room [of the master], and the old monk said, "This is no easy matter."
You have reached this state; it is a pity that you have died and cannot yet live. To have no doubt regarding words and phrases is a great illness. Have you not heard it said:
"Letting go at the edge of a precipice, one spontaneously accepts the responsibility"? Only after death can one revive; such a thing cannot deceive the world.
You must believe that there is this principle. This old man says of himself: "I rely solely upon my present realization."
This was joyful; I could no longer make sense of it. The Old Monk, however, assigned me to the Zemo Liao as an attendant for miscellaneous duties.
Every day, together with the Master, I had to enter the room three or four times.

He would simply raise the koan, "The phrase that has it and the phrase that does not, like a vine leaning against a tree," and as soon as I opened my mouth, he would say, "Not so. This continued for half a year.

In the interim, I simply continued my investigation. One day, while sitting with various officials in the abbot’s quarters for the medicinal meal, I held my chopsticks in my hand and completely forgot to eat.
The Old Monk said, "This fellow has attained 'yellow-amber wood Zen' (a Zen that shrinks back) and has instead retreated.
I then offered him a metaphor, saying, "Monk, this principle is just like a dog watching..."
It is like a cauldron of boiling oil: if you wish to lick it, you cannot; if you wish to abandon it, you cannot.
The Old Monk said, "Your analogy is excellent. This very thing is the Diamond Circle and the Thorny Jujube.
One day, he asked the Old Monk, "I have heard that when you were at Wuzu’s, you once asked about this same matter. The Old Monk replied, "Not so."

[The old man] asked, "Do you know how the Fifth Patriarch, the Venerable Master, answered? The Master was unwilling to speak. The old man said, 'The Master could not have questioned you alone at that time;
he must have questioned you before the great assembly. What harm is there in speaking of it now? The old master then said, 'I asked:

"What is the meaning of 'having a phrase and yet no phrase, like a vine leaning against a tree'? The Patriarch replied: "It can be painted, but it cannot be drawn."'"* *Note: This passage refers to a famous encounter between Mazu Daoyi (the "old master") and his teacher Baizhang Huaihai (the "Fifth Patriarch"). The dialogue concerns the nature of ultimate reality, which is beyond conceptualization yet expressible through metaphor.*
"It is not accomplished; it is like drawing a picture, yet the picture cannot be completed. He asked again, "What is it like when the tree falls and the vines wither?

Regarding your field: formerly there was only one Elder Jing who was your equal; he has simply passed away.

After some time had elapsed, you were appointed to conduct the ceremony for the installation of a monk. Later, while serving as the Head Seat at Yunju, you would frequently enter the room with your brothers during the night.

how would you deal with him? The old man replied, "How fortunate I am! It is just as Su Dongpo said:

"Pressed by me, you have been driven to the wall," the old monk laughed heartily.
Reflecting upon this old monk, even if one were to grind one's bones to powder, one could never repay his kindness.

Because I heard the Elder’s remark regarding how a man from Fuzhou eating lychees had a moment of sudden awakening, I have come to speak of this matter. This brother has been among the monastic communities.
Walking according to the compass and stepping according to the square, he was free from the faults of the patch-robed monks; yet, it is a pity that his "measuring foot" was too short.
However, were he to perform a somersault and emerge, one would certainly be unable to deceive him. I shall cite an ancient saying for the sake of the great assembly.
As it is said in the Teachings: "When I do not see, how can you see the place where I do not see? If you see this 'not seeing,' then naturally it is not that [other] thing."
The characteristic of seeing: if you do not see the ground of my non-seeing, it is naturally not a thing;
how could it not be you? Later, Master Zhantang offered this verse: "The Old Barbarian’s thoroughgoing grandmotherly heart / For Ānanda, his intention grew even deeper.
